story.title: Rosa and Isla and the Wall-Climbing Club
story.subtitle: A sticky, scratchy, slimy tour of animals who never fall down

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Ladybird
chapters.text:
Rosa lined up her toy ladybirds in a neat red row on the carpet.

Isla hung by her fingertips from the bookshelf, practicing her best climbing grip.

Then a real ladybird landed on the window and started to glow. Her spots blinked red, then gold, then red again. CLICK. CLICK. CLICK.

"Hello," said a tiny voice. "I'm Dot. Want to see how animals climb walls?"

Rosa gasped so hard she dropped a ladybird toy. Isla let go of the bookshelf and landed with a grin.

Dot tapped her wings, and the whole room seemed to grow — or maybe the girls shrank. Either way, they zoomed out the window, tiny as beetles, riding on Dot's back.

WHOOSH! They landed on a big window across the yard. A fat, friendly lizard sat upside down on the glass, waving one foot.

"That's a Tokay gecko," said Dot. "Say hi, Gordon."

"Hiya!" said Gordon, not falling off at all, even upside down.

Isla stared at his feet. "How does he stick to glass? Glass is so smooth!"

"Millions of tiny hairs," said Dot. "So small, you'd need a special magnifier to see even one. They grip the glass like a thousand tiny fingers."

Rosa reached up and pressed her own hand flat on the window. "Like my ladybird's feet stick to leaves!"

"Exactly like that," said Dot.

Gordon peeled one toe off the glass, slow and careful, like pulling up a sticker. Then another toe. Then he was free.

"No glue, no mess," said Gordon. "Just peel, and go!"

Isla tried it on the window glass too — press, press, peel! "It doesn't leave any sticky marks at all!" she laughed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Buzzing Sticky Feet
chapters.text:
BZZZZ! A fat fly landed on a flower pot wall, right above their heads.

Dot shrank them down even smaller, so the fly looked as big as a bus.

Isla peeked under its feet. "There's tiny shiny drops under there!"

"That's its secret," said Dot. "Flies and some beetles have little pads that ooze a sticky drop, like a tiny dot of glue, every time they step."

Rosa giggled. "Like honey on my toast!"

"Sort of," laughed Dot, "only this honey never gets on your fingers."

A round shiny beetle climbed up next to the fly, using the very same trick, drop by careful drop.

Isla watched closely, counting under her breath. "So that's two drops holding on, every single step?"

"Every step," said Dot. "Drop, stick, drop, stick, all the way up the wall."

The fly buzzed off, feet clean and ready for the very next wall.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Spider on the Glass Door
chapters.text:
A big spider sat perfectly still on a shiny glass door, not moving one bit.

"Spiders can climb glass too," said Dot. "Look close, Isla."

Isla leaned near the glass, careful not to touch the spider at all. "Its feet look fuzzy!"

"Thousands of teeny hairs," said Dot, "just like Gordon's, only spider-sized."

Rosa counted on her fingers. "One, two... eight sticky feet!"

"Eight indeed," said Dot. "So even if one foot slips, seven more are holding tight."

The spider scuttled sideways, up and over the glass, quick as a wink, never once wobbling.

Isla grinned. "No wonder spiders never fall off windows."

Rosa waved both hands at the spider as it vanished round the corner.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Claws or Sticky Feet?
chapters.text:
On the garden wall, a long line of ants marched straight up the rough bricks.

"Easy," said Dot. "Ants use tiny claws for bumpy walls like this one."

Then a cockroach scuttled onto a smooth tile nearby, and Isla leaned in close. "Wait, it's not using claws now, is it?"

"Sharp eyes," said Dot. "On smooth walls, ants and cockroaches switch to sticky pads instead."

Rosa clapped both hands. "Claws for bumpy, sticky for smooth!"

"That's the whole trick," said Dot, "like choosing the right shoes for the right ground."

Isla scratched her own climbing shoe on the rough brick, then pressed it flat on the smooth tile. "I get it now — different grips for different walls!"

Rosa tried the same thing with her little sneaker, giggling the whole time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Goats on the Cliff
chapters.text:
WHOOSH! Dot flew them high above a rocky mountain, where a goat stood on a thin, steep ledge.

Rosa's eyes went wide. "Isn't that too high? Won't he fall down?"

"Not this goat," said Dot gently. "Mountain goats never slip. Watch his feet."

Isla studied the goat's hooves. "They've got a hard edge... and something soft underneath?"

"Exactly right," said Dot. "The hard rim grips the rock, and the soft middle part squishes to fit every little bump."

The goat hopped from rock to rock, calm as could be, and Rosa let out a big breath. "Phew! He's fine!"

"Goats are some of the very best wall-climbers on the whole mountain," said Dot.

Rosa gave the goat a cheer so loud it echoed off the cliff.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Squirrel's Secret Claws
chapters.text:
SCRITCH SCRATCH! A squirrel zipped straight up a tree trunk outside their window.

"How does he grip wood that fast?" asked Isla.

"Sharp curved claws," said Dot. "They dig into tiny cracks you can't even see."

Rosa squinted hard at the bark. "I don't see any cracks at all!"

"That's because they're too small for our eyes," said Dot, "but not too small for squirrel claws."

Isla watched the squirrel leap onto a brick wall and scramble straight up that too. "He climbs walls the very same way!"

"Same claws, same trick," said Dot. "Bark or brick, it hardly matters to him."

The squirrel paused at the top, tail flicking, almost like he was taking a bow.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Frog on the Wet Leaf
chapters.text:
PLIP! Rain began to fall, and a small green tree frog hopped onto a wet leaf wall.

"Won't he slide right off?" asked Isla. "That leaf looks so slippery!"

"Watch his toes," said Dot. The frog's toes were flat and round, pressed wide against the shiny leaf.

"They're sticky, even in the rain," said Dot, "perfect for wet leaves, and perfect for wet glass too."

Rosa pressed her own fingers flat together. "Flat sticky toes, like little stickers!"

"Just like that," said Dot, smiling at her.

The frog hopped higher and higher, never sliding, never slipping, all the way to the top of the leaf.

Isla laughed. "He's basically got built-in climbing shoes."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Slow and Slippery Snail
chapters.text:
On the garden wall, a little snail inched upward, leaving a shiny trail behind it.

"That's slime," said Dot. "Snails glide along it, up and over the smoothest walls."

Isla tilted her head. "So the slime is like... his path?"

"And his grip," said Dot. "His whole foot ripples in little waves, pushing him along the slime."

Rosa giggled. "Slow and slimy, but it works!"

"Every single time," said Dot. "Slow is just fine, when you never, ever fall off."

The snail reached the top of the wall at last and tucked himself into his shell for a rest.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
Dot flew them home, right through the window, right back to Rosa's carpet.

"One more thing," said Dot. "People who study how animals climb are called scientists — folks who figure out how things work."

Isla's eyes lit up. "Like Kellar Autumn? He figured out the gecko's sticky trick!"

"That's him," said Dot. "And climbers like you use his ideas to make better climbing shoes and sticky gloves."

Isla looked down at her own climbing shoes and grinned. "Gecko power, right here on my feet."

Rosa yawned a great big yawn and lined her ladybird toys back up in a neat little row.

One small ladybird toy had a tiny new spot on its back, glowing soft and warm, just like Dot.

"Spotty but mighty," whispered Dot, folding in her wings. "Until next time, you two."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Rosa. Goodnight, Isla. Spotty but mighty — sleep tight, little climbers.

true_facts.text: Gordon the gecko climbs glass walls because his toes have millions of **tiny hairs**, so small you'd need a magnifier to see one.
A gecko's sticky grip isn't glue — he can **peel his toes off one at a time**, like pulling up a sticker.
Flies and beetles climb walls by **oozing tiny sticky drops** from the pads on their feet, step by step.
Spiders climb glass because each of their **eight feet** is covered in thousands of **tiny hairs**.
Ants and cockroaches use **sharp little claws** on bumpy walls, and switch to **sticky pads** on smooth ones.
Mountain goats never slip because their hooves have a **hard outer edge** and a **soft squishy middle**.
Squirrels climb using **sharp curved claws** that dig into tiny cracks too small for us to see.
Tree frogs have **flat sticky toes** that grip even wet, slippery leaves.
Snails climb smooth walls by gliding along a trail of **shiny slime**.
Real scientists study gecko feet to invent better **climbing shoes and sticky gloves** for people.

story.title: Finn, Nell, and Clover the Bee
story.subtitle: A sweet nighttime visit to the hive

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Jar
chapters.text:
Finn licked the last bit of honey off his toast.

Nell sniffed the honey jar. "It smells like sunshine," she said.

It was almost bedtime. One tiny drop of honey sat on Finn's plate.

The drop began to glow. It glowed gold, like a tiny sun.

Finn poked it with his finger. "Nell, look!"

POP! A tiny bee buzzed up out of the glow.

"Hello!" said the bee. "I'm Clover. Want to see where honey comes from?"

Nell clapped her hands. "Yes! Yes!"

Clover waved one tiny wing. The bedroom spun gold and soft.

When it stopped, Finn and Nell were small. Tiny as bees.

They stood in a field full of yellow flowers.

"Whoa," said Finn.

"My favorite color," Nell whispered. "Yellow, yellow, everywhere."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Nectar Straw
chapters.text:
A fat, fuzzy bee landed on a flower next to Nell.

SLLLURP! It drank deep from the flower's cup.

"What is it drinking?" asked Nell.

"Flower juice," said Clover. "We call it nectar. It's sweet, like juice."

Finn leaned in close. "It has a little straw!"

"That's right," said Clover. "Bees have a long tongue, just like a straw, for sipping up nectar."

Nell giggled. "Like my juice box straw!"

"Just like that," said Clover.

The bee's tummy began to look round and full.

"That nectar goes into a special tummy," said Clover. "A honey tummy, just for carrying nectar home. Bees even have two tummies — one for food, one for honey."

Finn's eyes went wide. "Two tummies? I only have one!"

Nell patted her own tummy. "One is plenty for me."

Clover laughed, a little buzzy laugh. "Follow that bee! She's heading home now."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Wiggly Dance
chapters.text:
Back at the hive, the bee began to wiggle.

She wiggled left. She wiggled right. She waggled her whole body.

"Is she stuck?" asked Finn.

Clover shook her head, smiling. "That's a dance! It tells the other bees where the flowers are."

"A dance can talk?" Nell asked.

"It can," said Clover. "Scout bees find the best flowers. Then they dance to show everyone the way."

Finn tried it. He wiggled his hips. He waggled his arms.

"Am I telling them where the kitchen is?" he asked.

Nell laughed so hard she flopped over in the grass.

Three bees watched Finn's wiggle. They buzzed off, straight toward a patch of yellow flowers by a fence.

"It worked!" Finn shouted.

"IT WORKED!" he shouted again, even louder.

Clover clapped two tiny legs together. "Not bad, for a bee with no wings."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Bee Kisses
chapters.text:
Inside the hive, it buzzed busy, like a kitchen before dinner.

A tired forager bee landed. She touched mouths with another bee.

"Ew!" said Nell. "A bee kiss!"

"That's how they share," said Clover. "The nectar passes mouth to mouth, bee to bee."

Finn frowned. "Isn't that a little yucky?"

"It's how honey gets started," said Clover. "Every bee who passes it helps make it sweeter."

Nell thought for a moment. "Like sharing a lollipop with your sister?"

"Just like that," laughed Clover. "A very long lollipop, passed around and around."

Finn watched one drop of nectar go from bee, to bee, to bee.

"It's a nectar train!" he said.

"CHOO CHOO!" yelled Nell, chugging her arms like train wheels.

Clover buzzed with laughter. "Buzz well, you two. Buzz well."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Six Little Sides
chapters.text:
They reached a wall covered in tiny rooms.

Each little room had straight sides, all neat and tidy.

"Count them with me," said Clover.

Finn counted on his fingers. "One, two, three, four, five, six!"

"Six sides," said Clover. "Every honey room has six sides, like a little stop sign."

Nell traced one with her finger. "So smooth."

"Bees make the wax for these rooms with their own bodies," said Clover. "Right out of their own tummies, like magic."

Finn gasped. "Wax from a tummy?"

"Bee magic," said Clover, grinning.

Nell pointed to a room filled with gold. "This one has honey in it already!"

"Good eye," said Clover. "That nectar went into this little room to turn into honey."

Finn peeked into an empty one. "Can I live in a six-sided room?"

"Only if you grow wings," laughed Clover.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Great Wing Wind
chapters.text:
A whole row of bees lined up beside the honey rooms.

They flapped their wings. Fast. Faster. FASTEST.

WHOOOOSH! A warm little breeze blew through the hive.

"Why are they flapping so hard?" asked Nell.

"They're drying the nectar," said Clover. "Flapping blows away the extra water. That turns watery nectar into thick, sticky honey."

Nell flapped her own arms. "I'm helping too!"

"Me too!" Finn flapped beside her, fast as he could.

WHOOOOSH! Their hair blew straight back.

Clover laughed so hard she nearly tumbled off her flower. "You two flap faster than some bees!"

Finn sniffed the air. "It smells like toast already."

"Honey smells like that," said Clover. "Sweet and warm."

Nell grinned and gave one more giant flap, just for good measure.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Little Wax Lid
chapters.text:
A bee patted something soft over a full honey room.

Pat, pat, pat. It looked like a tiny lid.

"What's that?" asked Finn.

"A wax cap," said Clover. "It seals the honey inside, keeping it clean and safe."

Finn patted the air, copying her. "Like closing a lunchbox!"

"Exactly like that," said Clover.

Nell looked around at all the capped rooms, rows and rows of gold.

"Why do they make so much?" she asked.

"For winter," said Clover. "When snow covers the flowers, bees can't go out to drink nectar. So they eat the honey they saved up."

Nell nodded slowly. "Like keeping cookies for later."

"Just like that," said Clover, smiling.

Finn tapped a capped cell gently. "Saved for later. Smart bees."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Queen's Big Family
chapters.text:
In the middle of the hive sat one very big bee.

Bees buzzed all around her, patting her gently with their legs.

"That's the queen," said Clover. "She's the busy mom of almost every bee here."

"Every single one?" Nell gasped.

"She lays eggs," said Clover. "Sometimes more than a thousand in one single day!"

Finn's mouth fell open. "A thousand? That's SO many."

"How many bees live here all together?" Finn asked.

"In summer, a hive can hold twenty thousand to sixty thousand bees," said Clover.

Nell tried to count them. "One, two, three... that's a lot of bees!"

"Too many to count," laughed Clover. "But every single one has a job."

The queen bee looked at Finn and Nell and gave a tiny wing-wave.

Nell waved back. "Goodnight, Queen Bee."

Clover's wings glowed gold. "Time to go home, little bees."

The field spun gold again, soft and warm, and then they landed back in their own beds.

On the nightstand sat the honey jar, lid shut tight.

Beside it lay one tiny yellow petal, soft as a whisper.

Nell picked it up and smiled. "A flower, just for me."

Finn looked at his toast plate. Only crumbs left now.

"Thank you for the honey," Finn whispered to all the far-away bees.

Clover's glow faded to a tiny gold spark, then winked out.

"Buzz well," her voice whispered, soft as a hum.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Finn. Goodnight, Nell. Buzz well.

true_facts.text: Bees slurp up sweet flower juice called **nectar** using a long tongue, just like a straw.
Nectar goes into a **second tummy** inside the bee, just for carrying it home.
Scout bees do a **wiggly dance** to show the other bees where the best flowers are.
Bees pass nectar from **mouth to mouth**, like sharing a very long lollipop.
Every little honeycomb room has **six sides**, neat as a stop sign.
Bees make the **wax** for their rooms right out of their own bodies.
Bees **flap their wings** super fast to blow away the water and turn nectar into sticky honey.
A tiny **wax lid** gets patted over each full honey room to keep it clean and safe.
Bees save up honey to eat all **winter**, when there are no flowers to drink from.
The **queen bee** can lay more than **a thousand eggs** in just one day.
In summer, one bee hive can hold **twenty thousand to sixty thousand bees**.

story.title: Omar and the Glowing Bike Chain
story.subtitle: A midnight ride through two hundred years of bicycles

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Running Machine
chapters.text:
Omar practiced his favorite BMX trick in the backyard, a wheelie down the ramp. A flashlight sat on the cooler. It was way past bedtime, but the trick needed one more try.

His bike's chain started to glow, silver and green, like it had swallowed a firefly. Omar froze. "Chains don't do that," he whispered.

The chain unspooled off the frame and stretched into a shining road of light. Omar grabbed his handlebars and rolled onto the glow.

WHOOSH! The yard melted away. Omar landed in a grassy field in Germany, back in **1817**. A man in a tall hat sat on a strange wooden two-wheeler with no pedals at all.

"Karl von Drais," the man said, tipping his hat. "Care to try my running machine?"

Omar stared at the wheels. "Wait — no pedals? How do you even go?"

"You push with your feet," Karl said, "like running, but sitting down."

Omar hopped on and pushed off, legs pumping fast. It wobbled, but it rolled. "This is basically a scooter with handlebars!" he laughed.

The glowing chain wrapped around his wrist like a bracelet, ready to pull him somewhere new.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Boneshaker
chapters.text:
The chain tugged, and WHOOSH, Omar landed on a bumpy cobblestone street in France. A man was bolting metal pedals straight onto the front wheel of a bike.

"Pierre Michaux," he said. "Pedals go right on the front wheel now. We call it the velocipede."

Omar climbed on and rode it over the bumpy stones. His teeth rattled the whole way. "This should be called the BONESHAKER," Omar said, "because it's shaking my bones!"

Pierre laughed so hard he nearly fell over. "Good name. That's exactly what everyone is already calling it."

Omar rubbed his sore arms. "You need something squishy on those wheels," he said. "Something that soaks up the bumps."

Pierre scratched his head. "Someday, somebody will think of that."

Omar grinned, already wondering who.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Giant Wheel
chapters.text:
Next stop: a street in the **1870s**, with a wheel taller than Omar's dad. A rider wobbled way up high.

"The penny-farthing," the rider called down. "Big wheel up front, named after two old coins — a big penny and a tiny farthing."

Omar squinted up. "One pedal turn and you go way farther with a wheel that big?"

"That's the whole idea," the rider said. "But sit this high, and a sudden stop can send you flying over the handlebars. We call that 'taking a header.'"

Just then the rider hit a bump and started to tip. Omar's BMX instincts kicked in. "Lean back! Don't grab the brake!" he shouted.

The rider leaned back hard and straightened right out, safe and still way up high. "Thanks, kid!" he called, pedaling off.

Omar laughed with relief. "Tallest bike I've ever seen, for sure."
chapters.shout_line: LEAN BACK! DON'T GRAB THE BRAKE!

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Safety Bicycle
chapters.text:
The glow chain pulled Omar to England, **1885**. A man named John Kemp Starley stood beside a bike with two wheels the same size, joined to the back wheel by a chain.

Omar grinned. "That's basically my BMX bike!"

"I call it the safety bicycle," John said. "Same-size wheels, chain driving the back one. No more giant wheel, no more headers."

Omar hopped on and pedaled a smooth circle around the yard. "This feels so much better!"

"People everywhere will want one," John said. "This shape will become the one bikes are built like, forever after."

Omar lifted his glowing wrist-chain. "My bike has a chain too, see?"

John Kemp Starley's eyes went wide. "Looks like yours already learned a thing or two from mine."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Squishy Air Tires
chapters.text:
Next, a workshop in Scotland, **1888**. A man named John Boyd Dunlop knelt beside a tricycle, wrapping a rubber tube around its wheel.

"My son's tricycle rides too rough on solid rubber wheels," John said. "So I filled a rubber tube with air instead."

Omar poked the tire with his thumb. It squished and bounced back. "Like my BMX tires! Bouncy air inside!"

"Exactly," John said. "Air soaks up every bump in the road."

Omar remembered the boneshaker from before. "This is what that guy in France needed!" he said. "Squishy wheels, just like you said!"

John Boyd Dunlop smiled. "Good thing word travels fast. Soon every bike in the world will roll on air."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Golden Age
chapters.text:
WHOOSH, and Omar stood on a busy street in the **1890s**, with more bikes rolling by than he had ever seen in one place.

A woman pedaled past confidently, wearing baggy trousers instead of a long skirt.

"These are called bloomers," she called to Omar. "Long skirts get caught in bike chains and wheels, so we made something safer to wear instead."

Omar nodded. "Smart. Function over fashion."

"Bikes gave women a way to go wherever we want, whenever we want," she said. "A famous American named Susan B. Anthony even said riding a bike set women free more than almost anything else in the world."

Omar watched her roll off down the street. "Cool," he said. "A bike that changes more than just how fast you go."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Bike Shop That Learned to Fly
chapters.text:
The chain dropped Omar into a bike shop in Dayton, Ohio, in the **1890s**. Two brothers, Wilbur and Orville Wright, were fixing a customer's wheel.

"We fix bikes here," Wilbur said, "but we tinker with other ideas too."

Omar noticed thin metal tubes and spoked wheels stacked on a shelf. "Those look like airplane parts," he said.

Orville grinned. "Good eye. Light metal tubes and spoked wheels work great on bikes. Turns out they work great on flying machines too."

"You're going to build an airplane?" Omar asked, eyes wide.

"In **1903**," Orville said, "we plan to."

Omar laughed. "From bike shop to the sky. That's wild."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Ramp
chapters.text:
The chain glowed one more time, and WHOOSH, Omar landed on dirt hills in California, the **1970s**. Kids like him raced small, sturdy bikes down bumpy trails, popping jumps off the dirt.

"BMX bikes," one rider said, skidding to a stop. "Built tough, like motocross motorcycles, but for us kids."

Nearby, other riders bolted wide, bumpy tires onto their bikes for rough trails. "Mountain bikes," someone said. "Perfect for riding down hills like these."

Omar laughed. "I knew my BMX bike had an awesome family tree!"

The glow chain tugged one last time. WHOOSH! Omar landed back in his own backyard, flashlight still sitting on the cooler.

His bike chain looked like plain metal again, just a little sparkle left in the moonlight. Omar grinned. "Over a billion bikes in the whole world now," he whispered, "and mine's got the best story of all."

He wheeled his bike into the garage, yawning big.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Omar. Pedal on.

true_facts.text: In **1817**, a German inventor named Karl von Drais built a wooden two-wheeler with no pedals — riders pushed it along with their feet.
Karl's invention was called the running machine and steered with handlebars, just like bikes today.
In the **1870s**, people rode the penny-farthing, with a giant front wheel taller than a grown-up and a tiny back wheel.
The penny-farthing got its funny name from two old coins — a big penny and a tiny farthing.
Riding so high up was risky — a sudden stop could send a rider flying over the handlebars, called 'taking a header.'
In **1885**, John Kemp Starley invented the safety bicycle, with two same-size wheels and a chain driving the back wheel.
The safety bicycle was much easier to balance than the penny-farthing, so it became the bike everyone wanted.
In **1888**, John Boyd Dunlop invented air-filled rubber tires, making rides much smoother than hard rubber wheels.
In the **1890s**, bikes gave women new freedom, and Susan B. Anthony said riding a bike helped set women free more than almost anything else.
Because long skirts were dangerous near bike wheels and chains, riders started wearing looser pants called bloomers instead.
Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio in the **1890s**, before they built the first successful airplane.
The Wright brothers used bike-building tricks, like light metal tubes and spoked wheels, to help build their flying machine.
Today there are more than a billion bicycles in the world — more than any other kind of vehicle.

story.title: Ada and the Magnet Robot
story.subtitle: A bedtime trip through pulling, pushing, and the giant magnet called Earth.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Fridge
chapters.text:
Ada lined up her fridge magnets into a wobbly robot shape on the kitchen fridge. She always built robots out of her favorite magnets before bed.

Tonight, one magnet buzzed under her finger. It felt warm, like a little heartbeat.

"Hello?" Ada whispered.

The magnet robot wiggled. Two tiny eyes blinked open. "Hello, Ada," it said in a clicky voice. "I'm Bolt. Want to see how I work?"

Ada grinned so big her cheeks hurt. "Yes!"

Bolt hummed, and the fridge door swirled like silver water. Ada stepped through — and landed somewhere humming with invisible pulls.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Push, Pull, Click!
chapters.text:
Two big magnets floated in front of Ada, sliding closer, then jumping apart.

"Why won't they touch?" Ada asked.

Bolt landed on one end. "Every magnet has two ends," he said. "We call them **poles** — a **north** end and a **south** end."

Ada poked the floating magnets. When she turned one around, it snapped straight to the other with a loud **CLICK!**

"Opposite poles **pull together**," Bolt said. "But two of the same kind **push apart**."

Ada flipped the magnet back and forth, giggling as it clicked and bounced, clicked and bounced.

"It's like a dance," she said. "A pulling, pushing dance!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Tiny Spinning Dancers
chapters.text:
Bolt pressed a button on his chest, and everything got tiny. Ada found herself standing inside a piece of metal.

Little dots spun everywhere, each one humming like a top.

"Those are **electrons**," Bolt said. "Tiny spinning bits inside every atom. When they spin the same way, they act like their own little magnets."

Ada watched clumps of electrons line up in neat rows, like kids holding hands.

"When lots of them point the same way," Bolt said, "the whole piece of metal becomes magnetic. We call each lined-up group a **domain**."

But in a wooden block nearby, the little dots pointed every which way, messy as scribbles.

"That's why wood isn't magnetic," Ada said. "Nobody's lining up!"

"Exactly," said Bolt, spinning with pride.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Invisible Hug
chapters.text:
Back at full size, Bolt set a magnet on the table. A paperclip zoomed across and stuck, even though nothing touched it.

"What's pulling it?" Ada asked.

"An invisible **magnetic field**," Bolt said. "It's the stretchy space around a magnet where its push and pull work."

"Can I see it?" Ada asked.

Bolt sprinkled tiny iron bits — like silver sugar — around the magnet. They curved into loops, swooping from one end to the other.

"Whoa," Ada breathed. "It's like the magnet is drawing itself!"

"That's the shape of its field," Bolt said, "from the north pole, curling all the way to the south."

Ada traced the loops with her finger, careful not to touch the magnet.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Rock That Pointed
chapters.text:
Bolt's fridge-door swirl opened onto a rocky hillside, long, long ago.

A traveler held up a strange black rock. It kept sticking to his iron knife.

"That's **lodestone**," Bolt said. "A rock from the ground that's already magnetic. People near a place called **Magnesia** found it first."

"Is that where the word magnet comes from?" Ada asked.

"Good guess," Bolt said. "Most people think so."

Later, Bolt showed her travelers floating a lodestone on a leaf in water. It turned, slow and steady, until it pointed the same direction every time.

"That's an early **compass**," Bolt said. "People used it to find their way, over two thousand years ago."

Ada spun the leaf herself, giggling as it swung back to the same spot, again and again.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Giant Magnet Called Earth
chapters.text:
Bolt zoomed them high into the sky. Below them, the whole Earth hung like a blue marble.

"Guess what," Bolt said. "This whole planet is a magnet too."

Ada's eyes went wide. "The whole Earth?"

"Deep, deep inside," Bolt said, "melted iron swirls around and around. That swirling makes Earth act like one giant bar magnet."

Bolt handed her a tiny compass. Its needle spun, wobbled, then settled, pointing the same way no matter how Ada turned around.

"The needle's north end gets pulled toward Earth's magnetic north," Bolt said.

Ada spun in a circle three times. The needle didn't budge. "It always knows the way!"

"That's how sailors never got lost," Bolt said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Magnet You Can Switch Off
chapters.text:
Bolt led Ada to a junkyard where a giant crane swung overhead.

CLUNK! It lifted a rusty old car straight off the ground, no hooks, no ropes.

Ada gasped. "How is it just staying up there?"

"That crane has an **electromagnet**," Bolt said. "Wrap wire in a coil, zap it with electricity, and it turns into a magnet — one you can switch on and off."

The crane operator flipped a switch. CLUNK! The car dropped gently onto a pile.

"On for pulling, off for letting go," Bolt said.

Then Bolt handed Ada a bar magnet and a tiny saw. "Cut it in half. Go on."

Ada did. Both halves instantly had their own north and south ends.

"Two whole magnets," Ada laughed, "out of one!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Trains That Float, Birds That Know the Way
chapters.text:
Next, Bolt showed Ada a sleek train gliding with no wheels touching the track.

"It's floating!" Ada shouted.

"Strong magnets push the whole train up," Bolt said. "Without rubbing on the rails, it can zoom super fast. We call that a **maglev** train."

Ada touched a gold ring and a penny nearby. Neither one stuck to her magnet.

"Gold and copper don't stick," Bolt said. "Only some metals, like iron, really answer a magnet's pull."

High above, a line of birds flew past in a V shape.

"Some birds, turtles, and fish," Bolt said, "can feel Earth's magnetic field too. It helps them find their way on long trips."

Ada waved at the birds. "Safe travels!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back to the Fridge
chapters.text:
The silver swirl opened once more, and Ada stepped back into her kitchen.

Bolt shrank down onto the fridge, settling among the other magnets.

"One last thing," Bolt said. "Fridge magnets like me are made from bendy rubber mixed with magnet powder. That's why I can bend without falling off."

Ada pressed Bolt flat, then let him spring back, round and happy.

She lined her magnets into a smiling robot face, right where she'd started.

"Goodnight, Bolt," she whispered.

Bolt's eyes blinked slow, like a sleepy wink. "Goodnight, Ada. Pull in close, and dream away."

Ada climbed into bed, feeling the whole humming, clicking, pulling world tucked safely behind her, on the fridge door.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ada. Pull in close, and dream away.

true_facts.text: Every magnet has two ends called **poles** — a north one and a south one.
Opposite poles **pull together**, and two of the same kind **push apart**.
Tiny spinning bits inside metal, called **electrons**, act like their own little magnets.
When lots of those tiny spinners line up the same way, metal becomes magnetic — that lined-up group is a **domain**.
A magnet has an invisible stretchy space around it called a **magnetic field**, where its pull works.
Sprinkling tiny iron bits near a magnet shows curvy loops — the shape of its magnetic field.
A naturally magnetic rock called **lodestone** was first found near a place called Magnesia.
People long ago floated a lodestone to make an early **compass**, which always pointed the same way.
Deep inside, Earth has swirling melted iron, which makes the whole planet act like a giant magnet.
A compass needle points north because it lines up with Earth's own magnetic pull.
Wrapping wire in a coil and running electricity through it makes an **electromagnet**, which can switch on and off.
Cutting a magnet in half does not make one north piece and one south piece — both halves become whole new magnets.
Fridge magnets are made from bendy rubber mixed with magnet powder, which is why they can bend without falling off.

story.title: Priya, Dev, and the Rainbow Inside the Raindrop
story.subtitle: A squirt of water, a secret window, and all the colors hiding in the sun.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Squirt That Started It
chapters.text:
Rain had just stopped. The sun poked through the clouds, bright and nosy.

Dev loaded his water pistol with puddle water. "Watch this, Priya!"

He squeezed the trigger. Mist burst out — SPLOOSH!

Right in the spray, a tiny rainbow flickered. Red was on the outside. Purple was on the inside.

Priya gasped. "Dev, your water pistol made a rainbow!"

"The sun did that," said Dev. "I just sprayed water with the sun behind us."

The little rainbow stretched wide. It glowed so bright the whole yard turned gold and pink.

"Why is it getting bigger?" Dev whispered.

"I don't know," said Priya, "but I'm not missing this."

She grabbed his sleeve. They stepped into the glowing mist — and the backyard disappeared.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Inside the Drop
chapters.text:
They landed with a soft BOING on something squishy and clear.

"Where are we?" Dev asked, poking the curved, wobbly wall.

"Not glass," said a tiny, sparkly voice. "Water!"

A speck of light zoomed over, flickering every color at once. "I'm Fizz. Welcome to a raindrop!"

"We're INSIDE a raindrop?" said Priya.

"Watch," said Fizz. A beam of plain white sunlight shot into the drop. It bent sideways the second it touched the water.

"That bending is called **refraction**," said Fizz. "Light changes direction when it moves from air into water."

The beam bounced off the back wall like a ball off a trampoline, then bent again on its way out.

"It bounces AND bends?" said Dev. "Just like my water pistol shots off the fence!"

"Exactly like that," said Fizz, grinning.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Secret Colors Hiding in White
chapters.text:
The sunbeam that bent through the drop came out looking strange. It wasn't white anymore. It was stripes of color.

"Wait," said Priya, squinting. "Sunlight isn't white. It's colors!"

"White light was never just white," said Fizz. "It's every color, all mixed together, like paint before you squeeze it out."

The artist in Priya loved that.

"A scientist named **Isaac Newton** proved it," said Fizz. "Back in the **1660s**, he shined sunlight through a triangle of glass. All the colors spread out, just like this."

Dev squirted a little mist into the sunbeam. Tiny rainbow sparkles floated in the air.

"I'm basically Isaac Newton," he announced.

"With a water pistol," said Priya, laughing. "Sure, Dev."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Red Goes First, Violet Goes Last
chapters.text:
The color stripes lined up in careful order, like a parade.

"Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and two purples," Priya counted on her fingers.

"Indigo and violet," said Fizz. "People remember the order with a name: **Roy G. Biv**."

"Why does red always go on the outside?" asked Priya.

"Red bends the least going through water," said Fizz. "Violet bends the most. That's why violet lands on the inside edge."

Priya loved that. "It's a color recipe! Red first, violet last, every time."

Dev tried to shuffle the colors with his hands, like cards. "What if I want purple first?"

"You don't get to choose," said Fizz. "Light always lines up the same way."

"Boring," said Dev. Then he grinned. "Kind of cool, though."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Rainbow That's Actually a Circle
chapters.text:
Fizz led them out of the drop into a sky full of floating raindrops, each one catching light.

"Okay, weird question," said Dev. "Why do rainbows look like an arch, not a whole circle?"

"Because they ARE a whole circle," said Fizz. "You just can't see the bottom part. The ground is in the way."

Priya's eyes went wide. "So there's rainbow underground?"

"Not underground," laughed Fizz. "The ground just blocks your view of the lower half."

"People in airplanes sometimes see the whole circle," Fizz added, "because there's no ground below them to block it."

Dev gasped. "I want to see a circle rainbow from a plane!"

"Someday," said Priya, patting his head. "For now, let's keep floating."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Everybody's Own Rainbow
chapters.text:
A cluster of floating drops twinkled nearby. Two faint arcs appeared, one bright, one pale above it.

"Two rainbows?" said Priya.

"Sometimes light bounces twice inside a drop," said Fizz. "That makes a second, fainter rainbow, with the colors flipped."

Dev squinted. "The second one's backwards!"

"Good eye," said Fizz. "Also, no two people ever see the exact same rainbow. Yours and Priya's come from totally different raindrops, because you're standing in slightly different spots."

"Wait, so MY rainbow is mine?" said Dev. "Priya can't have it?"

"All yours," said Fizz.

"Finally," said Dev, "something Priya can't borrow."

Priya rolled her eyes. "I didn't even want your rainbow."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Moonbows, Bridges, and a Pot of Gold
chapters.text:
Fizz floated them toward a shimmering waterfall made of light.

"Rainbows aren't only in rain," said Fizz. "They show up in waterfall mist, garden hoses, even moonlight."

"Moonlight rainbows?" said Priya.

"Moonbows," said Fizz. "Usually too faint for your eyes to see color, just soft and silvery. Cameras can catch the colors hiding inside."

"People have told stories about rainbows forever," Fizz went on. "Some called it **Bifrost**, a bridge for gods to cross. Others told of a rainbow after a big flood, a sign of a kept promise."

"And some say there's a pot of gold at the end," said Fizz, "though that part's probably just a fun story, since a rainbow's end moves whenever you do."

Dev aimed his water pistol at the nearest arc. "I'm gonna touch it!"

He sprayed. His hand passed right through. No gold. No end.

"Told you," said Fizz, smiling. "You can look, but you can never actually touch one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Backyard
chapters.text:
Fizz's light began to fade, scattering into mist. "Time to go home, you two."

"Wait!" said Dev. "Will we see you again?"

"Whenever the sun meets the spray," said Fizz. "Just look for the colors."

A soft SPLOOSH of light, and the backyard reappeared. The grass was damp. The sun was warm.

Dev looked at his water pistol, completely ordinary again. "Did that really happen?"

Priya grabbed her sidewalk chalk and drew a careful arc: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet, in just the right order.

"Proof," she said, grinning.

Dev squirted one last cloud of mist into the sunlight. A small rainbow blinked back at them, like a tiny, private wave goodbye.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Priya. Goodnight, Dev. Spray well, and dream in every color.

true_facts.text: A rainbow forms when sunlight goes into a raindrop, bends, bounces off the back, and bends again on the way out.
That bending is called **refraction** — light changes direction when it moves from air into water.
Plain white sunlight is really all the colors mixed together, like paint before you squeeze it out.
Rainbow colors always line up the same way: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet — remembered as **Roy G. Biv**.
Red sits on the outside of a rainbow and violet on the inside, because red bends the least and violet bends the most.
To see a rainbow, the sun needs to be behind you and rain or spray needs to be in front.
A rainbow is really a full circle — we usually only see an arch because the ground blocks the bottom half.
From an airplane, with no ground in the way, people can sometimes see a whole circle rainbow.
No two people ever see the exact same rainbow, because everyone is standing in a slightly different spot.
Sometimes a fainter second rainbow shows up above the first one, with its colors flipped.
Rainbows can also form in waterfall mist, garden hose spray, and even in moonlight, where they're called moonbows.
A scientist named **Isaac Newton** used a triangle of glass to split sunlight into rainbow colors back in the **1660s**.
Old stories talk about rainbows too, like **Bifrost**, a rainbow bridge in an old tale.
Some stories say there's a pot of gold at the end of a rainbow, but a rainbow's end always moves when you do, so you can never really get there — or touch a rainbow at all.

story.title: Jack, Ellie, and the Night the Mermaid's Purse Hatched
story.subtitle: A bedtime dive through four hundred million years of sharks.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Purse That Glowed
chapters.text:
Jack's bath was over, but his shark tooth necklace was still dripping on the rug.

Ellie sat crisscross on her bed, cradling a little shell night light. She called it her "mermaid's purse," because the pet store lady once said real mermaids tuck baby sharks inside things exactly like it.

"That's not even true," Jack said, grinning, because winding up Ellie was basically his job.

"It is TOO true," Ellie said, and hugged the shell tighter.

That was when the shell went warm in her hands. It crackled, soft and green, like a glow stick waking up.

CRRRK.

The shell split down the middle, and something small and silver slipped out onto the blanket. It had fins. It had a tail. It blinked up at them with two shiny black eyes.

"That," Jack whispered, "is a baby shark."

"I TOLD you mermaid's purses were real," Ellie said, triumphant.

The little shark flipped a somersault and landed on Jack's pillow. "Hiya," it said. "I'm Pip. Sorry about the mess — hatching is messy business. Want to see where sharks really come from?"

Jack didn't need asking twice. He grabbed Ellie's hand, and the bedroom folded away like wet paper, and —

WHOOOSH — they were swimming.

"Whoa," Jack said, looking down at himself. "Why don't I have bones?"

"You do," said Pip, looping around them. "But mine are different. A shark's skeleton is made of something called **cartilage** — it's bendy, like the squishy part on top of your ear. Go on, feel your ear."

Ellie felt hers. "Squishy!"

"Exactly," said Pip. "That's why sharks bend and twist so easily. Now hang on tight — we're going way back. Sharks have been swimming in the sea for more than **400 million years**. That's before dinosaurs. That's before trees."

"Before TREES?" Jack said. "What did sharks even hide behind?"

Pip grinned, all teeth. "Nothing. Nobody could catch them anyway."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Giant Tooth
chapters.text:
A shadow slid under them, bigger than a school bus.

Ellie grabbed Jack's arm. Jack grabbed it right back, which, for once, he didn't mind admitting.

"Don't worry," said Pip. "That one's ancient history. Literally."

The shadow became a giant shark with a mouth like a cave, and then it faded away, like mist.

"That was **Megalodon**," said Pip. "The biggest shark anyone's ever found. It's **extinct** now — that means every single one is gone. None left anywhere."

"Then how do people even know it was real?" Jack asked.

"Good question," said Pip. "Shark skeletons are bendy, remember? Bendy skeletons don't turn into **fossils** easily — a fossil is old bones or teeth that turned hard as stone over a very long time. But teeth do turn into fossils."

Pip nudged something half-buried in the sandy sea floor. Jack scooped it up: a tooth, shaped like a triangle, as long as his own hand.

"That's a Megalodon tooth," said Pip. "Almost everything we know about Megalodon comes from teeth exactly like that one."

Ellie measured the tooth against her palm. "It's bigger than my whole hand!"

"Hands are small when you're six," Jack said.

"Teeth are big when you're a Megalodon," Ellie shot back, and Jack laughed so hard he nearly dropped the tooth.

He tucked it into his pocket instead. "Souvenir," he said.

"Good call," said Pip. "Hang on — next stop is a shark so big it makes Megalodon's cousins look small, and so gentle it wouldn't hurt a shrimp."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
Something enormous glided out of the blue, spotted like a leopard, calm as a cloud.

"That," Jack breathed, "is the biggest fish I have ever seen."

"It's the biggest fish in the whole world," said Pip. "A **whale shark**. Over **40 feet long**."

Ellie tried counting its spots as it passed. "One, two, three — I give up, there's too many!"

"Good thing it's gentle," said Pip, "because with a mouth that big, you'd expect trouble."

"Does it eat boats?" Jack asked, only half joking.

"It eats **plankton**," said Pip. "Plankton is just tiny floating specks of food, way smaller than a crumb. The whale shark opens its huge mouth and strains them out of the water, like a colander catching noodles."

Jack studied the giant shark's slow, lazy swim. "It doesn't even look hungry."

"That's because it's been doing this a long time," said Pip. "Some whale sharks live past **100 years old**."

"A hundred?" Ellie said. "That's older than Grandpa!"

"Way older," Jack said, impressed.

The whale shark drifted close enough for Ellie to wave at it, slow and polite, the way Pip had shown them. The shark didn't seem to mind one bit. It just kept gliding past, like it had all the time in the world, which, Jack figured, it basically did.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Rows and Rows of Teeth
chapters.text:
A fin sliced the water ahead, sharp as scissors.

"Now THIS one," Jack said, "is the shark I've been waiting for."

The **great white shark** turned, slow and curious, showing off a mouth lined with rows of pointy, saw-edged teeth.

"Whoa," Jack said. "How many rows is that?"

"Count them," said Pip.

Jack counted, careful, the way he counted stairs at home. "Looks like... a whole bunch!"

"Good guess," laughed Pip. "A great white loses and grows **thousands of teeth** over its whole life. New ones are always lined up behind, ready to slide forward the second an old one falls out."

"Like a vending machine," Jack said. "Teeth keep coming."

"Exactly like that," said Pip. "Great whites grow up to about **20 feet long**, and those teeth are perfect for catching seals and fish."

Ellie, who had been quiet, suddenly pointed. "Jack — is that a tooth down there?"

Jack swam down and found a shed tooth, small and white, resting in the sand. "She's right! It really does just fall out and leave a spare lying around."

"Told you," Ellie said, smug, and for once Jack didn't even mind losing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Sandpaper Skin and Secret Sparks
chapters.text:
"Touch the water near its side," Pip said. "Careful — just a feel, not a pat."

Jack brushed his fingers near the great white's side as it swam off. "It feels... rough? Like sandpaper!"

"Good hands," said Pip. "Shark skin is covered in tiny, tooth-shaped bumps. They make it rough, but they also help the shark slip through the water smoothly, almost like a race car's paint."

"Sharks have sandpaper race-car skin," Jack said. "Officially the coolest animal alive."

Ellie tilted her head. "How does it find stuff to eat if its eyes are so tiny?"

"Ah," said Pip, spinning a loop. "Sharks have a secret trick. Every living thing makes tiny electric sparks, even you. Sharks feel those sparks through jelly-filled holes in their snout."

"So it can feel my heartbeat?" Ellie asked, eyes wide.

"From close by, maybe," said Pip. "Which means a shark can find a fish hiding in the sand, even in the dark, even with its eyes shut."

Jack tried to imagine feeling someone's heartbeat through his own nose, and immediately tried to wiggle his nose at Ellie.

"Stop it," Ellie giggled, swatting him away, which was exactly the reaction Jack had been fishing for.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Walking Shark and the Fastest Fin
chapters.text:
Something small scuttled across the coral below them, using its fins like tiny paddles.

"Is that shark... walking?" Ellie asked.

"It sure is," said Pip. "That's an **epaulette shark**. It scoots across reefs and puddles using its fins, and it can hold its breath a surprisingly long time when the water around it runs low."

"Like when the pool gets shallow," Jack said, "and you have to army-crawl to the deep end."

"Exactly like that," said Pip.

A wide, strange head swung into view, eyes stuck out on either end like handlebars.

"Whoa, its head is a hammer!" Jack said.

"**Hammerhead shark**," said Pip. "That wide head spreads its eyes far apart, so it can look almost all the way around while it hunts."

Ellie waved both arms out like handlebars, giggling. "Can I have a hammerhead?"

"Ask Mom," Jack said.

A streak of silver blurred past them so fast it left a ripple. "WHOA, slow down!" Jack shouted.

"That's a **shortfin mako**," said Pip. "Fastest shark there is. It bursts forward in quick sprints to catch speedy fish like tuna."

"Faster than you, Jack, in the pool," Ellie said.

"Nothing's faster than me in the pool," Jack said, and Pip just laughed and let him have that one.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Mermaid's Purses and River Sharks
chapters.text:
Something leathery and black drifted past, shaped like a little pillow with curly strings on each corner.

Ellie gasped. "Pip — is that a real mermaid's purse?"

"It sure is," said Pip. "Some sharks lay eggs inside cases exactly like that one. Other sharks don't lay eggs at all — their babies are born alive, ready to swim right away."

Ellie cradled the empty case gently. "So my night light really was one."

"It really was," said Pip, and Ellie shot Jack the smuggest look a six-year-old has ever shot anyone.

"Fine," Jack muttered. "You were right."

A thick gray shark swam past them, heading toward water that tasted strangely fresh.

"That's a **bull shark**," said Pip. "Most sharks need salty ocean water, but bull sharks can swim in rivers too. Some have turned up a very long way upstream."

"So it could swim near actual houses?" Jack asked.

"Way, way upriver, sometimes," said Pip.

Below them, a shark lay still on the sandy bottom, barely moving.

"Is it sick?" Ellie asked, worried.

"Just resting," said Pip. "That's a **nurse shark**. It pumps water over its gills while it lies there, so it doesn't have to keep swimming just to breathe."

"Lucky," Jack said. "I have to keep moving or I sink."

"You'll learn," said Pip, patting him with a fin.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Shark Lady and the Way Home
chapters.text:
A small, round shark drifted by, taking a single, perfect, cookie-shaped bite out of a passing shape in the distance, then zipping off.

"Okay, that one's just rude," Jack said.

"That's a **cookiecutter shark**," Pip laughed. "Tiny, lives down deep, and yes — it really does take round bites out of animals much bigger than itself, even whales. Don't worry, nobody's hurt badly. It's just a very small, very strange lunch habit."

Ellie wrinkled her nose. "Weird."

"Sharks are a little weird," Pip agreed. "That's the best part."

A woman in an old diving suit swam past, smiling, surrounded by curious sharks that bumped her gently like puppies.

"That's **Eugenie Clark**," said Pip. "People called her the Shark Lady. She spent years studying sharks and proved they're curious, and that they can even learn tricks."

"Like a dog?" Ellie asked.

"Kind of like a dog," said Pip.

"One more thing before you go home," Pip added. "Sharks sit near the very top of who-eats-who in the ocean. That helps keep everything else down there balanced and healthy. And even though they look scary, a shark hurting a person is very, very rare. People cause sharks far more trouble than sharks cause us."

Jack nodded slowly. "So they're not monsters. They're just... important."

"Exactly," said Pip. "Ready for home?"

The ocean folded away like wet paper again, and —

CRRRK — they landed back on Ellie's bed, the little shell night light glowing soft green between them.

Jack's Megalodon tooth sat warm in his pocket. Ellie hugged her shell tight.

"Goodnight, Pip," Ellie whispered.

"Swim well, you two," Pip said, and the light dimmed to a sleepy glow.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Jack. Goodnight, Ellie. Swim well.

story.title: Nora and the Tile from Pompeii
story.subtitle: One tiny mosaic piece opens a whole buried town.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Tile
chapters.text:
Nora sat on her bedroom floor, sorting bright mosaic tiles into piles. Blue, red, gold — she loved building little pictures from tiny squares. It was way past bedtime, but one more pattern wouldn't hurt.

Then she noticed it: a chipped red tile, warm under her finger. She tapped it once, twice, three times, like a knock on a door.

CLICK. The tile glowed like a tiny sun.

"Hello," said a small voice. "I'm a tessera — that's what Romans called a little mosaic tile. Want to see where I came from?"

Before Nora could answer, the glow swallowed the room.

She landed on a sunny street lined with stone buildings. Market sellers called out. Dogs barked. Everything smelled like fresh bread.

"Welcome to Pompeii," said the tessera. "A real Roman town, near where the city of Naples is today. About eleven to fifteen thousand people once lived right here."

"Pompeii," Nora whispered. "Why's it called that?"

"Some say it comes from an old word, *pompe*, meaning 'five' — maybe because five little villages joined to make one town."

Nora grinned. "Five pieces making one picture. Just like a mosaic."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Stones in the Street
chapters.text:
Nora skipped ahead and stopped. Big stone blocks crossed the road, with gaps on either side.

"What are these for?" she asked.

"Stepping stones," said the tessera. "People hopped across without getting muddy feet. Carts rolled right through the gaps between them."

Nora counted the gaps. "One, two... just enough for wheels!"

Nearby, water trickled from a stone fountain shaped like a face.

"Pompeii had pipes under the streets," the tessera said, "carrying water to fountains all over town. People filled their jugs right here."

Nora cupped her hands under the spout. Cool water splashed her fingers.

"Smart town," she said. "They thought of everything."

"They did," said the tessera. "Come on — I want to show you where people cheered the loudest."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Loudest Seats in Town
chapters.text:
A huge oval building rose ahead, bigger than any building Nora had seen.

"What's THAT?" she asked, tipping her head back.

"An amphitheater," said the tessera. "That's an open-air stadium. People built it almost one hundred fifty years before the town was buried — one of the oldest ever found."

Nora climbed onto a stone step. "What did they watch here?"

"Gladiator games," the tessera said. "Brave fighters, roaring crowds, lots of noise."

Nora cupped her hands and shouted into the empty rows. "GO TEAM!"

Her voice echoed back three times.

"I think they heard that one in Naples," laughed the tessera.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: A Strange Cloud
chapters.text:
The sky turned a strange grey-brown. Nora pointed at the mountain across the bay.

"Why is there smoke way up there?"

"That's Mount Vesuvius," said the tessera. "It's a volcano — a mountain that can blow out hot ash and rock. On **August 24th, in the year 79**, it erupted."

Nora felt a flutter of worry. "Are we safe?"

"We're just watching, like a boy named Pliny the Younger did," the tessera said gently. "He stood far across the bay and wrote down everything he saw, like a careful reporter. His letters are why scientists still call this kind of eruption 'Plinian' today."

"So writing can be brave too," Nora said.

"Very brave," said the tessera. "Let's see what the ash left behind."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Frozen in Time
chapters.text:
The glow shimmered, and years rushed by in a blink.

Ash and light rock called pumice had rained down, covering the whole town — as deep as a two-story house.

"That's SO much," Nora gasped.

"It happened fast," said the tessera, "fast enough to keep things exactly as they were. Come look."

Inside a stone bakery, Nora spotted a round loaf, still marked with the baker's own stamp, sitting in the oven.

"That bread is thousands of years old?" Nora asked.

"Baked the same day the ash fell," said the tessera. "Paintings on walls, even silly messages people scribbled outside shops — all kept safe too."

Nora touched the cool stone gently. "It's like a time capsule."

"Exactly like one," said the tessera.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Lost and Found
chapters.text:
The light flickered again. Now workers with shovels stood in a dusty field.

"Where are we now?" Nora asked.

"Many years later," said the tessera. "Pompeii was forgotten for a long, long time — until **1748**, when workers digging here found old walls and ancient things buried below."

Nora watched a worker brush dirt from a stone step — the very one she'd hopped across earlier.

"They found the stepping stones!" she said.

"People called archaeologists kept digging carefully after that," said the tessera. "That's what we call people who dig up the past to learn from it."

Nora clapped. "Pompeii came back."

"In a way," smiled the tessera, "it never really left."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Wooden Doors and Painted Walls
chapters.text:
The tessera led Nora to a smaller town by the sea.

"This is Herculaneum," it said. "Buried by the same eruption, but by a different kind of hot ash. Here, even wooden furniture and old scrolls survived."

Nora peeked into a doorway. "A whole wooden door, after all this time?"

"Amazing, right?" said the tessera.

Back near Pompeii, Nora found a wall covered in bright paintings.

"These are frescoes," said the tessera, "paintings made right onto wet walls. One famous set, in the Villa of the Mysteries, shows a mysterious ceremony nobody's fully explained."

Nora studied the colors — reds, golds, deep blues — and grinned.

"It's like a giant mosaic," she said, "just painted instead of tiled."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Whole Picture
chapters.text:
"One last stop," said the tessera, and the glow swirled again.

Now Nora stood above Pompeii, looking down at stone streets stretching far below.

"Millions of people visit here every year now," said the tessera. "It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site — that means a group of countries agreed to help protect it forever."

"Is it all dug up?" Nora asked.

"Only about two-thirds," said the tessera. "New paintings and rooms are still being found."

"And the volcano?"

"Still there," said the tessera. "Scientists watch it closely, every single day, to keep everyone nearby safe."

Nora nodded slowly. "Every tiny tile tells a story."

"Every tiny tile tells a story," the tessera agreed, and the glow folded back into the little red tile.

Nora blinked. She was back on her bedroom floor, her finished mosaic glowing faintly in the lamp light — tiny stepping stones, a fountain, a round loaf of bread, all pieced together.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Nora. Every tiny tile tells a story. Sleep well, and dream in mosaics.

story.title: Maya and the Race to the Moon
story.subtitle: A splashy trip through the Space Age, with Barnacle the seal along for the ride.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beep in the Water Cup
chapters.text:
Maya had swim practice that morning, and now her arms ached in a good, floppy way. She sat cross-legged on her bed, painting a little rowboat, her paintbrush dipped in a cup of water on the nightstand.

It had been a whole week since the glow from the hum-bridge had faded off her windowsill. Tonight the glow was back, but this time it came from her water cup.

**BEEEEP.** The water fizzed like soda. Up popped a round, whiskery head.

"All aboard, Maya!" said Barnacle the seal, water sloshing onto her sketchbook.

"Barnacle! You're in my cup!"

"Technically," he said, "I'm in a little slice of outer space. Listen." The beep came again, steady as a heartbeat.

"That sounds like boat code," Maya said. "Like when ships blink their lights."

"Close! On **October 4, 1957**, the Soviet Union launched something called **Sputnik 1** — the first satellite ever to fly around the Earth." Barnacle explained a satellite is just a machine that circles a planet, around and around, like a toy on a string with no string at all.

"Sputnik was only about as wide as a **beach ball**," he went on, "and all it did was send out that simple beep, over and over. Anybody with an ordinary radio could hear it."

Maya grinned. "People all over the world heard a little beach ball beeping from space?"

"Paws-itively true," said Barnacle.

Maya cupped her hands around the glowing water. It spun into a tiny whirlpool, bright as stars.

"Hold on tight," said Barnacle.

**SPLOOSH.** The cup swallowed them whole.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Laika and the New Space Team
chapters.text:
They landed with a soft *thump* on something cold and metal. Above them hung a shiny silver ball with a tiny round window.

Maya pressed her face close. Inside sat a small, bright-eyed dog.

"Why is there a dog in space?" Maya asked.

"On **November 3, 1957**," said Barnacle, "the Soviets launched **Sputnik 2**, and a brave dog named **Laika** became the very first living creature to circle the Earth."

Maya waved through the window, careful not to touch the glass. "Hi, Laika. You're so brave."

"The whole world fell in love with her," Barnacle said. "She became famous everywhere."

A siren of sorts wailed in the distance — not scary, just busy and important, like a school on the first day.

"Everyone over in America got a big surprise," Barnacle said. "They didn't want to be left behind, so they built a brand-new space team."

"What's it called?"

"**NASA**. It started working on **October 1, 1958**."

Maya thought about her own swim team, how they'd all gotten matching caps once. "Did they get a cool name because of Sputnik?"

"Exactly because of Sputnik," said Barnacle, clapping his flippers. "You could say Sputnik beeped, and NASA answered."

Maya giggled. "That's a good one. For a seal."

"I have my moments," said Barnacle, and the silver ball above them began to spin into a new, glowing circle of light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Invisible Belt
chapters.text:
This time they landed on a launch pad with a tiny satellite shaped like a long pencil.

"This one's American," said Barnacle. "**Explorer 1**. Launched **January 31, 1958**."

Maya tilted her head. "What did it find?"

"Something nobody could see before. An invisible ring of fizzy energy wrapped all the way around the Earth. Scientists named it the **Van Allen belt**, after the man who figured it out."

"A belt made of energy, not for pants?" Maya asked.

"Not for pants," Barnacle agreed. "Just a glowing ring, circling our whole planet, like a hula hoop made of light."

Maya loved this. She flipped open her sketchbook and started drawing: Earth in the middle, a glowing ring looping around it.

"Can I keep this drawing?" she asked.

"You'll want to," said Barnacle, with a wink that seals probably shouldn't be able to do. "It might come in handy."

Maya tucked her pencil behind her ear. "Where next?"

"Somewhere a person finally gets to go, not just a satellite," said Barnacle, and the drawing in her lap began to glow at the edges.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The First Person Up There
chapters.text:
They tumbled out beside a tall rocket, steam hissing from its sides.

A man in a round white helmet waved from a hatch, grinning so big his whole face seemed to smile.

"That's **Yuri Gagarin**," said Barnacle. "On **April 12, 1961**, he became the very first human to fly in space. He zoomed all the way around the Earth once, in about **108 minutes**."

"That's faster than my whole swim practice!" Maya said.

"Much faster," said Barnacle.

Maya asked, "Was he scared?"

"He smiled the entire way," said Barnacle. "That's why people loved him so much."

Then the scene shifted, quick as a wave, to a smaller capsule bobbing nearby.

"And that one?" Maya asked.

"**Alan Shepard**. On **May 5, 1961**, he became the first American in space. His trip was shorter — he didn't make it all the way around the Earth like Gagarin did."

Maya thought of boat races back home, how sometimes one boat went all the way around the buoy and another just went partway.

"So Gagarin did the whole lap," she said, "and Shepard did half?"

"A fair way to think about it," said Barnacle, clearly impressed.

Maya grinned. "I want to see who finishes the whole race."

"Funny you say that," said Barnacle. "Someone's about to announce exactly that."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: A Dare to the Moon
chapters.text:
A crowd gathered around a podium. A man in a dark suit stood tall, speaking in a clear, booming voice.

"That's President **Kennedy**," Barnacle whispered. "Listen."

"We choose to go to the Moon," the voice rang out, "and to do it before this decade is out."

Maya's mouth fell open. "The actual Moon? Like, land on it?"

"On **May 25, 1961**, he dared his whole country to do exactly that," Barnacle said.

Maya grabbed her pencil and, right under her drawing of the glowing belt, wrote one big word: MOON.

"What's that for?" Barnacle asked.

"It's our mission plan," Maya said. "If we're going to see everything, we need to know where we're headed."

Barnacle looked at the word, then at Maya, clearly delighted. "A captain who plans ahead. I like it."

"All boats need a destination," Maya said proudly.

"Then let's follow your map," said Barnacle, and the word MOON on her page began to shimmer like moonlight on water.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Valentina's Forty-Eight Laps
chapters.text:
They landed beside yet another rocket, smaller flags painted along its side.

A woman climbed out, hair pushed back, eyes bright with excitement.

"On **June 16, 1963**," said Barnacle, "**Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman ever to fly in space. She circled the Earth aboard a ship called **Vostok 6**."

Maya's eyes went wide. "A whole lady astronaut? Like, by herself?"

"All by herself," said Barnacle. "She used to work in a factory before this. Then she went and orbited the Earth **forty-eight times**."

Maya tried to picture swimming forty-eight laps of her pool and nearly fell over giggling. "That's SO many laps!"

"She never got tired of the view," Barnacle said.

Maya waved up at Valentina, who waved right back before her rocket rumbled off the pad.

"I want to go around the whole Earth someday too," Maya said.

"One lap at a time," said Barnacle gently. "You've already got the forty-eight-lap spirit. That's the important part."

Maya beamed, tucking that thought away like a shell in her pocket.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Secret Superhero
chapters.text:
The next landing was quiet and dark, stars thick overhead.

A spaceship floated nearby, and a figure in a puffy suit drifted slowly outside it, tethered by a long cord, like a balloon on a string.

"That's **Alexei Leonov**," said Barnacle. "On **March 18, 1965**, he became the first person ever to float outside his spaceship. That's called a **spacewalk**. He floated out there about **ten minutes**."

"Why doesn't he fall?" Maya asked.

"No gravity up here to pull him down," said Barnacle. "Nothing to fall toward. He just floats."

Maya watched, amazed, as Leonov tumbled gently, slow as a leaf in a pool.

"Who built all these rockets, anyway?" Maya asked. "Somebody has to design them."

"Ah," said Barnacle, lowering his voice like it was a secret — which, it turned out, it was. "On the Soviet side, one man led it all: **Sergei Korolev**. But nobody outside his country even knew his name until after he died, in **1966**. It was kept completely secret."

Maya gasped. "A secret superhero behind everything?"

"Exactly that," said Barnacle. "And on the American side, a rocket builder named **Wernher von Braun** led the team that built the giant rockets for NASA."

Maya nodded slowly, piecing it together like puzzle edges. "So there were two secret rocket wizards, racing each other."

"You found it," said Barnacle, clearly proud. "Nobody told you that. You worked it out yourself."

Maya grinned so wide her cheeks hurt.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Whole Earth in a Photo
chapters.text:
They drifted now, not toward a planet but around one. Through a round window, Earth hung small and blue and swirled with white clouds, like a marble floating in black water.

"This is **Apollo 8**," Barnacle said. "In December **1968**, these astronauts became the first people ever to circle the Moon. And look — right there."

An astronaut lifted a camera to the window.

"That's **William Anders**," said Barnacle, "taking what people now call the **Earthrise** photo — our whole Earth, rising over the edge of the Moon."

Maya pressed her hands to the glass, awestruck. "It looks so small. And so pretty."

"From up here," Barnacle said softly, "it's the only home anybody has."

Maya didn't say anything for a moment. Then she grabbed her pencil and began to draw it exactly as she saw it — round, blue, rising over gray Moon dust.

"Keep that one safe," said Barnacle. "It's a good one to bring home."

Maya folded the drawing carefully into her sketchbook, right next to her glowing belt and her MOON plan.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: One Giant Leap
chapters.text:
The ground shook. A rocket taller than any building Maya had ever seen stood waiting, smoke curling from its base.

"That's the **Saturn V**," said Barnacle. "**363 feet tall** — taller than the Statue of Liberty!"

Maya craned her neck all the way back. "That's bigger than my whole street."

**WHOOOOSH.** The rocket climbed into the sky, and the scene swept forward to a dusty gray surface, a ladder, and a boot stepping down.

"On **July 20, 1969**," Barnacle said, "**Neil Armstrong** became the first person to ever walk on the Moon. He called it a giant leap."

Maya watched Armstrong's boot press into the dust, leaving a perfect print.

"**Buzz Aldrin** walked there too," Barnacle added, "while their friend **Michael Collins** stayed up above, all alone, flying the ship called **Columbia** in circles around the Moon."

"Wasn't he lonely?" Maya asked.

"Maybe a little," said Barnacle. "But somebody had to keep the ship safe for the ride home. That's its own kind of brave."

Maya thought of staying home to keep a boat tied up steady, while others went ashore. "That's a good job too," she decided.

She looked at the boot print, perfect and still, and whispered the words right along with Armstrong.

"ONE GIANT LEAP!" Maya shouted, and her voice echoed clear across the quiet gray Moon.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Splashdown, and Shaking Hands
chapters.text:
The next rocket did not look right. A bang, far off and muffled, rattled the little ship, and a warning light blinked red.

"Uh-oh," said Barnacle, calm as ever. "This is **Apollo 13**, **1970**. An oxygen tank broke, way out past the Moon."

Maya's stomach tightened for one second. "Are they okay?"

"They are," Barnacle said right away. "Everybody on the ground worked together and figured out a fix using only what the astronauts already had on board. The whole crew made it safely home."

Maya let out a breath. "Like patching a torn sail with whatever's in the boat."

"Exactly like that," Barnacle said, and the worry melted off Maya's shoulders like morning fog.

"By the end of it all," Barnacle went on, "**twelve** astronauts had walked on the Moon."

"Twelve whole people!" Maya said, wiggling with delight.

Then the sky filled with two ships, one Soviet, one American, drifting slowly toward each other.

"**July 17, 1975**," said Barnacle. "The last chapter. American and Soviet spaceships **docked** together, right there in orbit, and the crews climbed through and shook hands."

Maya watched the astronauts grin at each other, shaking hands in space the way she shook hands after a swim meet.

"That's a nice way to end a race," she said.

"The nicest way," said Barnacle, and the stars around them began to swirl and fold, pulling gently back toward home.

**SPLOOSH.** Maya landed softly on her own bed, paintbrush still in her hand, her water cup calm and still beside her.

On her sketchbook sat a drawing she didn't remember finishing: the whole Earth, rising blue over gray Moon dust, with a tiny paper rocket tucked beside it.

Barnacle's flipper-print glistened, just once, on the rim of the cup, and then the water went quiet.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. The stars are still up there, circling along, same as always. SPLOOSH, and play well, little astronaut.
