story.title: Zara and the Fire Inside the Earth
story.subtitle: A rock-hunting, lava-glowing bedtime adventure

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Geode That Glowed
chapters.text:
Zara sat on her bedroom floor. Her rock box was wide open. Shiny stones covered the carpet like stars.

She picked up her favorite rock. It was round and gray, with a secret hiding inside. She tapped it twice. "Hello, Geode," she whispered.

The rock wiggled. Then it cracked open all by itself. Warm orange light spilled out, like a tiny campfire.

A glowing purple crystal floated up from the crack. It had sparkly edges and two blinking eyes.

"Finally!" it said. "I've been waiting in that rock for ages. I'm Ember. I know all about rocks that get *really* hot."

"Rocks that get hot?" Zara leaned closer, eyes wide.

"The hottest rocks on Earth," said Ember. "Want to see where they live?"

Zara did not need to think twice. She grabbed her toy rock hammer and reached for Ember's glow.

WHOOOSH! The light pulled them down, down, down, through the floor, through the dirt, deep underground.

They landed softly on warm, bumpy rock.

"Where are we?" Zara asked, looking around.

"Inside a volcano story," said Ember. "A **volcano** is a hole in the ground. Hot melted rock can escape through it."

"Melted rock?" Zara poked the ground. It was warm, not burny.

"While it's down here, we call it **magma**," said Ember. "Once it comes out on top, it gets a new name. We call it **lava**."

Zara grinned. "Magma inside, lava outside. Like me in my coat!"

"Exactly like that," laughed Ember. "Now hold on. We've got a fiery world to see."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Crack in the World
chapters.text:
The ground shivered under Zara's sneakers. A thin crack zigzagged across the rock, right by her toes.

"Whoa," she said. "Did I do that?"

"Not you," said Ember. "The whole ground is doing it. Earth's outside is made of giant puzzle pieces. We call them **plates**."

"Like dinner plates?" Zara tilted her head.

"More like puzzle plates," Ember said. "They float around, super slowly. Sometimes they push together. Sometimes they pull apart. Sometimes they slide past each other."

Zara crouched and pressed two pretend pieces together with her hands. "And volcanoes pop up at the cracks?"

"Most of them do," said Ember. "There's a giant loop of volcanoes that circles the whole Pacific Ocean. Grown-ups call it the **Ring of Fire**."

"A ring made of fire mountains," Zara whispered. "That is the coolest necklace ever."

"Here's a wobbly number for you," Ember said. "About **75 out of every 100** of the world's active volcanoes sit somewhere on that ring."

Zara counted on her fingers, then gave up and just grinned. "That's basically all of them!"

"Almost all," Ember agreed. "Follow the crack. I bet it leads somewhere loud."

Zara followed the zigzag line across the rock floor. It glowed faintly, like a dropped string of fairy lights. She skipped along it, humming, until the light brightened ahead.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Country With the Most
chapters.text:
The crack led them up through warm fog. When it cleared, Zara stood on a green, bumpy island.

Mountains poked up everywhere, some smoking gently at the top like sleepy teakettles.

"Where's this?" Zara asked, counting the smoking peaks. One, two, three, four — she lost count at seven.

"This is **Indonesia**," said Ember. "Guess how many volcanoes it has, compared to every other country."

Zara thought hard, tapping her chin. "A hundred?"

"Close in spirit," said Ember. "It has more active volcanoes than any other country on Earth."

"More than ANY other country?" Zara spun in a circle, trying to see them all at once.

"The most of all," Ember said. "All those smoking peaks are sitting on cracks where puzzle plates meet."

Zara pointed to the smallest, smokiest mountain. "That one looks like it's making tea."

"Good eye," said Ember, chuckling. "Some of these puff a little smoke almost every day. It's just how they breathe."

Zara waved at the smoking peaks, the way she'd wave at a shy new friend. "Hi, mountains. Nice steam."

"Ready for the gentlest volcanoes in the world?" Ember asked. "I know exactly where to find them."

"Yes!" Zara said, already running toward Ember's glow.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Hawaii's Gentle Giants
chapters.text:
The crack of light led down into warm, blue water, then back up onto black sand, warm from the sun.

Zara's sneakers sank into the sand. Steam puffed softly from little cracks nearby.

"Where are the plate edges here?" Zara asked, looking around. "I don't see any cracks at all."

"Good catch," said Ember. "Hawaii's volcanoes don't sit on an edge. They sit over a **hotspot** — a patch of extra-hot rock, way down deep, that keeps pushing heat up in the exact same spot."

Zara pressed her palm flat on the warm ground. "Like a stove burner that never turns off?"

"Just like that," Ember said, grinning.

A low rumble rolled across the island. Far off, bright orange lava crept slowly down a hillside, glowing like a river made of candy.

"That's **Kilauea**," said Ember. "It has been erupting almost without stopping, for years and years and years."

"Years and YEARS?" Zara's mouth fell open. "Doesn't it ever get tired?"

"Volcanoes don't get tired," Ember laughed. "They just keep going."

They climbed a wide, gentle hill nearby. It rose and rose but never got steep, like a giant had smoothed it with a spoon.

"This whole hill is one volcano," said Ember. "It's called **Mauna Loa**. By one way of measuring, it's the biggest active volcano on the whole planet. It rises over **4,000 meters** above the sea — picture about forty soccer fields, stacked one on top of another."

Zara tried to picture forty soccer fields stacked straight up and gave up, giggling. "That's a LOT of grass."

She looked down at the wide, gentle slope under her sneakers, then thought of a picture in one of her books — a mountain with steep, pointy sides, wearing a little hat of snow.

"This one is round and squishy-looking," Zara said slowly. "Like a shield lying flat on the ground."

"Exactly right," said Ember, delighted. "Wide, gentle volcanoes like this one are called **shield volcanoes**. The tall, steep, pointy kind — like Japan's Mount Fuji — are called **stratovolcanoes**. You just worked out the difference all on your own."

Zara puffed up proudly, hands on her hips. "I'm basically a volcano scientist now."

"Basically," Ember agreed, laughing. "Now let's go somewhere with a much older, much louder story to tell."
chapters.shout_line: LIKE A STOVE THAT NEVER TURNS OFF!

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Writer Who Watched
chapters.text:
The light swirled, and the warm island melted away. Zara landed on a cool, grassy hillside above a sparkling blue bay.

Across the water, a huge mountain loomed, puffing a thin gray cloud from its top.

"Where are we now?" Zara whispered.

"Italy, a very long time ago," said Ember. "That mountain is **Vesuvius**. Back in the year **79**, it woke up big and loud. It buried two whole towns, **Pompeii** and **Herculaneum**, under thick, soft ash."

Zara hugged her knees to her chest. "Buried? All the way?"

"All the way," said Ember gently. "But here's the neat part of this story. Across the water, a young man named **Pliny the Younger** sat and watched the whole thing happen. He didn't run away. He wrote down everything he saw, in letters to a friend."

"He just... watched, and wrote?" Zara asked, tilting her head.

"He did," said Ember. "And he wrote it so well that scientists still use his words today. When a volcano blasts ash way up high, in a huge puffy cloud shaped like a mushroom, they call that a **Plinian eruption** — named after him."

Zara looked at the thin cloud puffing from the mountain's top, far across the water. It did look a little like a mushroom, if she squinted.

"He got a whole type of eruption named after him," Zara said, "just for watching and writing it down?"

"Just for that," said Ember. "Not every hero swings a hammer or digs a hole. Some heroes just pay very close attention."

Zara pulled her little notebook from her coat pocket — the one she always carried for drawing rocks — and scribbled a wobbly mushroom cloud at the top of a blank page.

"I'm watching too," she announced. "Maybe someday they'll call it a Zara eruption."

"Someday," Ember laughed, glow bobbing happily, "maybe they will."

Across the bay, the mountain puffed once more, soft and far away, and then settled back into quiet.

Zara closed her notebook carefully, like she was keeping a secret safe inside it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Loudest Bang Ever
chapters.text:
Ember's glow zipped them out over a wide, wild ocean, dotted with green islands.

"Cover your ears," Ember said, "just in case."

"In case of what?" Zara asked, hands already halfway to her ears.

"In case you ever meet the loudest bang anybody has ever heard," said Ember. "In **1883**, a volcano named **Krakatoa** exploded so loudly that people heard it about **3,000 miles** away, on a tiny island called Rodrigues."

Zara's eyes went huge. "Three thousand miles? That's like shouting all the way across an ocean!"

"Pretty much exactly that far," said Ember. "Imagine shouting in your backyard, and someone hearing you on the other side of the whole country — and then some more besides."

Zara cupped her hands and shouted into the breeze. Her voice barely carried past her own sneakers. She giggled. "I've got some practicing to do."

They floated on, over more green islands, until they landed on a quiet, grassy slope.

"This one is called **Tambora**," said Ember. "In **1815**, it had the biggest eruption anyone has ever written down. It threw so much ash and dust up into the sky that the whole sky changed, for a long while."

"Changed how?" Zara asked, looking up at the clear blue sky above her.

"The dust floated all the way around the world and blocked some of the sunlight," said Ember. "The very next year, **1816**, summer barely showed up in places far away, like Europe and America. People even called it the **Year Without a Summer**."

Zara frowned, thinking hard. "One mountain made a whole YEAR go cold? Everywhere?"

"Pretty much everywhere that mattered to the story," said Ember. "One volcano, one whole summer, gone fuzzy and gray and cold."

Zara looked down at the quiet, grassy mountain beneath her sneakers. It was hard to imagine it ever being that loud, or that powerful.

"You're sneaky," she told the mountain, patting the air above the grass like she might pat a big, sleepy dog. "You don't look like you could do all that."

"That's volcanoes for you," said Ember, glow twinkling. "Even the quiet, grassy ones keep big secrets."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Mountain That Lost Its Top
chapters.text:
The sky turned cloudy and cool. Zara stood on a ridge, looking across a valley at a tall, snow-capped mountain.

"This one is called **Mount St. Helens**," said Ember. "Watch closely. Something big happened here."

"Is it going to erupt right now?" Zara asked, taking half a step back.

"Not today," said Ember quickly. "This already happened, a long time ago. We're only watching the story. We're safe and sound."

Zara relaxed, and leaned forward instead, curious.

"Scientists had been watching this mountain for weeks," Ember explained. "They used special tools — ground-wiggle machines that feel tiny shakes under the dirt, and pictures from satellites, flying machines way up above the clouds, to spot the ground swelling up like a balloon. Those are warning signs that a volcano might be waking up."

"Smart," said Zara. "Like listening for a tummy rumble before lunchtime."

"Exactly like that," Ember laughed. "On **May 18, 1980**, the whole side of the mountain suddenly slid away — a wall of rock and snow, in the biggest landslide anyone has ever recorded. Right after that, the volcano blew its top clean off."

"Blew its WHOLE top off?" Zara gasped.

"About **1,300 feet** of mountain, just gone, in moments," said Ember. "But because scientists had been watching so closely, and warning people early, most everyone nearby was already somewhere safe."

Zara looked at the mountain, now missing a chunk at the very top, like a cake with a big slice cut out of it.

"So watching the warning signs kept people safe," Zara said slowly, working it out.

"That's exactly the point," said Ember. "One of the scientists who studied this mountain, named **David Johnston**, spent his work watching it closely, so he could help warn everybody else. Paying close attention can be its own kind of brave."

Zara nodded firmly, like she was filing that thought away somewhere important and safe.

"Rocks and mountains have good stories," she said. "But the people watching them have good stories too."

"They sure do," said Ember, glowing a little brighter. "Now — one more stop. The sleepiest giant of them all is waiting."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Sleeping Giant, the New Island, and the Biggest Mountain of All
chapters.text:
The next stop was a wide, golden field, dotted with steamy little pools that burped soft puffs of steam.

"This is **Yellowstone**," said Ember. "Under all this pretty land sits a giant volcano — so giant, people call it a **supervolcano**, which just means the biggest kind of volcano there is."

Zara looked around at the peaceful field, the lazy steam, a few sleepy-looking bison grazing far away.

"It doesn't look very super-scary," she said.

"It isn't, right now," said Ember. "Its last really giant eruption happened about **640,000 years ago**. Scientists watch it closely, with those same ground-wiggle machines, and right now they see no sign at all that it's getting ready to erupt again."

"So it's basically just... napping," said Zara.

"Basically napping," Ember agreed. "For a very, very long nap indeed."

They floated north, over cold gray water, until a tiny new island poked up from the waves, steaming and hissing softly.

"This is **Surtsey**," said Ember. "Back in **1963**, this whole island rose straight up out of the sea near Iceland, while a volcano underwater kept right on erupting."

"A brand-new island? It just... appeared?" Zara leaned over, carefully, to watch steam curl off the fresh black rock below.

"Iceland sits right where two puzzle plates are slowly pulling apart," said Ember, "so new islands and new volcanoes pop up there more than almost anywhere else on Earth."

Zara looked, but never touched the steaming new rock. She just grinned at it from a careful distance.

"I want to come back when it's cooled all the way down," she said. "Then maybe I could add a tiny piece to my rock box."

"Noted," Ember said, smiling. "One more stop before we go home. Close your eyes."

Zara squeezed her eyes shut. When Ember said "open," she was floating up among the stars, looking down at a huge, red, dusty planet.

"That's **Mars**," said Ember. "And right there is **Olympus Mons** — the biggest volcano anyone has ever found, anywhere. It stands about **13.6 miles** high. That's almost three Mount Everests, stacked straight up on top of each other."

Zara tipped her head back, trying hard to imagine a mountain that enormous. "My neck hurts just thinking about climbing that one."

"Good thing nobody has to," Ember laughed. "One last fact, and it's a happy, cozy one. After ash falls and settles down, it breaks apart into rich, dark dirt, perfect for growing all sorts of plants. That's part of why so many farmers choose to live near volcanoes, even the risky ones. The ground says thank you, in its own quiet way."

Zara smiled, thinking of her own rock box, full of cool, quiet, sleeping stones waiting back home.

"I think I'm ready to go home now," she said softly. "I've got a lot of rocks to look at differently tomorrow."

"Home it is," said Ember, glowing warm and steady. "Shine on, Zara."

WHOOOSH! The stars, the red planet, and the warm night air all swirled together into one long streak of light.

Then Zara was sitting on her bedroom floor again, rocks scattered across the carpet exactly like always.

Her geode sat closed in her hand, quiet and gray, just like it had been at the very start. But when she turned it over, one tiny new fleck of sparkly purple crystal glinted from a crack that hadn't been there before.

"Thank you," Zara whispered to it.

The little rock didn't answer. But somewhere deep inside, just for one second, it almost seemed to glow.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Zara. Shine on.

story.title: Ben and the Glitch Block: A Trip Through Game History
story.subtitle: One pixel cube, nine levels, and about sixty years of games.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Green Glow at Brookhaven
chapters.text:
Ben was lying on his bedroom floor, flashlight propped against a pillow, finishing a pixel-art dragon on his tablet. Pixel by pixel, he dragged each tiny square into place. It was way past bedtime, but the dragon only needed one more wing.

Then the desk lamp flickered green.

On his shelf, a blocky gray cube he'd built out of cardboard — leftover from an old Minecraft art project — started to hum. Static crackled across its sides like TV snow. Ben sat up so fast his tablet slid off his knees.

"Hello?" he whispered.

The cube blinked open like a tiny door, and green light poured out, the exact green of his dragon's eyes.

"Finally," said a small voice. Out popped a creature made entirely of square pixels, about the size of a guinea pig, with two blinking eyes. "I've been waiting for someone who likes **blocks** as much as I do. I'm Byte. Want to see where games came from?"

Ben looked at the glowing cube, then at his half-finished dragon. "Is this part of the art?"

"Nope," said Byte. "This is real. Grab my hand — well, my pixel."

The moment Ben's finger touched Byte's square hand, the room melted into green lines, and then — **WHOOOSH!**

They landed in a room full of humming machines the size of refrigerators, wires snaking everywhere. A man in a white coat squinted at a round glowing screen that showed nothing but wobbly green lines.

"That's a funny TV," Ben said.

"It's not a TV," the man said, smiling. "It's an **oscilloscope** — a screen scientists use to look at wobbly lines. I'm William. I thought, why not make the wobbles into a game?"

Ben leaned closer. The green line bounced back and forth like a tiny dot playing catch with itself. "Is that... tennis?"

William grinned. "Good eye. I call it **Tennis for Two**. Built it right here at **Brookhaven National Laboratory**, in **1958**. Turn that knob to hit the ball back."

Ben turned it. The dot bounced. **BOING!**

"I WIN!" Ben yelled, even though nobody had kept score.

Byte laughed, a sound like a dial-up modem giggling. "First game thousands of people ever played on a screen, and you already want a rematch."

"Obviously," said Ben. "Where next?"

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Fridge-Sized Computer
chapters.text:
**WHOOOSH!** Green lines spun again, and when they stopped, Ben stood in a room that smelled like hot metal. A machine as big as three refrigerators stacked together blinked rows of lights across one whole wall.

"Whoa," Ben breathed. "That's one computer?"

"One computer," said Byte. "Back in **1962**, computers didn't fit in your pocket. This one's called a **PDP-1**, and it needed its own room just to say hello."

A college student in glasses typed fast at a console, two blobs of light drifting on a round screen nearby.

"Steve Russell, at your service," the student said, not looking up. "Or I will be, once this works."

Ben squinted at the screen. Two triangle-shaped dots floated near a scatter of tiny dots. "Are those... spaceships? And that's stars?"

Steve looked up, surprised. "That's exactly what they are. My friends and I are building a game called **Spacewar!** You fly a ship, dodge the star's pull, and try to shoot the other ship."

"Can I fly one?" Ben asked.

Steve slid him a control box with one switch and one button. "Thrust and fire. Try not to fly into the sun."

Ben flicked the switch. His triangle swung wide around the little star, barely missing it. "Whoa, close one!"

"Too close," laughed Steve. "That star pulls ships in if you're not careful — but nobody really gets hurt, it's just pixels."

Byte floated beside Ben's shoulder. "This was one of the very first computer games anybody could actually play against a friend. Right here, on a computer that needed its own air conditioner."

Ben pressed fire. A tiny dot streaked across the screen and Steve's ship spun away, untouched.

"Missed," said Steve cheerfully.

"Next time," Ben said, already grinning at the screen like it was the best arcade machine he'd ever seen — even though arcades didn't exist yet.

Byte tugged his sleeve. "Speaking of which. Let's go meet the man who put games on an actual television."

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Brown Box in the Basement
chapters.text:
Green light again, and this time Ben landed in a basement that smelled like solder and coffee. A man with thick glasses hunched over a tangle of wires connected to a plain brown wooden box, plugged into a small television.

"Who turned my TV into a drawing board?" Ben asked, pointing at two white squares bouncing a white dot between them on the screen.

"I did," said the man, not looking annoyed at all. "Ralph Baer. People are going to call me the **father of video games** one day, though right now I'm just the guy whose wife keeps asking when dinner's happening."

"You made a game come out of a regular TV?" Ben said. "That's not supposed to work."

"That's exactly the idea," Ralph said, flipping a switch. The dot bounced again. "I built this **Brown Box** in my basement in the late **1960s**. Before this, if you wanted to play a game on a screen, you needed a whole room full of machines like your friend here probably showed you."

Byte nodded proudly, like he'd personally built the PDP-1.

Ben leaned over the controls, two knobs that moved the paddles up and down. "People are gonna want this in their living rooms," he said. "You should sell it."

Ralph grinned like Ben had read his mind. "Funny you say that. A company called Magnavox thought the same thing."

**FLASH** — the basement blinked away, replaced by a toy-store shelf lined with boxes showing a family gathered around their TV, controllers in hand.

"In **1972**," Byte explained, "Ralph's basement invention became the **Magnavox Odyssey** — the first video game console anyone could buy for their own home."

Ben picked up a box, grinning at the cartoon family on the cover. "So before this, nobody could play a TV game at home at all?"

"Nobody," Byte confirmed. "Now everybody could."

Ben set the box back on the shelf carefully. "Byte, I think I just watched my living room get invented."

Byte snorted. "Wait till you see what happens in the arcades."

chapters.heading: Level 4: Quarters Everywhere
chapters.text:
The green light dropped them into a dim, noisy room full of beeping machines and the smell of popcorn. In the corner stood a wooden cabinet with a small screen showing two white paddles and a bouncing square ball.

"Now THIS looks like an arcade," Ben said, already reaching for the coin slot — empty.

Two men stood nearby, one holding a clipboard, the other grinning like he'd just won something.

"Nolan Bushnell," said the grinning one. "This is Ted Dabney. We started a company called **Atari**, and this little machine is called **Pong**. Table tennis, but electric."

Ben peered at the coin slot. It looked stuffed, like someone had tried to feed it way too many snacks. "Is it... broken?"

Ted laughed. "Story goes that this very machine got so popular, so fast, people shoved in quarters till it actually jammed shut. Couldn't fit one more coin."

Byte leaned in. "Nobody's totally sure that part's true — it might be a bit of a tall tale — but it tells you how wild people went for it."

Ben grinned, imagining a machine stuffed to bursting with coins like a birthday piñata. "Can I try it even without quarters?"

Nolan flipped a hidden switch. "For you? Free game."

Ben gripped the knob and spun it. The little square ball bounced off his paddle — **BOP!** — zipped across the screen, and bounced past Ted's paddle entirely.

"POINT!" Ben shouted, pumping his fist like he'd scored the winning goal.

"That's **1972** for you," said Nolan, shaking his head good-naturedly. "Two guys, one simple game, and suddenly everybody on the block wants a turn."

Byte tugged Ben toward the green glow waiting by the door. "Speaking of wanting a turn — wait till you see what happens when games start coming on little plastic cartridges you can swap like trading cards."

Ben was already following, rubbing his hands together. "Swap like Minecraft skins?"

"Kind of," said Byte. "Just plastic instead of pixels."

chapters.heading: Level 5: One Box, A Thousand Games
chapters.text:
They landed in a living room bathed in TV light, a stack of flat plastic cartridges fanned across the carpet like a hand of cards.

"Whoa, it's like a chest full of discs," Ben said, picking one up. It had a cartoon spaceship on the cover.

"Close," said Byte. "In **1977**, Atari released a console called the **Atari 2600**. Before this, most home games only had one or two built-in games. This one let you swap **cartridges** in and out, like changing which world you load up."

Ben slid a cartridge into the slot. **CLICK.** The TV flickered to a new game entirely — rows of blocky aliens marching sideways across the screen, slowly creeping down.

"Those guys look mad," Ben said, squinting at the screen.

"They're from **Space Invaders**," said a new voice. A man adjusting dials behind the machine bowed slightly. "Tomohiro Nishikado. I made this game in **1978**, for arcades in Japan. Aliens march down, you shoot up. Simple."

Ben grabbed the controller, counting the alien rows out loud — "one, two, three, four rows!" — as they inched closer, faster each time one got shot.

"They speed up the fewer there are," Tomohiro said. "Keeps everybody's heart pounding — in a fun way."

Ben fired. **PEW PEW!** Two aliens blinked out. The rest sped up, marching a little quicker.

"They're getting faster!" Ben said, grinning instead of worried, mashing the button with both thumbs.

The last alien dropped. **BZZT — victory jingle!**

"Cleared the whole screen," said Byte. "This game got so popular in arcades, some places ran out of coins for change."

Ben set the controller down, buzzing with pride. "Okay, that one's going straight to the top of my favorites list."

"Careful," said Byte, pixels flickering with a grin. "Your list is about to get a lot longer."

chapters.heading: Level 6: Pizza, a Glitch, and a Buried Treasure
chapters.text:
The green light dropped them outside a pizza parlor, the smell of melted cheese drifting into the alley. Byte pointed at a round pizza missing one triangle slice. "Look familiar?"

Ben looked at the pizza, then pictured the little yellow circle from his game memory. "Wait. Is that supposed to be—"

"**Pac-Man**!" said a man carrying a sketchpad, grinning as he circled the pizza outline with a napkin. "Toru Iwatani, nice to meet you. Some people say I got the idea for this shape from a pizza missing a slice — that part's a little fuzzy, but the shape sure looks right, doesn't it?"

Ben compared the pizza and his memory of the game. "Pretty much exactly."

"I made **Pac-Man** in **1980**," Toru said, "for a company called Namco. Little yellow circle, eats dots, runs from ghosts."

"Runs from ghosts but never gets actually caught, right?" Ben checked.

"Never for long," Toru said with a wink. "Just a quick time-out and tries again."

Byte tugged Ben's sleeve toward the green glow. "Fast forward a few years, and things get bumpy."

They landed in a warehouse stacked to the ceiling with boxes of game cartridges, dust thick on top.

"By **1983**," Byte explained, "so many rushed, not-very-good games had been made, people stopped buying as many. The whole business shrank for a while — kind of like a party that got too crowded and everyone went home early."

Ben picked up a cartridge labeled E.T. "What happened to all these, then?"

"Funny you ask," said Byte, grinning. "A famous story says a bunch of unsold cartridges, including this exact game, got buried out in a New Mexico landfill — basically a giant trash dump. For years, people thought it was just a rumor."

"Was it true?" Ben asked.

"In **2014**," said Byte, "diggers actually went out there and found them. Cartridges, buried for decades, dug right back up."

Ben grinned, holding the dusty cartridge up like buried treasure. "So the games didn't disappear. They were just waiting."

"Exactly," said Byte. "Good thing too, because the comeback's about to be huge."

chapters.heading: Level 7: A Plumber and Some Falling Blocks
chapters.text:
The green glow cleared into a toy store wrapped in a red-and-white cardboard display, a mustached cartoon plumber jumping across the box art.

"In **1985**," Byte said, "the video game business needed a comeback. Nintendo brought out a console called the **NES**, and it came packaged with a brand-new game."

Ben grabbed the controller, a rectangle with a cross-shaped pad and two round buttons. "This looks way simpler than that PDP-1 thing."

"Way simpler," agreed a cheerful man polishing the display, pencil tucked behind his ear. "Shigeru Miyamoto. I designed the game inside that box — **Super Mario Bros.** Press the pad to run, the button to jump."

Ben pressed. On the screen, a small mustached man in overalls hopped clean over a gap and landed on a floating brick.

"He just jumped over a hole like it was nothing!" Ben said.

"That's **Mario**," Shigeru said proudly. "Probably the most famous character in any video game, ever."

Ben jumped Mario onto another brick, grinning. "He's basically the mascot of all gaming, huh?"

"Pretty much," Byte confirmed. "A **mascot** — a character everybody recognizes the second they see him, kind of like your Minecraft skin."

A soft electronic melody chimed from the next aisle over — falling square blocks tumbling down a screen, stacking into neat rows that vanished when they filled completely.

"Oh, I know this one," Ben said, eyes lighting up. "Tetris!"

A man adjusting the screen smiled. "Alexey Pajitnov. Built it in **1984**, at a computer center in Moscow. Just falling shapes — turn them, stack them, clear the lines."

Ben grabbed the controls and rotated a falling L-shaped block, sliding it into a gap. The row filled and vanished with a satisfying **ZAP**.

"That's so satisfying," Ben said, already reaching for the next block.

"Careful," Byte said, pixels flickering with amusement. "People have lost entire afternoons to that sound."

Ben didn't look up. "One more row."

chapters.heading: Level 8: Faster, Shinier, Wavier
chapters.text:
The green light this time came with actual speed — a blue blur streaked past before Ben even landed.

"Whoa, who was that?" Ben said, spinning around.

"That," said Byte, "was **Sonic the Hedgehog**, released by Sega in **1991**. They built him fast and blue specifically to race against Nintendo's Mario."

A looping track unspooled nearby with a small blue figure zipping through it, curling into a ball to roll through loops.

"Race you," Ben told the screen, grabbing the controller. Sonic zipped through a loop so fast the screen blurred. "He's basically Mario but turbocharged."

"Exactly the plan," said Byte.

The scene shifted to a living room glowing with a different console, a shiny silver disc spinning inside.

"In **1994**," Byte explained, "Sony jumped into consoles with the **PlayStation**. It used **CDs** — shiny discs — instead of cartridges, which meant games could look and sound a lot fuller."

Ben held the disc up to the light, rainbow colors swirling across it. "It's like a tiny rainbow."

Next, a cluster of computers sat connected by a tangle of cables, kids typing eagerly at each one.

"**1993**," said Byte. "A game called Doom got people linking their computers together with cables — called a **LAN party** — just to play against each other in the same room."

Ben glanced at the tangle of wires. "That's basically a sleepover, but for games."

"Pretty much," Byte laughed.

Finally, the room shifted again — a cozy living room, and someone waving a white remote around like a tennis racket.

"**2006**," Byte said. "Nintendo's **Wii** used a controller you actually wave around, instead of just pressing buttons. Even people who'd never touched a game before wanted a turn."

Ben grabbed the remote and swung it like a bat. On screen, his tiny cartoon self swung a bowling ball down a lane. **CRASH!** Pins scattered everywhere.

"STRIKE!" Ben yelled, swinging the remote again just because it felt good.

Byte floated beside him, pixels glowing warm. "One more stop, player one. This one, I think you're really going to like."

chapters.heading: Level 9: Back to the Block
chapters.text:
Green light swirled once more, and this time Ben landed somewhere that looked almost exactly like... a giant cube world, blocky trees and blocky hills stretching to a blocky sunset.

"Wait," Ben said slowly. "This is—"

"**Minecraft**," Byte confirmed, grinning wide. "Released in **2011** by a developer named Markus Persson — everybody just calls him **Notch**. Built entirely out of blocks you can place and break."

Ben reached out and touched a blocky tree. It felt oddly familiar, like the cardboard cube back on his shelf. "This one's basically made of the same stuff as Byte."

"Fair point," said Byte, patting his own square chest. "This game ended up becoming the **best-selling video game ever made**. Billions of blocks, placed by millions of people."

Ben grinned, already itching to build something. "Can I just — five more minutes?"

"We'll see," said Byte. "One last stop first."

The scene shifted to a quiet museum hall, glass cases lined with old controllers, cartridges, and consoles Ben now recognized — the Brown Box, the Odyssey, an Atari cartridge, a Game Boy.

"In **2015**," Byte said, "a museum called The Strong, in Rochester, New York, opened the **World Video Game Hall of Fame** — a place that keeps all these old games safe, so nobody forgets where it all started."

Ben peered into a case holding a dusty cartridge that looked a lot like the one he'd pulled from the landfill pile. "So all of it — the TV tennis, the spaceships, the pizza guy, all of it — just kept building up to now?"

"Every single level," said Byte, "led to the next one."

The green light swirled one final time, softer now, and Ben blinked — back on his bedroom floor, flashlight still glowing, tablet beside him. The cardboard cube on his shelf sat dark and still again, just cardboard.

Except now, propped against it, sat one tiny pixel-art brick Ben hadn't built — painted brown, just like a certain basement prototype.

Ben picked it up, grinning, and set it carefully beside his dragon drawing before finally switching off the flashlight.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ben. Game over — for tonight. Sleep tight, player one.

story.title: Lena and the Wandering Ball
story.subtitle: A keeper's tour through two thousand years of soccer

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Ball Under the Bed
chapters.text:
Lena was supposed to be asleep. Instead she was diving across her bedroom carpet, socks sliding on the rug, tipping an invisible shot wide of an invisible post.

She was good at this. Her coach said she had the best hands on the team, and most nights she practiced saves against her wall with a rolled-up sock, since her real ball lived in the garage.

Tonight there was a second ball. Scuffed brown leather, stitched in big clumsy panels she'd never seen in any store. It sat under her bed like it had always been there, which was strange, because she definitely had not left a ball under her bed.

She picked it up. It was warm. Then it hummed, a low note like a kicked drum, and glowed the exact green of a referee's flag. **WHOOOOSH.**

When the glow let go, Lena was standing on hard-packed dirt. A crowd of kids her own age were kicking a leather ball between two bamboo poles, laughing every time it went through.

"China," said the ball, which, it turned out, could talk, in a voice like a ref who'd seen everything twice. "Han dynasty, give or take. This game is **cuju** — it means 'kick ball.' People here have been playing it for over **2,000 years**."

Lena watched a girl flick the ball up without ever touching it with her hands. "That's basically soccer."

"That," said the ball, "is basically the point."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Game the King Banned
chapters.text:
The glow yanked them sideways, and Lena landed in a muddy English street, watching what looked like half the town kicking one ball at the same time.

There were no teams. There were no rules. There was just a mob of grown-ups shoving, yelling, and occasionally falling into a fence.

"This is **mob football**," the ball said, sounding delighted. "Whole villages play. The point is just to get the ball to the other end of town, however you can."

Lena ducked as someone sailed past, chasing a ball that had bounced into a vegetable stall. "This seems like a terrible idea."

"King **Edward II** agreed with you. He banned it in London in **1314**, because it kept wrecking the streets."

"Did that work?"

"Does banning a game ever work?"

Before they left, the ball rolled her past a glass case in a castle up in Scotland, holding a small, lumpy ball so old its stitching had gone soft and gray.

"That one might be from the **1540s**," the ball said, quieter now. "Some people call it the oldest football in the world."

Lena looked at it a long moment. Older than any rule. Just a ball, waiting for someone to kick it. Not so different from the one glowing in her own hands.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Rules, Finally
chapters.text:
They landed in a university courtyard full of arguing students, which Lena decided was probably normal for a university.

"Every school plays this differently," the ball explained. "Some let you carry it. Some don't. Nobody agrees on anything."

"So how does anyone play anyone else?" Lena asked.

"Exactly the problem," said a student nearby, scribbling furiously. In **1848**, he said, Cambridge students wrote down one shared rulebook, so two different schools could finally play each other without an argument first.

It helped. It didn't finish the job.

Fifteen years later, the ball rolled her into a smoky London pub, where a serious man with excellent sideburns wrote by candlelight.

"**Ebenezer Cobb Morley**," the ball said. "Founded the **Football Association** right here, on **26 October 1863**. He wrote the first official rulebook himself."

Lena leaned over his shoulder. "No carrying the ball?"

"No carrying the ball," Morley agreed, not looking up, the way a man agrees with something he has already decided six times that evening.

"So that's why it's soccer and not handball," Lena said.

"Actually," said the ball, "it's officially called association football. Schoolboys in the 1880s started calling it '**assoc**' for short. Say that fast enough, enough times, and—"

"Soccer," Lena finished.

"There it is."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The First Real Games
chapters.text:
"Now things get fast," said the ball, and it wasn't kidding.

One blink later, Lena was in a crowd watching two teams chase a trophy nobody had ever competed for before. "The **FA Cup**," the ball said. "First played in **1871-72**. It is still going. Oldest football competition on Earth."

Another blink, and Lena stood on a muddy pitch in Glasgow, watching two national teams face off for the very first time. "Scotland versus England," said the ball. "**1872**. First official international match ever."

The final whistle blew. Lena checked the score. Nothing. Zero. Zero.

"That's it? Nobody scored?"

"Nobody scored."

"**NIL-NIL!**" Lena shouted, half outraged, half delighted, because apparently some things about soccer never change.

One more blink dropped them into a meeting room, where a man named **William McGregor** unrolled a long list of team names. "In **1888**," the ball said, "he organized the first football league in the world — one proper season, same clubs, every week."

Lena counted twelve teams on the list. "So this is where it stops being one game," she said, "and starts being a sport."

"Look at you," said the ball. "Figuring things out."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: One Cup for the Whole World
chapters.text:
"Soccer had rules. Soccer had leagues," the ball said. "What it didn't have was one big competition for the whole planet."

They landed in Paris, 1904, in a room with seven men arguing in four different accents.

"**FIFA**," the ball said. "Soccer's world organization. Founded right here, by seven countries who finally agreed on something."

Lena's eyebrows went up. "Seven countries agreeing on anything sounds harder than Cambridge."

"You have no idea."

The glow carried them to Uruguay, where a stadium roared loud enough to rattle Lena's teeth. A man in a sharp suit held up a small golden trophy.

"**Jules Rimet**," said the ball. "He's the reason this exists at all — the first **FIFA World Cup**, played in **1930**."

On the field below, Uruguay beat Argentina in the final, and the home crowd went so loud that pigeons left the stadium roof in one panicked wave.

Lena laughed. "They take this seriously."

"Everyone always has," said the ball. "That's sort of the whole story."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Keepers They Tried to Stop
chapters.text:
The next stop smelled like cut grass: a women's match, thousands of fans packed along the sideline.

"**Lily Parr**," the ball said, nodding at a tall player blasting a shot a grown man would've struggled to stop. "One of the biggest stars English football had. Her team drew bigger crowds than plenty of men's teams."

Lena watched Parr's shot rip the net. "She's incredible. Why haven't I heard of her?"

The ball's hum dropped, just slightly. "Because in **1921**, the people running English football banned women's teams from their grounds. For fifty years."

Lena's stomach dropped, the way it does on a missed save. "That's not fair."

"No," the ball agreed. "It wasn't."

"So what happened?"

"They kept playing anyway, wherever they could. In **1971**, the ban was finally lifted." The light warmed. "Twenty years after that, in **1991**, the first official **Women's World Cup** was played, in China."

A stadium rose around them, bright and loud. On the field, a goalkeeper in gloves not so different from Lena's own dove full length and turned a shot around the post.

"Who won?" Lena asked, already grinning.

"The United States. First ever."

Lena pulled on an invisible glove of her own. "Good."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Stolen Cup and the Colored Cards
chapters.text:
"This one has a dog in it," the ball said. "You're welcome."

They arrived in London, **1966**, days before the World Cup, to find reporters in an uproar. The trophy had been stolen clean out of its display case.

"Stolen? The whole trophy?"

"Vanished. For about a week, nobody in England could find it anywhere."

"So how'd they get it back?"

The ball rolled toward a scruffy little terrier sniffing at a garden hedge. "A dog named **Pickles** found it. Wrapped in newspaper. Under a bush."

Lena stared at the dog, who looked thoroughly unimpressed with himself. "That's it? That's the big save?"

"Almost. Watch." The scene shifted to a packed stadium, England's players lifting that very same trophy months later. "England hosted the **1966 World Cup**. And won it. Their only title, so far."

One more blink dropped them into 1970, a referee reaching into his pocket and holding up a square of colored plastic.

"**Ken Aston**," the ball explained. "A referee who got the idea from a traffic light. Yellow means slow down. Red means stop completely. He brought **yellow and red cards** to the World Cup in **1970**, and every referee on Earth still uses them."

"**RED CARD!**" Lena shouted, pointing dramatically at nothing, because some lines deserve to be shouted whether or not anyone's around to hear them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Going Home
chapters.text:
The last stop was loud with drums and one player everyone in the stadium seemed to be watching at once.

"**Pele**," the ball said. "Brazilian forward. The only player ever on three World Cup-winning teams — **1958**, **1962**, and **1970**."

Lena watched him glide past two defenders like they were cones in a drill. "He makes it look easy."

"Everyone says that. Nobody could do what he did."

Brazil won again in 1994 and 2002, the ball added — five titles total, more than any other country. And because Brazil had kept that original trophy for good after their third win, FIFA had to make an entirely new one, in **1974**, for everybody else to chase.

"So the trophy's not even the original anymore?"

"Nope. Still counts."

The glow rose around them, gentler this time, like full time instead of a red card. Lena felt carpet under her socks before she saw her own room again.

The scuffed ball sat in her hands, ordinary brown leather, not glowing anymore. On her wall, the dent from a thousand practiced saves looked exactly the same as it had three hours and two thousand years ago.

She set the ball down carefully under her bed, in case it had somewhere else to be next time.

"Goalkeepers," she told it, "always expect a second shot."

The ball didn't answer. But she was fairly sure it was smiling.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow there was a scrimmage, and Lena already knew exactly which save she wanted to practice first.

true_facts.text: **Cuju**, a kicking game played in China over **2,000 years ago**, is one of soccer's oldest known ancestors.
Medieval **mob football** in England got so wild that King **Edward II** banned it in London in **1314**.
The **Football Association** was founded in London on **26 October 1863**, and from then on players couldn't carry the ball.
The word "soccer" comes from "**assoc**," a short nickname schoolboys used for association football in 1880s England.
The **FA Cup**, first played in **1871-72**, is the oldest soccer competition still running anywhere in the world.
**FIFA**, soccer's world organization, was founded in Paris in **1904** by seven countries.
The first **World Cup** was played in Uruguay in **1930**, with the host country beating Argentina in the final.

story.title: Arjun and the Midnight Innings
story.subtitle: A bedtime journey through the strange, true science of sleep.

chapters.heading: Over One: The Last Panel
chapters.text:
Arjun was not asleep. He was under the blanket with a flashlight, finishing the comic he'd drawn himself, the one with a blank last page he hadn't inked in yet.

"Five more minutes," he whispered, which is what he always said, to nobody in particular.

The blank panel answered. It flickered green, and ink crawled across the page on its own, sketching wide eyes, a long white coat, and a small silver bell where a whistle should be. An owl climbed out of the page and straightened his umpire's coat.

"Umpire Hoot," he said. "Lights out means stumps drawn. But I'll strike you a deal. One full innings through the science of sleep. Then straight to the crease of your pillow."

"What's an innings got to do with sleeping?"

"Everything," said Hoot. "A night's sleep isn't one long stretch. It's **cycles about ninety minutes each**, back and forth between quiet sleep and busy, dreaming sleep, all night. Like overs."

Arjun sat up. "Then let's see all the overs."

The bell rang. The bedroom folded like a page turning.

chapters.heading: 1953: The Boy Whose Eyes Twitched
chapters.text:
They landed in a dim room in **Chicago**, where a boy slept and a young scientist watched him by flashlight, writing in a notebook.

"That's **Eugene Aserinsky**," said Hoot, "working with his teacher, **Nathaniel Kleitman**, at the University of Chicago. Watch the boy's eyelids."

Arjun leaned close. Under the closed eyelids, the eyes were darting side to side, fast.

"His eyes are moving," Arjun said. "Like he's watching something."

"He is, in a way," said Hoot. "In **1953**, that twitching led Aserinsky and Kleitman to discover what we now call **REM sleep** — eyes darting under closed lids, during the most dream-filled part of the night. Kleitman spent his whole life studying sleep. People call him the father of modern sleep research."

The scientist in the room smiled at his notebook like he'd just won a match.

"Not out," said Hoot, ringing his bell softly. "He's just dreaming."

chapters.heading: The Dream Innings
chapters.text:
The scene spun, and suddenly Arjun was standing at a cricket crease in a dream of his own, bat raised, ball sailing toward him.

He swung for six. Nothing happened. His arms stayed still, heavy as sandbags.

"Try wiggling your toe," said Hoot, watching from the boundary rope.

Arjun tried. Nothing moved.

"During **REM sleep**," Hoot explained, "your brain gets almost as busy as when you're awake. But your muscles go limp, so you can't actually act out what you're dreaming."

"Good thing," said Arjun. "Or I'd knock the lamp off my nightstand every night."

"There was an old idea, back in **1899**, that dreams were secret wishes hiding in disguise. A scientist named **Sigmund Freud** wrote a whole book about it. It's a fun idea. Most scientists today think he got carried away."

The ball from Arjun's dream froze mid-air, as if waiting for the next over.

chapters.heading: The Growing Overs
chapters.text:
They dropped onto a practice ground at dawn, where young players bowled and batted in long, slow shadows.

"Why here?" Arjun asked.

"Watch the deepest part of the night," said Hoot. "The deepest stage of quiet, non-dreaming sleep is when the body releases the most **growth hormone** — the signal that tells a body to grow. It's one reason growing kids need extra sleep."

Arjun thought about the pencil marks on his doorframe at home, each one a little higher than the last.

"So if I want to bowl from higher up," he said, "I need my overs."

"Now you're thinking like an umpire," said Hoot.

Arjun grinned and marked an invisible line in the grass with his toe, like he was setting his own personal best.

chapters.heading: The Body's Umpire Clock
chapters.text:
Next came a strange little control room, glowing behind Arjun's own closed eyes, with a tiny clock ticking above where two nerves crossed.

"That," said Hoot, "is the **suprachiasmatic nucleus**. A tiny spot just above where your eye nerves cross. It works like your body's master clock, telling you when to feel sleepy and when to feel awake."

"That's a mouthful."

"Call it the body's umpire clock. It runs on a **circadian** rhythm — roughly a day long, reset by light."

Arjun noticed a thin beam of light hitting the clock through a crack, and the ticking sped up.

"It's listening to light," he said, and reached out to block the beam with his hand. The ticking slowed right down.

"Good eye," said Hoot. "In **2017**, three scientists — **Hall, Rosbash, and Young** — won the Nobel Prize for finding the genes that keep that clock ticking."

chapters.heading: The Sleepy Juice and the Night Rinse
chapters.text:
They landed in a cluttered little lab, where a small glowing bottle sat on a shelf, bubbling faintly.

"Sleepy juice," said Hoot. "Properly called **melatonin**. A scientist named **Aaron Lerner** first pulled it out in a lab in **1958**. It's the signal that tells your body it's nearly bedtime."

Arjun picked up the bottle and sniffed it. It smelled like nothing at all.

"And this," Hoot went on, pointing to a tiny door in the wall, "is where your brain files the day away. Sleep helps sort everything you practiced or learned into memories that stick."

"Like cricket drills?"

"Exactly like cricket drills. And after the filing's done, a cleaning crew called the **glymphatic system** gives your brain a nightly rinse, flushing out the day's gunk."

"So my brain gets a shower every night," said Arjun, "and I don't even get wet."

"Lucky you," said Hoot.

chapters.heading: The Sleep Records
chapters.text:
The lab door opened onto a strange little zoo. A dolphin drifted past with one eye open.

"Dolphins and some seals sleep with half their brain at a time," said Hoot, "so one eye can stay open for danger, or just to keep swimming."

A giraffe dozed standing up, barely for a moment. "Giraffes get by on under two hours some days," said Hoot. "Shortest sleepers of any big animal."

A bat hung nearby, snoring. "Some bats sleep up to twenty hours. And even fruit flies rest like they're sleeping, which tells scientists sleep is incredibly old — maybe as old as animals themselves."

"What's the record for staying awake, then?" Arjun asked.

"A teenager named **Randy Gardner**, in **1964**, stayed awake about eleven days for a school science project. One of the longest ever recorded."

Arjun's eyes went wide. "Eleven days? I could beat five more minutes easy."

"Doctors say never to try it," said Hoot firmly. "Going without sleep wrecks your mood, your focus, your memory, fast. Gardner's story is interesting. It is not a dare."

Arjun nodded slowly. "Noted, umpire."

chapters.heading: Stumps Drawn
chapters.text:
The bell rang one last time, and Arjun's bedroom folded back into place around him, flashlight still warm in his hand.

"One more thing," said Hoot, already fading into the page. "Sleepwalking happens during the deepest, quietest sleep, not during dreaming. So sleepwalkers usually aren't acting out a dream at all."

"Good to know, in case I meet one in the hallway."

"And here's the big score," Hoot added. "Most people spend roughly a third of their whole life asleep. It's not wasted time. It's overtime for growing, remembering, and cleaning house."

The owl sketch stilled on the last page, grinning.

Arjun looked at his comic, then at his flashlight, then closed the book himself.

"Stumps drawn," he said, and clicked off the light without being asked.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow there was a net session to bowl in, and sleep, it turned out, was how he'd get there.

story.title: Tom and the Humming Bell
story.subtitle: A midnight ride through two hundred years of bicycles

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Bell in the Toolbox (1817)
chapters.text:
Tom was supposed to be asleep an hour ago.

Instead he was on the garage floor, flashlight between his teeth, truing the back wheel of his mountain bike. The brake pads kept rubbing. He loved the puzzle of it — the kind of problem that had an actual answer if you looked hard enough.

Digging for a spoke wrench, his hand closed on something cold and round at the bottom of his grandfather's old tool bin. A brass bell, dented, green with age, with letters worn almost smooth. He rubbed it with his thumb.

It hummed. Then it glowed, the way a phone screen glows in a dark room, except this light was alive.

"Careful with that," said a voice made of clicking gears. A shape stood in the light — part rider, part bicycle, spokes for ribs, flickering like a projector running low on bulb. "Not every bike had brakes you could trust. I'm Revel. I ride the whole two hundred years. Tonight you're coming with me."

Before Tom could ask a single sensible question, the garage folded away like a page turning.

He landed on a cobbled German street in **1817**, next to a man straddling a wooden frame on two wheels — with no pedals at all. The man pushed off the ground with both feet, like running while sitting down.

"That's not a bicycle," Tom said. "That's barely a bicycle."

"Fair," said Revel. "Karl von Drais calls it his *Laufmaschine* — his 'running machine.' No pedals yet. But look at the front wheel."

It turned on a handlebar, just like Tom's own bike at home.

"He steers it," Tom said slowly. "That's the part that matters."

"Everyone will nickname it the hobby horse," Revel said. "You're looking at the great-great-grandfather of your mountain bike."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Boneshaker (1860s)
chapters.text:
The next stop rattled Tom's teeth before he even landed.

He was standing — bouncing, really — on cobblestones, watching a man wobble past on a machine with pedals bolted straight onto its front wheel.

"No chain," Tom said, tracking the mechanism with his eyes. "The pedals just turn the wheel directly. One crank, one turn."

"Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement built it that way in the **1860s**," Revel said. "People call it the velocipede. You'll like its other nickname better."

The rider hit a rough patch of stone and his whole body shuddered like a jackhammer.

"The boneshaker," Tom guessed, grinning.

"Lallement even patented the design over in the United States, in **1866**," Revel added. "First pedal bike with American paperwork."

Tom watched the rider's spine rattle over another cobble and winced in sympathy. "Somebody needs to invent a wheel that doesn't feel like a jackhammer."

"Patience," Revel said. "That's a few stops away yet."

Tom crouched to look at the front wheel up close, turning the pedal with one finger, feeling how directly the force traveled — no gears, no chain, just push and go. As an engineer-in-training, he respected the honesty of it. Simple. Just extremely uncomfortable.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Taking a Header (1870s)
chapters.text:
The next machine made Tom actually laugh out loud.

It had a front wheel taller than the rider — taller than Tom, even — and a back wheel the size of a dinner plate.

"That looks like it's going to fall over," Tom said.

"It's called a penny-farthing," Revel said, "named for two old British coins — the **big penny** and the **tiny farthing**. One big wheel, one small one, same idea."

"Why would anyone build it that tall?"

"One turn of the pedals," Revel said, "and that giant wheel covers way more ground than a small one would. Bigger wheel, more speed per push."

Tom understood that instantly — it was just gear ratios, a century before anyone called them that.

The rider hit a rut. For one breathless second he pitched forward over the handlebars.

"He's going to—" Tom started.

The man threw his arms out and rolled it into a clumsy stop, upright, unharmed, grinning like he'd meant to do that.

"They call that *taking a header*," Revel said. "Sitting that high above the wheel, if you stop fast, you go over the front. Happened all the time."

"So it's basically a tall, wobbly catapult," Tom said.

"Popular anyway, in the **1870s**," said Revel. "People love going fast more than they fear falling down."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Safety Bicycle (1885)
chapters.text:
The next bike looked almost normal, and that was exactly the surprise.

Two wheels, roughly the same size. A chain looping from the pedals back to the rear wheel. Tom crouched by it, tracing the chain with one finger.

"Now we're talking," he said. "The pedals don't even touch the wheel they're turning. The chain does the work."

"John Kemp Starley built this in **1885**," Revel said. "He calls it the Rover Safety Bicycle. Lower seat, even wheels — no more getting thrown over the handlebars."

"Safety." Tom tested the word. "They named it after the thing it fixed."

"Exactly. And it worked. Within a few years, this is the only design anyone wants."

A rider rolled past, both feet nowhere near the ground, completely steady, completely unremarkable — which, Tom realized, was the whole point. Nobody needed nerve to ride this one. Just legs.

He swung a leg over a spare frame leaning against a fence, feeling the low seat, the close ground. It felt, for the first time all night, like a bike he actually recognized.

"Finally," Tom said. "Something I'd actually ride down a hill."
chapters.shout_line: SOMETHING I'D ACTUALLY RIDE DOWN A HILL!

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Smooth Ride (1888)
chapters.text:
Three years on, and the wheels had changed again.

Tom knocked a knuckle against a tire and felt it give, soft and springy, instead of clanging like the solid rubber ones before it.

"That's air in there," he said, surprised. "It's a balloon."

"A Scottish vet named John Boyd Dunlop figured that out in **1888**," Revel said. "He wanted a smoother ride for his son's tricycle, so he wrapped the wheels in rubber tubes full of air. A pneumatic tire — just means air-filled."

Tom pressed the tire again, feeling it bounce back. "So instead of the wheel bashing every bump straight into you, the air soaks it up first."

"Exactly that," Revel said. "His company is still around today, under his name. You've probably seen it on tires — bike tires, car tires, all sorts."

Tom thought of his own mountain bike tires, wide and knobby, cushioning every root and rock on the trail. All of it traced back to a vet trying to stop his kid's tricycle from rattling him senseless.

"Smart," Tom said. "Fix the problem for one kid, fix it for the whole world by accident."

"That happens more than you'd think," said Revel.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Golden Age (1890s)
chapters.text:
Suddenly the street was full of bicycles — dozens of them, all different riders, all grinning.

"This is the **1890s**," Revel said. "People call it the Golden Age of Bicycles. Millions sold, across Europe and America both."

Tom noticed something else: women riding, dressed in loose trousers instead of long skirts, pedaling fast and sure.

"Long skirts used to tangle in the chain and the wheels," Revel explained. "So the bicycle craze helped push those looser trousers — bloomers — into fashion. More than that: a bike meant a woman could go wherever she wanted, whenever she wanted, without asking anyone for a ride."

"That's not nothing," Tom said.

"The reformer Susan B. Anthony put it stronger than that," Revel said. "She said cycling had done more to set women free than anything else in the world."

Tom watched a woman overtake two men without even glancing at them, laughing the whole way past.

"A machine that just... changes how free you are," Tom said. "That's a wild kind of engineering. You're not just building a faster wheel. You're building a door."

"Now you're getting it," Revel said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Bicycle Shop in Dayton (1903)
chapters.text:
The next street smelled like oil and sawdust. A sign read BICYCLE SHOP, and two brothers stood behind the counter, surrounded by wheels, spokes, and metal tubing.

"Wilbur and Orville Wright," Revel said. "Run a bike shop here in Dayton, Ohio, through the **1890s**."

Tom picked up a length of the tubing, light as a pencil in his hand. "This is way too light for a bike frame."

"It's exactly light enough for something else," Revel said. "These two take what they learn here — light metal tubing, spoked wheels, balance — and use it to build the first machine that actually flies. **1903.**"

Tom set the tube down carefully, newly respectful of it. "So the bicycle basically taught people how to build an airplane."

"Same year," Revel said, "something else starts in France. A bike race, start to finish, across the whole country. They call it the Tour de France. These days it runs about **3,500 kilometers** — over **2,000 miles** — in about three weeks."

"Three weeks on a bike," Tom said. "My legs hurt just imagining it."

"Wait till you see what they ride it on," said Revel, already pulling him forward through the light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Garage Floor
chapters.text:
The last stop felt almost like home — bikes with gears that clicked under a lever, flipping the chain between different-sized wheels to climb hills without destroying your knees.

"Derailleurs," Revel said. "Common by the **1930s**. Then in the **1970s**, riders in California start building bikes tough enough for dirt trails — wide tires, strong frames. Mountain bikes. Around the same time, kids are racing small, sturdy bikes modeled on motorcycle dirt tracks. BMX."

Tom looked down at himself and realized, grinning, that he was still wearing his own riding gloves from an hour — or two hundred years — ago.

"There are more than a **billion bikes** on Earth right now," Revel said. "More than any other vehicle humans have ever built. In places like the Netherlands and Denmark, some cities have more bikes than cars."

The light folded again, and the garage floor came up to meet Tom's sneakers, solid and familiar.

His mountain bike leaned against the wall exactly where he'd left it, brake pads still slightly rubbing. The old brass bell sat in his palm, warm now instead of cold, letters a little clearer than before.

He set it gently on his workbench, right next to the spoke wrench.

"Same bike," Tom said. "Completely different bike."

Somewhere behind him, faint as a bell fading, he thought he heard one word: *ride.*

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, that back wheel was finally getting fixed.

true_facts.text: In **1817**, Karl von Drais built a wooden two-wheeler with no pedals at all, pushed along with the feet.
Von Drais's machine got steered with handlebars and was nicknamed the hobby horse.
In the **1860s**, pedals got bolted straight onto the front wheel, making the rattly ride nicknamed the boneshaker.
In the **1870s**, the penny-farthing had a giant front wheel and a tiny back one.
It was named after two old coins of very different sizes — the big **penny** and the small **farthing**.
Falling forward off a penny-farthing was nicknamed **taking a header**.
In **1885**, John Kemp Starley built the Rover Safety Bicycle, with two even wheels and a chain.
In **1888**, John Boyd Dunlop invented the air-filled tire, making rides far smoother.
Bicycles gave women new freedom in the **1890s**; Susan B. Anthony said cycling helped set women free more than anything else.
Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio, before building the first flying airplane in **1903**.
The Tour de France bike race began in **1903** and today covers about **3,500 kilometers** across France.
Mountain bikes with wide, tough tires were built in the **1970s** by riders in California.
Today there are more than a **billion bicycles** on Earth — more than any other kind of vehicle.
