story.title: Hana and the Compass That Would Not Point North
story.subtitle: A journey through the engineering marvel — and the real story — of the RMS Titanic

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Keel in Belfast
chapters.text:
Hana was supposed to be asleep an hour ago. Instead she lay on her bedroom floor with every map she owned spread out like a quilt, tracing shipping lanes across the Atlantic with one finger, the lamp turned down low so the hallway light wouldn't give her away.

On the rug beside her sat the brass compass she'd found at a flea market last month, the one that never quite pointed north. Tonight its needle spun in a slow, lazy circle, and the glass over its face began to glow a blue-green the exact color of deep ocean on a map.

"That's new," Hana said.

The compass hummed like a ship's bell struck underwater. Ink seemed to spill up out of her Atlantic map and swallow the room, and when it cleared, Hana was standing in a shipyard so loud her teeth buzzed. RAT-TAT-TAT-TAT went a thousand rivet hammers, driving hot metal into the ribs of something enormous.

"Belfast, Ireland," said the compass, its voice a dry little tick-tick-tick. "The year is **1909**. That skeleton in front of you doesn't have a name yet. It's about to get a very big one."

Hana walked the length of the dry dock, counting her paces the way she measured distances on her maps at home. She ran out of ground before she ran out of ship. "This is going to be huge," she said. "Bigger than anything."

A shipwright wiping grease from his hands overheard her and grinned. "Smart girl. This is the **Harland and Wolff** shipyard, and we're building for the **White Star Line**. Today we laid her keel — that's the long backbone at the very bottom that the whole ship gets built around. **March 31st, 1909.**"

"So the keel is like... the spine," Hana said, "and everything else hangs off it, like roads hang off a river on a map."

The shipwright laughed so hard he had to sit down on a crate. "Never heard it put that way, but you're not wrong, miss."

The compass warmed against Hana's palm, pleased with her, the way a dog is pleased when you throw the right stick.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Four Funnels, Three Real
chapters.text:
Two years slid by in a blink of blue light, and when the ink-fog cleared, Hana was gripping a rail above a crowd that stretched farther than she could map in her head.

"**May 31st, 1911**," the compass ticked. "Launch day."

Someone cut a rope. The great hull — still just a hull, no decks or funnels yet, dark and slick with grease to help her slide — began to move. Then she hit the water with a SPLOOOOSH that soaked the front three rows of spectators, and the whole crowd roared.

"She's not finished," Hana said, surprised. "Where are the rest of her insides?"

"They build the outside first, then finish her afloat," said the compass. "Come back in a year."

It did that thing again, where a year disappeared like a page turning, and now Hana stood on a finished deck under four enormous funnels, black smoke pouring from three of them into a gray sky.

Hana counted. Then she counted again. "That fourth one isn't smoking."

"Correct," said the compass, sounding almost proud of her. "**Only three of her four funnels carried real smoke.** The fourth was mostly there to look grand and keep her balanced to the eye."

"They built a whole fake smokestack because it looked better?"

"People have built stranger things for looks," said the compass. "At about **882 feet long**, she was the largest ship in the world — and she had two sister ships, **Olympic** and **Britannic**, built from almost the same plans. You could say she was the middle child."

Hana grinned, thinking of her own little brother, who also insisted on being taller than he actually was. "What's her name?"

The compass's needle finally settled, for just a second, on one word etched into the bow in gold letters.

"**Titanic**," it said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Sixteen Rooms That Don't Talk to Each Other
chapters.text:
The ink-fog swirled again, and this time it dropped Hana onto a gangway crowded with trunks, hatboxes, and a brass band somewhere playing something cheerful.

"**April 10th, 1912**," said the compass. "Southampton, England. She's leaving for New York City. First voyage. Everyone's favorite kind of nervous."

Hana loved this part — the part where a map stops being lines on paper and becomes an actual plan somebody is about to follow. She found a posted diagram of the ship's insides near the gangway and traced it with her finger the way she traced coastlines at home.

"There are walls down here that don't look like normal walls," she said, pointing at thick lines running crosswise through the lower decks.

"**Watertight compartments**," said the compass. "Sixteen of them. Picture the inside of the ship cut into sixteen separate boxes, each with doors that can seal shut. Flood one box, and in theory the rest stay dry and she keeps floating."

Hana counted the boxes on the diagram, the same careful way she counted countries on a map she hadn't memorized yet. "Sixteen," she confirmed. "That's why everyone's calling her —"

"—**nearly unsinkable**," the compass finished. "That word *nearly* is doing a lot of work in that sentence."

Hana looked up sharply. "What do you mean, *nearly*?"

The compass's glow flickered, almost like a shrug. "Sixteen strong rooms is a very good number. It is not an infinite number. Hold that thought."

Hana held it. She didn't love how it felt in her hands.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Night the Sea Went Flat
chapters.text:
Four days later — though for Hana it was the space between one blink and the next — the air turned sharp and cold, and the ocean outside the rail had gone strangely still, like a map with no waves drawn on it at all.

"Something's wrong," Hana said. "It's too quiet."

"**Eleven forty at night, April 14th, 1912**," said the compass, quieter than usual. "Keep watching."

Far ahead, something pale rose out of the dark — not a cloud, not a wave. A shape taller than the deck rail, drifting silent as a held breath.

"Iceberg," Hana breathed.

A bell rang three times somewhere above. The ship shuddered, one long scrape Hana felt through the soles of her shoes more than heard, and then — nothing. No crash, no alarm, no shouting. Just the engines going quiet, one by one, like a held note finally ending.

"That's it?" Hana asked. "That's the whole collision?"

"That's the whole collision," said the compass. "No drama you can see from here. The real trouble is happening below the waterline, where five of those sixteen rooms we talked about are filling up with water nobody invited."

"Five," Hana repeated. "You said sixteen could flood and —"

"I said she could take some flooding and keep floating. Five was more than *some*." The compass's tone stayed level, almost gentle. "Nobody on deck is panicking yet, Hana. Right now, it just looks like a very large, very calm ship, standing still under the stars."

Hana let out a breath she hadn't realized she'd been holding. Calm. For now, calm was true, and she decided to believe it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Dots, Dashes, and a Very Old Song
chapters.text:
Below deck, a small room clattered with a sound like hail on a tin roof — dots and dashes, fast and urgent, tapped out by two men hunched over a glowing dial.

"That's **Morse code**," the compass said. "A message made of short beeps and long beeps instead of letters. Those two are **Jack Phillips** and **Harold Bride**, and they're using the **wireless** — a radio, basically, except in 1912 the word *wireless* still sounded like magic."

Hana leaned toward the dial, picking out a pattern she half recognized from an old scouting badge. "Dash-dot-dash-dot, dash-dash-dot-dash... that's C-Q-D, isn't it? Then... S-O-S?"

The compass actually sounded impressed. "Good ear. **CQD** was the old distress call. **SOS** was the brand-new one, simpler to send and simpler to hear. That night, Phillips and Bride sent out both, just to be sure every ship listening would understand."

"Belt and suspenders," Hana said, quoting her dad.

Up on the boat deck, faint over the clatter, came music — a violin, then more instruments joining in, steady and almost cheerful, as people climbed into lifeboats in the cold.

"Legend says the ship's band, led by a man named **Wallace Hartley**, kept playing right through all of this," said the compass. "Survivors really did report hearing music. Nobody's completely sure which songs, or for how long — that part's gotten polished up over a hundred years of retelling. But the music itself seems to be true, and it must have helped, a little, to have something ordinary playing while everything else turned strange."

Hana listened to the thin, brave little tune drifting up through the cold and found she believed every note of it, polished or not.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Not Enough Boats, Just Enough People
chapters.text:
On deck, ropes creaked as wooden lifeboats swung out over black water, lowering a few dozen people at a time while a thousand more still waited.

Hana did what she always did with a map she didn't like the shape of: she counted. Boat after boat, person after person, the same math turning uglier each time. "There aren't enough," she said. "Not even close."

"You're right," said the compass, no softening it. "The lifeboats on board had room for about **1,178 people** — nowhere near everyone aboard that night. It's one of the plainest lessons this whole voyage has to teach."

A woman in a fur-trimmed coat elbowed her way to an oar in one half-loaded boat, ignoring the sailor who tried to take it from her. "I can row as well as any man here," she announced, and started rowing.

"**Margaret Brown**," the compass said. "Everyone will end up calling her 'the Unsinkable Molly Brown' after tonight, and she will have earned every letter of it."

Hana grinned, already planning to steal that nickname for herself someday.

In the boat ahead, a woman settled two trembling, fluffy shapes under her coat before anyone could stop her.

"Pomeranians," the compass explained, before Hana could ask. "Small dogs. A couple of passengers tucked their pets right in with them, and nobody had the heart to argue. Not every small thing aboard that night was lost."

Hana reached down and scratched the glass over the compass's face, the closest thing it had to a head. "You'd have smuggled yourself into a lifeboat too, wouldn't you."

"I prefer to think I'd have been useful," said the compass. "A compass is exactly what a lifeboat needs."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Lights That Finally Came
chapters.text:
By the time the sky began to pale into gray, Titanic herself was gone from the water — she had gone down at about **2:20 in the morning**, not even three hours after that first quiet scrape against the ice.

"**Captain Edward John Smith** stayed aboard until the very end," the compass said simply. "He'd commanded ships for the White Star Line for years. That night, he chose not to leave."

Hana didn't ask any more questions about that part. Some facts don't need picking apart; they just need a moment of quiet, and she gave it one.

What she did instead was scan the horizon the way she scanned a map for a town she knew had to be there somewhere. "There," she said, pointing at a single light, steady where everything else was only gray water and gray sky.

"**Carpathia**," the compass confirmed, ticking faster now, almost excited. "She picked up the distress call and turned around, running flat out through an ice field in the dark to get here. By morning, she'd pulled every lifeboat's survivors up out of the cold."

From the lifeboats, a thin, ragged cheer went up — tired people finding just enough breath left to be glad.

Hana watched the little boats row toward that one steady light, and thought that if she ever drew a map of this night, that single dot of light would be the only thing she'd bother marking.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Finding Her Again
chapters.text:
The ink-fog swirled one last time, and Hana half expected the cold deck again. Instead she landed somewhere entirely different: a dim room full of screens, grainy footage crawling across every one of them, pale shapes drifting through water so dark it looked like ink itself.

"**September 1st, 1985**," said the compass. "An explorer named **Robert Ballard** finally found her, sitting on the seafloor about **12,500 feet** down — that's deeper than four Empire State Buildings stacked on top of each other."

Hana leaned toward a screen showing a long, dark shape split cleanly into two pieces. She pulled out her own folded map of the Atlantic from her pocket — she always kept one somewhere — and matched the coordinates scrolling past against the blank ocean near Newfoundland, Canada.

"Here," she said, tapping the spot. "About **370 miles** off the coast. That's where she's been this whole time."

"Exactly there," the compass agreed. "You'd have made a fine member of Ballard's crew."

"What happened after they found her? After all of it, I mean."

"People finally fixed what needed fixing," said the compass. "A new rule called **SOLAS** said every ship had to carry enough lifeboats for everyone aboard, no exceptions. An **Ice Patrol** started watching the North Atlantic for icebergs, so no other ship would be surprised the way she was. A museum shaped like a ship's bow opened in Belfast in **2012**, right on the old shipyard site. A film came out in **1997** that practically everyone on Earth has now seen. And plates, shoes, all sorts of ordinary little things pulled up from the wreck sit behind glass in museums, so people never quite forget."

The ink-fog rose one final time, soft as a held breath, and set Hana down gently back on her own bedroom floor, maps still spread around her, lamp still glowing low.

The compass sat quiet in her palm, its needle finally pointing somewhere steady — not quite north, but close enough.

On her map of the North Atlantic, in pencil, a small dot now marked a spot that hadn't been there before.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow she had a whole ocean left to chart.

true_facts.text: The Titanic was built in **Belfast, Ireland**, by Harland and Wolff for the White Star Line.
Her **keel** — the ship's backbone — was laid on **March 31st, 1909**, and she was launched into the water on **May 31st, 1911**.
She left **Southampton, England**, on **April 10th, 1912**, heading for New York City on her very first voyage.
At about **882 feet long**, she was the biggest ship in the world, and she had two sister ships, Olympic and Britannic.
Of her four funnels, only **three actually let out smoke** — the fourth was mostly there to look balanced and grand.
Her hull was divided into **sixteen watertight compartments**, strong rooms that led people to call her nearly unsinkable.
At about **11:40 p.m. on April 14th, 1912**, she struck an iceberg in the icy North Atlantic.
She sank at around **2:20 a.m. on April 15th, 1912**, less than three hours after the collision.
Her radio operators sent out both the old **CQD** signal and the brand-new **SOS**, tapped out in dots and dashes.
Survivors reported hearing the ship's band keep playing music that night, though which songs exactly has always been a little fuzzy.
There was only room in the lifeboats for about **1,178 people** — far fewer than everyone aboard.
Passenger **Margaret Brown** helped row her lifeboat and earned the nickname 'the Unsinkable Molly Brown.'
The steamship **Carpathia** raced through the night and pulled survivors from their lifeboats by morning.
The wreck was finally found on **September 1st, 1985**, by explorer Robert Ballard, resting about **12,500 feet** deep off Newfoundland, Canada.

story.title: Max, Sami, and the Brick That Started Everything
story.subtitle: A journey through ninety years of clicking plastic, with one competitive brother and one extremely patient one.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Carpenter in Billund (1932)
chapters.text:
Max was three gear ratios into building a robot arm out of LEGO Technic pieces, and Sami was on the floor beside him, drawing the next version before Max had even finished the first. That was how it always went. Max built. Sami designed something better. Max got competitive about it.

"I just need a stronger elbow joint," Max muttered, digging through the bin for a longer axle. His hand closed around something that wasn't an axle at all — a single old brick, gray and scratched, way heavier than plastic should be.

"Where'd that come from?" Sami asked, looking up from her sketchbook.

Neither of them knew. But when Max pressed it against one of Sami's bricks, just to see if it would even click, the brick went warm, then hot, then it lit up amber from the inside, like a tiny lightbulb had switched on under the studs — the little round bumps on top.

**WHOOOSH.**

The bedroom folded away like a page turning. When it unfolded again, Max and Sami were standing in a small wooden workshop that smelled like fresh-cut pine, sawdust drifting in a shaft of sunlight.

A man in a carpenter's apron looked up from a half-finished stepladder, not even surprised. "You're earlier than most," he said. "I'm Ole Kirk Christiansen. Welcome to Billund."

"Billund... Denmark?" Sami said. She'd seen the word on the bottom of a LEGO box.

"The very one," Ole Kirk said. "**1932.** I make wooden toys here. Ducks, mostly. And stepladders, because wooden ducks don't pay all the bills."

Max picked up a little wooden duck from the workbench and turned it over, checking the joints like he checked his Technic builds. "No wheels. No gears. Just... wood?"

"Just wood," Ole Kirk agreed. "For now."

Sami noticed he said *for now* like a man already thinking about his next idea. She liked that. It was the same look she got right before a drawing turned into something completely different from what she'd planned.

The brick in Max's pocket gave a small, impatient pulse of warmth, like it was saying: *keep going.*

"There's more, isn't there," Max said. It wasn't really a question.

Ole Kirk smiled and went back to his stepladder. "Oh, there's a lot more."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Play Well (1934)
chapters.text:
The workshop was the same, but the sign over the door was new — somebody had just finished painting it, and the paint still looked wet.

**LEGO**.

"That's a weird word," Sami said, head tilted, already imagining how she'd draw the letters bigger, bolder, with little bricks for serifs.

Ole Kirk clearly loved that question. "**1934.** I squashed together two Danish words — *leg godt*. It means **'play well.'**"

Max said it out loud a few times, the way you test a part before you trust it. "Leg-oh. Lego. Huh. That actually works."

"There's a rumor going around," Ole Kirk added, lowering his voice like he was sharing a secret, even though he was clearly enjoying this part, "that in Latin, an old language people used to use for serious things, *lego* means **'I put together.'** Some people think I planned that too."

"Did you?" Sami asked.

"I did not," Ole Kirk admitted, grinning. "But it's a good story, and I'm not about to correct anyone."

Max snorted. "So it's basically a happy accident."

"The best kind," Ole Kirk said.

Sami had already flipped to a blank page and was sketching the sign, the wet paint, the whole scene, the way she did whenever something felt worth keeping. Max watched her draw the letters and noticed something.

"You wrote it like it clicks together," he said. "The L locks into the E."

Sami looked down at her own drawing, surprised. She hadn't meant to do that. But now that Max said it, she couldn't unsee it, and she liked it better that way.

The brick in Max's pocket pulsed again, warmer this time, like it approved.

"Play well," Ole Kirk said again, like it was a promise he intended to keep for a very long time. "Now go on. Things are about to get a lot less wooden."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Plastic and the First Little Bricks (1947–1949)
chapters.text:
The next WHOOOSH dropped them into a workshop that buzzed and clanked, full of machines Max immediately wanted to take apart.

"**1947,**" said a voice, and this time it was a different, younger man wiping his hands on a rag — Ole Kirk's son, broad-shouldered, clearly the kind of person who liked fixing things himself. "I'm Godtfred. My father bought one of the first plastic-squirting machines in Denmark." He patted a hulking metal contraption that hissed steam. "It melts plastic and shoots it into a mold, and out comes whatever shape the mold is."

"That's basically a 3D printer's great-great-grandfather," Max said, impressed despite himself.

By **1949**, the machine was spitting out small hollow bricks with bumps on top — studs, Sami noted, just like in her drawing. Godtfred called them **Automatic Binding Bricks**, which Sami thought was a terrible name for something so good-looking.

"They don't bind anything," she said, picking one up. She pressed two together. They sat there. Unimpressed. Then she pulled, and they came apart with a soft, sad little pop.

"They're a little loose," Godtfred admitted, rubbing the back of his neck. "We're working on it."

Max, who had spent an entire weekend arguing with his robot arm's elbow joint until it finally held tight, understood the problem immediately. "You need something underneath. Not just bumps on top — something on the bottom that grabs them."

Godtfred went very still, the way people do right before a good idea lands on them. He grabbed a pencil and a scrap of paper. "Say that again."

"Something underneath," Max repeated, feeling, for one brief and extremely satisfying moment, like the smartest engineer in Denmark. "Tubes. Hollow tubes that hug the bumps on the brick below."

Godtfred stared at the sketch forming under his own pencil like he hadn't quite believed it would look that simple.

"Come back in a few years," he said. "I think you just saved me some time."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Click Heard Around the World (1958)
chapters.text:
When the brick pulsed them forward again, the workshop had grown into something closer to a real factory, and Godtfred was older, calmer, holding a single brick up to the light like a jeweler inspecting a diamond.

"**January 28th, 1958,**" he said. "Today I filed the **patent** — that's a kind of legal promise that says this design is mine, and nobody else gets to copy it without asking. Tubes underneath, studs on top. Take a look."

He flipped the brick over. Sami leaned in and gasped, delighted, because there they were — the exact tubes Max had described, hollow and round, waiting to grab the next brick's bumps.

"Try it," Godtfred said.

Max pressed two bricks together. **CLICK.** He pulled. Nothing happened. He pulled harder. Still nothing. He turned to Sami with the particular smugness of an older brother about to win an argument neither of them was having. "It holds."

"Everyone can hear that it holds, Max," Sami said, rolling her eyes, but she was grinning.

Godtfred reached into his coat pocket and pulled out something small and gray. He set it on the table next to a shiny new one, fresh off the machine.

"Try this one too," he said.

Max clicked the old scratched brick — the very same kind of brick that had started this whole adventure — onto the brand-new one. It locked in exactly the same way, snug and certain, like no time had passed between them at all.

"That old brick in your pocket," Godtfred said, nodding at the one Max had carried through three different years, "was made the same year as this one. And it still fits a brick made decades later, because the design barely changed. A **1958** brick clicks into a brick made this morning."

Sami looked down at the two bricks locked together and thought about how her sketchbook had a drawing from first grade and a drawing from last week, and how different they looked, and how nothing she owned fit together across that much time except, apparently, this.

"That's kind of amazing," she said quietly.

"IT CLICKS!" Max yelled, because somebody had to say it out loud, and it might as well be him.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Fire, Plastic, and a Park Full of Bricks (1960–1968)
chapters.text:
The next landing was colder. Sami smelled smoke before she saw anything, and her stomach dropped — but Godtfred was standing calmly in front of them, arms crossed, watching the last curls of smoke drift up from a burned-out warehouse a safe distance away. Nobody was near the building. Nobody was in danger.

"**1960,**" Godtfred said. "That warehouse held every wooden toy we had left in storage. Fire got it overnight. Everyone got out fine — it was just the toys."

"That's terrible," Sami said.

"It was," Godtfred agreed. "But it also made the decision easy. We stopped making wooden toys after that and put everything into the plastic bricks instead."

Max understood that kind of thing better than he expected to. "Like when your first robot design fails and you just... start the next one better."

"Exactly like that," Godtfred said.

By **1963**, the company had switched to a tougher plastic called **ABS** — it didn't crack as easily and it kept its color instead of fading, which Sami appreciated immediately, since faded colors were the enemy of any good drawing.

Then the brick pulsed them forward one more time, into bright sunshine and the sound of hundreds of kids laughing. A model windmill built entirely out of bricks spun lazily nearby, taller than Max.

"**1968,**" Godtfred said, spreading his arms. "Welcome to the first LEGOLAND, right here in Billund, built on the same ground as my father's old workshop."

Max looked around at kids running between giant brick sculptures and felt, for once, like competing with Sami over who built the better robot arm seemed delightfully small. "You built an entire park out of this stuff."

"We built an entire park out of *your* idea," Godtfred said, pointing at him, "roughly. The tubes. Don't let it go to your head."

"Too late," Max said, and Sami laughed so hard she nearly dropped her sketchbook.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Gears, Faces, and a New Boss (1969–1979)
chapters.text:
This time the brick deposited them in a nursery full of much bigger, chunkier bricks, clearly built for much smaller hands.

"**1969,**" Godtfred explained, handing Sami a fat plastic brick she could have worn as a bracelet. "**DUPLO** — sized for toddlers, but it still clicks onto regular bricks. Nobody gets left out."

Sami immediately pictured her baby cousin building alongside her someday and decided this was the single best invention so far, which was saying something.

Then — and this was the moment Max had secretly been hoping for the entire trip — the scene shifted to a table scattered with gears, axles, and long gray beams.

"**1977,**" said a new voice. A younger designer held up a beam with holes down its length. "We call it **Technic**. Real gears. Real moving parts. Bricks that do things, not just sit there looking good."

Max picked up a beam like he was greeting an old friend. "This is... this is literally what I build with. Every weekend. This exact stuff."

"Good," the designer said. "Then you already know what to do with it."

One table over, Sami found something even better: a little yellow figure with movable arms, a round head, and a separate hat that popped right off.

"**1978,**" the designer said. "First **minifigure**. Swap the hats, swap the faces, make a thousand different people out of the same little body."

Sami swapped the hat for a different one, then a third, already redesigning the figure's whole personality with each change. "I could draw a hundred different outfits for this guy."

"People have drawn a lot more than a hundred," the designer said.

Last stop: a confident young man shaking hands with half the factory floor at once. "**1979,**" he said. "Kjeld Kirk Kristiansen. Ole Kirk's grandson. I grew up playing with these exact bricks, and now I'm running the place."

"Family business," Max said approvingly.

"The best kind," Kjeld agreed, echoing his grandfather without knowing it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Tires, Space Battles, and a Very Close Call
chapters.text:
The brick's next jump skipped forward fast, like flipping through years instead of walking through them.

"Quick fact before we move on," Kjeld said, catching them mid-WHOOOSH. "Because the company makes so many tiny rubber tires for sets, some people say LEGO is one of the biggest tire makers in the world — just counting how many tires, not how big they are. We're not out there making truck tires. Just a lot of very, very small ones."

"That might be a slight exaggeration," Sami said, "but I love it anyway."

"**1999,**" Kjeld continued, as shelves around them filled with tiny spaceships and figures Max actually recognized. "First LEGO Star Wars sets. People went a little crazy for those."

Around the year 2000, a glowing newspaper headline floated past calling the LEGO brick a **Toy of the Century** — which Max thought was a fairly big claim for something that started as a wooden duck.

Then the mood shifted. The factory looked quieter, a little worried.

"Early 2000s," Kjeld said, more serious now. "We hit a hard time. Spent money on too many different things at once and nearly ran out. It was close."

"Did it... shut down?" Sami asked, and for a second the question hung there, genuinely uncertain.

"No," said a new man stepping forward, calm and direct. "I'm Jorgen. Became the person in charge — the **CEO** — in **2004**. We went back to basics. Focused on the bricks. It worked."

Max exhaled, surprised at how relieved he actually felt.

By **2014**, a giant screen lit up showing a movie theater packed with kids watching tiny plastic people have an enormous adventure.

"**The LEGO Movie**," Jorgen said, smiling now. "Turns out everyone still loved the bricks. They just needed reminding."

"I could've told you that," Max said, nodding at the Technic beam still in his pocket.

"Next time," Jorgen said, "call us first."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Bedroom Floor
chapters.text:
The final WHOOOSH was gentler than the rest, like the brick knew they were almost home.

Max and Sami landed back on the bedroom carpet exactly where they'd started, the half-built Technic arm still sitting between them, Sami's sketchbook still open to the page she'd been drawing on. No time had passed at all, as far as the clock on the wall was concerned.

But the old gray brick in Max's hand had gone cool and quiet now, like it was resting after a long trip.

"Headquarters is still in Billund," Sami said slowly, piecing it together out loud, the way she did when a drawing was finally coming together. "Same ground as the old workshop."

"And it's still a family thing," Max added. "Kirkbi — that's them, Ole Kirk's family — they still own most of it."

Sami looked down at the brick, then at the half-finished robot arm, then at her own sketchbook full of redesigns Max hadn't built yet.

"You know what's funny," she said. "Every single idea we saw back there started because somebody looked at a brick and thought, *this could be better.*"

Max picked up the old brick and clicked it onto the elbow joint of his robot arm, right where the weak spot had been bugging him for days. It held. Properly held, the way Godtfred's bricks had held sixty-some years ago, because apparently nothing about that part had ever really needed fixing.

"Elbow's done," Max said, testing it with a satisfied grin.

"Then draw me the next part," he added, nudging Sami's sketchbook toward her.

Sami was already uncapping her pencil.

Tomorrow, there was a shoulder joint to figure out — and, knowing the two of them, an argument about whose idea it had really been.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, there was a shoulder joint to figure out.

true_facts.text: **Ole Kirk Christiansen** started the company in **Billund, Denmark**, in **1932**, making wooden toys and stepladders.
In **1934** the company got the name **LEGO**, short for two Danish words meaning **'play well.'**
People sometimes say *lego* means **'I put together'** in an old language called Latin — fun, but probably just a coincidence, not the real reason for the name.
In **1949** the company made **Automatic Binding Bricks** — early plastic bricks with bumps on top, but they didn't hold together very well yet.
**Godtfred Kirk Christiansen** added hollow tubes underneath the bricks to grip the bumps below, and that design was officially promised as his own — a **patent** — on **January 28, 1958**.
A brick made in **1958** still clicks perfectly onto a brand new brick today, because the design has barely changed.
A **1960** fire burned up the company's leftover wooden toys, and afterward they decided to make only plastic bricks from then on.
The very first LEGOLAND theme park opened in **Billund** in **1968**, right next to the original workshop.
**LEGO Technic**, with gears and moving parts, came out in **1977**.
The very first LEGO minifigures, with swappable hats and heads, showed up in **1978**.
The first LEGO Star Wars sets came out in **1999**.
A man named **Jorgen** became the person in charge of the company in **2004** and helped it focus back on bricks after a hard, money-tight stretch.
**The LEGO Movie** came out in **2014** and showed the whole world how much people still loved the bricks.
The LEGO company's main office is still in **Billund, Denmark**, on the exact same ground where the first workshop stood.

story.title: Isla and the Stone of Vesuvius
story.subtitle: A dig kit, a grey rock, and a city buried for seventeen hundred years.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Grey Stone on the Shelf
chapters.text:
Isla was supposed to be asleep. Instead she was lying on her bedroom floor, labeling pretend pottery shards with a tiny paintbrush, the way real archaeologists do. A lamp with a cracked shade threw long shadows across her dig tray.

On her shelf sat a rock the size of a fist. Her aunt had brought it back from a trip to Italy, light as a sponge and full of little holes, like it had been frozen mid-bubble. Isla had never thought much about it. Tonight, it hummed.

She froze. The rock was buzzing, faintly, like a phone on silent. She picked it up. It was warm.

"Okay," she whispered. "That's new."

The hum got louder. The holes in the stone began to glow a dull orange, like the last coals of a fire. Isla's bedroom wall rippled like water, and through it she could see sunlight, white stone, and a street full of people in togas, shouting over each other to sell bread and fish and wine.

"Go on, then," said a voice behind her — dry, polite, faintly amused, like someone reading out loud from a letter. "You wanted a mystery. I happen to have one that's been waiting seventeen hundred years."

Isla turned. Nobody was there. Just the stone, glowing in her palm.

"Are you... in the rock?" she asked.

"I'm in the story," said the voice. "The rock is just the door. Call me your guide. Or don't call me anything — I'll still show up."

Isla, who had read every mystery book in her school library twice, was not about to say no to an actual door. She stepped through the rippling wall and the glow swallowed her whole.

She landed on warm stone, in bright sun, in the middle of a street that smelled like baking bread and horses. A cart rattled past over raised stepping-stones laid across the road, with gaps underneath just wide enough for its wheels. People walked across the tops of the stones to keep their sandals out of the mud and water running down the gutters.

"Where," Isla said carefully, "and also *when*, am I?"

"Pompeii," said the voice, now walking beside her as a tall young man in a plain white tunic, ink-stained fingers, and the look of someone who always carried a notebook. "A real town, near a city you'd call **Naples**, in what's now southern **Italy**. And the *when* is the good part. You've got a little under two thousand years to go before you were born."

Isla grinned. A real place. A real time. This was, officially, the best Tuesday night of her life — and it was turning into the best Wednesday morning in Roman history, too.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Five Villages and a Name
chapters.text:
The young man introduced himself as he walked. "Pliny," he said. "Pliny the Younger, to be exact. There's an older Pliny too — my uncle. Try to keep us straight, it matters later."

Isla filed that away the way she filed every clue. A name mentioned twice in one sentence was never an accident in a mystery book.

The street opened into a square crowded with shoppers, stray dogs, and a man shouting about olive oil prices. Isla counted doorways as they passed — bakery, bathhouse, another bakery, a shop selling little clay oil lamps.

"How many people even live here?" she asked.

"Somewhere between **eleven and fifteen thousand**,
 depending who's counting," Pliny said. "Nobody kept perfect records. But it's a real town. Shops, theaters, temples. Not a backwater."

Isla noticed something painted across a wall in faded red letters, words she couldn't read. "What does that say?"

"An advertisement," Pliny said. "And next to it, a bit of political campaigning — someone wants their friend voted into office. Walls were the internet of their day. People painted ads and slogans right on the outside of buildings for everyone to see."

Isla laughed. "So Pompeii had billboards."

"Pompeii had everything," Pliny said. "Which brings me to your first real clue. Nobody's entirely sure where the name *Pompeii* comes from. But one good guess involves an old local word, *pompe*, which might mean **'five.'** As if five small villages joined together to make one town."

Isla stopped walking. "Might. You said might twice now."

"I did," Pliny said, not even a little embarrassed. "Some of history is a fact you can hold in your hand. Some of it is a very good guess wearing a fact's coat. Part of your job tonight is telling which is which."

Isla liked that. A mystery where even the guide admitted he didn't know everything — that was more honest than most.

"Five villages," she said, testing the idea out loud. "Count the hills. Maybe I can find five of something."

Pliny's mouth twitched, almost a smile. "Now you're doing this properly."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Water, Baths, and the Big Stone Bowl
chapters.text:
They turned a corner and Isla heard it before she saw it: water, splashing steadily into a stone basin at chest height, right in the middle of the street.

"A public fountain," Pliny said. "There are dozens across town. Pompeii had a proper water system — pipes made of lead, running under the streets, feeding fountains and bathhouses and private homes that could afford the fee."

Isla dipped two fingers in. Cold, clean, and still running, nearly two thousand years before her own kitchen tap. "That's better plumbing than some old houses back home," she said.

"Rome was proud of its water," Pliny said. "Follow it, and it usually leads somewhere interesting."

It led them to a long, low building with steam curling out of a doorway. Inside, men lounged in warm pools, scraping oil off their skin with curved tools, chatting like it was any other Tuesday. "Bathhouse," Pliny explained. "Part gym, part spa, part the place you went to hear the town gossip."

Further on, the street climbed toward a huge oval building, stone seats rising in rings around a sandy floor. Isla's stomach did a small flip of recognition. "Is that—"

"An amphitheater," Pliny said. "A big open stadium for watching shows. This one went up around **70 BC**. One of the oldest of its kind that's survived anywhere. People packed in to watch gladiator contests."

Isla climbed a few stone steps and sat, imagining the roar of a crowd where now there was only wind. "How many seats?"

"Thousands," Pliny said. "Enough for most of the town, if everyone showed up at once."

Isla looked out at the oval floor, then back at the stepping-stones, the fountain, the bathhouse steam. "This isn't a sleepy little village," she said. "This is a whole working city. Shops, baths, sports, water on tap. People here had actual lives."

"That," Pliny said, "is exactly the point I was hoping you'd land on. Everyone remembers how Pompeii ended. Almost nobody stops to notice how ordinary it was right up until it wasn't."

The sentence hung there, a little heavier than the ones before it. Isla noticed. She was good at noticing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Walls Talk Back
chapters.text:
"You said 'right up until it wasn't,'" Isla said, catching up to Pliny on a narrow side street. "That's a mystery-book sentence if I ever heard one. What aren't you telling me?"

Pliny kept walking, hands behind his back. "Seventeen years before the end, in **62 AD**, the ground shook. Hard. A strong earthquake cracked walls, knocked statues flat, scared half the town into rebuilding."

"And nobody figured out why?" Isla asked.

"Nobody connected it to the mountain," Pliny said, nodding toward a dark peak rising green and calm over the rooftops. "Vesuvius hadn't erupted in living memory. People thought it was just a mountain. A good one for grapevines, actually."

Isla studied the wall beside her — more painted words, half-faded. "More ads?"

"Read it as a clue, not decoration," Pliny said. "A mix. Some advertising, some politics, some just graffiti someone scratched for fun. People here left their fingerprints everywhere, on purpose and by accident. That's a gift for anyone who shows up later wanting to understand them."

Isla crouched by a patch of plaster with faint scratches in it — a name, a joke, maybe a complaint about dinner. She couldn't read the words, but she understood the impulse. People two thousand years ago left notes on walls for the same reason she doodled in the margins of her homework: because they were there, and they wanted someone to know it.

"So the earthquake was a warning," she said slowly, "and nobody read it right."

"Warnings are only obvious afterward," Pliny said. "That's not a flaw in the Romans. That's just how warnings work."

He glanced at the mountain again, and for just a second his dry, amused voice went quiet and careful. "Keep that earthquake in your notes, though. It matters for what's coming. I promise you this part of the story doesn't dwell where it doesn't need to."

Isla nodded. She trusted him on that. Mostly because he'd already admitted, twice, when he wasn't sure of something — and a guide who admits his doubts is usually the one telling you the truth about the rest.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Letter-Writer on the Hill
chapters.text:
The stone in Isla's hand flickered, and the street dissolved into a hillside across the bay, grass underfoot, the sea glittering far below. Pliny stood beside her, older now by a heartbeat, a scroll and stylus in hand instead of a lounging stroll.

"This is where I actually was," he said. "Watching from across the water, on **August 24th, in the year 79**, when the mountain let go."

Isla looked toward Vesuvius. A column of ash rose from its top like a tree made of smoke, spreading flat at the crown, climbing impossibly high into the blue sky.

"I wrote two letters about it afterward," Pliny said. "Described it carefully — the shape of the cloud, the ash falling like snow, the ground trembling. I was trying to get every detail right, the way a careful witness should. Scientists still use my description today. They even named a whole kind of eruption after it — a **Plinian eruption** — any time a volcano blasts ash that high, that fast."

Isla stared at the cloud, caught somewhere between awed and unsettled. "Were you scared?"

"A little," Pliny admitted. "My uncle wasn't, though. He commanded ships nearby, and when word came that people needed rescuing, he sailed *toward* the mountain instead of away from it, to help bring people to safety by boat. That's the kind of brave I'd like to be, if I'm honest."

Isla watched the ash column a moment longer. "Is this the scary part?" she asked, direct, the way she liked mysteries to be direct with her.

"It's the serious part," Pliny said. "Many people did not get away in time, and that's simply true. But plenty did. My uncle's ships carried people to safer shores that same day. We're not going to sit here and watch the worst of it — that's not what this stone is for. We're going to go see what it left behind. That's where your kind of mystery actually lives."

Isla nodded, grateful, and let the stone pull them forward through the ash cloud — not into the moment itself, but past it, the way you'd skip the saddest page of a book to find out how the story turned out.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: What the Ash Kept Safe
chapters.text:
They landed in quiet. No carts, no shouting, no splashing fountains — just still air and soft grey ground, crunching faintly underfoot like old snow.

"The eruption buried the whole town," Pliny said, "under as much as **four to six meters of ash and rock** — that's roughly as deep as a two-story house. It happened fast enough to seal the place like a jar."

Isla crouched and brushed ash off something pale. A loaf of bread, round and scored into eight wedges, sitting exactly where a baker had left it in an oven nearly two thousand years ago. "It's still got the baker's mark on it," she whispered.

"Baked, scored, and never eaten," Pliny said. "Preserved mid-bake. The ash fell so thick and so fast it froze ordinary moments exactly as they were — bread in ovens, paintings on walls, jokes scratched into plaster. A town interrupted, not erased."

Further along, inside a grand house with painted columns, Isla found a wall of figures in deep red, dancing, holding strange ritual objects she didn't recognize. "What is this place?"

"They call it the **Villa of the Mysteries**," Pliny said, and Isla's whole face lit up at the word. "These wall paintings — **frescoes**, made by painting straight onto wet plaster so the color sinks in and lasts — show some kind of ceremony. Nobody today is entirely certain what it means. It's one of archaeology's genuine open questions."

"A mystery nobody's solved," Isla said, delighted. "That's basically the best kind."

She traced the edge of a painted figure's robe, still vivid red after all this time, and thought about how strange it was that a disaster could also be the reason something survived. The ash that buried Pompeii in silence had also locked its secrets in a box nobody could open — until somebody eventually would.

"Who found it, in the end?" Isla asked. "Who opens the box?"

Pliny's eyes glinted. "Patience. That's a later chapter. Right now, there's a second buried town you should see first — smaller, by the sea, and preserved in an even stranger way."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Town Next Door
chapters.text:
The stone carried them along the coast to a quieter town, tucked close to the water, with houses that still had their rooftops.

"**Herculaneum**," Pliny said. "Smaller than Pompeii, and caught by the same eruption — but buried under a different kind of volcanic material, more like a thick, fast-moving flow instead of falling ash."

Isla stepped inside a doorway and stopped. The wood was still there. An actual wooden bed frame, a shutter on its hinges, even a wooden screen, dark and brittle but unmistakably furniture, not dust.

"Pompeii kept bread and paintings," she said slowly. "Herculaneum kept... wood?"

"And scrolls," Pliny said. "Rolled-up books made of a material like paper, charred black on the outside, but with the writing still trapped inside, layer after layer. People are still working out clever ways to read them without unrolling them, since unrolling would crumble them to nothing."

Isla turned slowly in the little room, taking it in — a house, basically untouched, just... paused. "It's like two different photographs of the same terrible day," she said. "One town got ash. The other got something else. And together they show you different pieces of the same story."

"That's precisely it," Pliny said, sounding genuinely pleased, like a teacher whose best student had just shown their work. "Disasters aren't tidy. They don't preserve everything the same way. Which is exactly why archaeologists need both towns, not just one."

Isla ran a hand along the edge of the wooden shutter, careful not to press too hard. It felt impossibly fragile and impossibly real at the same time, like touching a held breath.

"Okay," she said. "Now I really want to know who found all this. Somebody had to be the one who looked at a buried wall and went, wait a second."

Pliny smiled, properly this time. "Finally," he said. "The part where someone does the finding."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Found Again
chapters.text:
The stone's glow shifted, warmer now, and the scene around them changed to workers in old-fashioned clothes, digging carefully with shovels and brushes in a dusty field.

"**1748**," Pliny said. "Workers digging in this area struck old walls and strange objects underground. Word got around. People realized there was an entire ancient town sitting quietly beneath the dirt, waiting."

"After how long?" Isla asked, though she could already do the math.

"Nearly **seventeen hundred years**," Pliny said. "Forgotten, then found again."

Isla watched the diggers work, slow and careful, brushing dust from a curved shape that might have been a jar, might have been a roof tile. It looked exactly like her own dig tray at home, just scaled up to the size of a city. "That's basically what I do with my pretend shards," she said. "Except real. And huge."

"It's still going," Pliny said. "Only about **two-thirds of Pompeii** has ever been properly dug up. The rest is still under there, waiting its turn. People find new frescoes, new rooms, new surprises most years."

"So it's an unfinished mystery," Isla said. "Still open."

"In **1997**, the whole site was named a place the world agreed to protect and care for forever — a list for the planet's most important places," Pliny said. "Millions of people visit every year now, to walk the same stepping-stones you walked tonight."

"And the mountain?" Isla asked, looking one last time at Vesuvius, calm and green against the sky.

"Still there. Still active," Pliny said. "Scientists watch it closely today, because a great many people live nearby now. Nobody's taking their eyes off it again."

The stone pulsed warm in Isla's palm, and the hillside folded away like a page turning. She landed back on her bedroom carpet, dig tray still scattered beside her, lamp still humming its ordinary electric hum.

She looked down. On top of her plastic pottery shards sat one new thing: a small, curled scrap of blackened material, thin as old paper, with the faintest ghost of writing pressed into it.

A message, it seemed, from a town that had never quite finished telling its story.

Isla picked it up carefully, the way you'd hold something that had waited seventeen hundred years to be noticed, and set it beside the grey stone on her shelf. Two mysteries now, side by side, both patiently unfinished.

Tomorrow, she had some reading to do.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, she had some reading to do.

true_facts.text: **Pompeii** was a real Roman town near the modern city of **Naples**, in what's now southern **Italy**.
On **August 24th, in the year 79**, the mountain **Vesuvius** erupted and buried the town.
Before that, Pompeii was a busy place with somewhere between **eleven and fifteen thousand** people, shops, baths, and theaters.
The ash and rock piled up **four to six meters deep** — about as tall as a two-story house.

A young Roman named **Pliny the Younger** watched the eruption from across the bay and wrote careful letters describing it, which is why this kind of fast, tall eruption is now called a **Plinian eruption**.
The eruption happened so fast it froze ordinary moments in place — like bread left baking in an oven.
Pompeii was mostly forgotten until **1748**, when workers digging there struck old walls and realized a whole buried town was underneath.
A nearby smaller town called **Herculaneum** was buried too, but by a different kind of volcanic material that preserved wooden furniture and even rolled-up scrolls.
A house called the **Villa of the Mysteries** has colorful paintings, made straight onto wet plaster, showing a ceremony nobody today fully understands.
Pompeii had a real water system, with pipes carrying water to public fountains all over town.
The town's big stone **amphitheater**, built around **70 BC**, is one of the oldest of its kind still standing, and was used for gladiator shows.
Archaeologists found an actual loaf of bread, still marked by its baker, preserved inside a Pompeii oven.
Pompeii's streets had raised stepping-stones so people could cross without getting their feet wet, with gaps for cart wheels to pass through.
Vesuvius is still an active volcano today, and scientists keep a close watch on it because so many people live nearby now.

story.title: Theo and the Terrible Lizard Level
story.subtitle: Player One boots up the oldest game ever made.

chapters.heading: Level 1: Spawn Point of Everything (230 Million Years Ago)
chapters.text:
Theo's bedroom floor was covered in sticky notes, each one a half-built level for his new Roblox game. Midnight had come and gone twice.

It had been exactly one week since the words THE NEXT LEVEL IS YOURS TO BUILD faded off his screen, and he still hadn't built it. He was stuck on what to make next.

His laptop flickered green and black, the way it did right before something good happened.

**BZZZT.**

A square green guy popped up, pixelated edges jittering. "Player One," squeaked Bit. "Miss me?"

"Bit!" Theo sat up so fast he knocked over a cup of pencils. "Where've you been?"

"Loading your next level," Bit said. "You wanted something bigger than Roblox Studio could hold. So tonight — dinosaurs."

The screen swallowed the room whole. Theo's chair, his rug, his soccer trophy — all of it dissolved into green code, and when it rebuilt itself, he was standing on cracked red dirt under a bruise-colored sky. A loading bar blinked in the corner of his vision: LEVEL 1 — SPAWN POINT OF EVERYTHING.

"Where are we?" Theo asked. "This looks like nowhere."

"**Two hundred thirty million years** back," Bit said. "This is when the **first dinosaurs** showed up — the very first players to ever join this server."

Theo turned in a slow circle. No grass, no trees. Just ferns, and something small scuttling between two rocks, barely bigger than a cat.

"That's a dinosaur?" Theo said. "It's tiny. I built scarier mobs in my last map."

"Everybody starts at level one," Bit said. "Even dinosaurs."

A golden coin blinked into existence at Theo's feet, spinning slowly. He picked it up — warm, heavier than it looked.

"One coin per level you clear," Bit reminded him. "Same rules as always."

Theo turned it over. "Okay. So who named these guys 'dinosaurs'? Sounds like a boss-fight title."

"Good question. A scientist named **Richard Owen** came up with it in **1842**," Bit said. "It's Greek. It means 'terrible lizard.'"

"Terrible like scary, or terrible like my free throws?"

"Scary," Bit said. "Mostly. Some of them were about the size of a chicken, but don't tell them that."

Theo laughed and pocketed the coin. "Okay. Terrible Lizard Simulator. I'm in. What's level two?"

The ground rumbled under his sneakers — not an earthquake, just a save point loading.

"Follow the cliffs," Bit said. "There's someone I want you to meet. She found more dinosaur bones than almost anyone who ever lived — and she was younger than you when she started."

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Girl Who Found Monsters (Lyme Regis)
chapters.text:
The cliffs were gray and crumbly, and the ocean smacked into them in roaring, repeating waves.

On the beach below, a girl in a long coat chipped at a rock with a small hammer, like she was debugging a dragon.

"Watch this," Bit said. "She's about to find something huge."

"Who is she?"

"**Mary Anning**. Born **1799**, right here in **Lyme Regis**, England. She hunted for fossils on this beach her whole life."

"Fossils," Theo repeated. "Like old bones turned to rock?"

"Exactly that," Bit said. "An animal dies, gets buried fast, and over thousands of years minerals swap in for the bone, bit by bit, until the whole thing turns to stone. Like a save file copying itself over, except it takes forever."

Theo crouched next to the girl, careful not to step on anything. "What are you looking for?"

Mary didn't look up. "Sea monsters," she said simply. "There's one in this rock. I can feel it."

Theo squinted at the gray stone. To him it looked like every other rock on the beach. "How do you even know where to dig?"

"You learn the shapes," she said. "A curve here means a rib. A bump there means a tooth."

Theo picked up a loose rock nearby and turned it over, copying her. He found a groove in it, a thin curling line like a spiral.

"Is this one?" he asked.

Mary took it from him, turned it in the light, and smiled. "That's a good eye for a boy who just arrived."

"I build maps," Theo said. "You learn to spot the glitch before it happens."

"Same thing," Mary said, "just with rocks instead of code."

She went back to her hammer, and a few taps later the stone split clean in half, revealing the curved shape of a long-necked sea reptile pressed into it like a stamp.

"WHOA," Theo said.

A second golden coin appeared, spinning next to the first in his pocket like it had been waiting for the reveal.

"She found some of the most important sea-reptile bones anyone ever dug up," Bit said, "and she wasn't even a grown-up when she started."

Theo looked back at the beach, at hundreds of plain gray rocks stretching in every direction. "How did nobody notice before her?"

"Nobody else was looking that close," Bit said. "You have to want to find it."

chapters.heading: Level 3: The First Name on the Leaderboard (1824)
chapters.text:
The level reloaded into a stone room stacked with bones, like a storage chest nobody had sorted in years.

A man in a long coat muttered over a huge jawbone on a table, turning it this way and that.

"Who's the NPC?" Theo whispered.

"Not an NPC. **William Buckland**," Bit said. "In **1824**, he gave the very first dinosaur an official name — **Megalosaurus**. Before him nobody had a word for any of this."

"So this is like the first entry in the dinosaur database," Theo said.

"Basically," Bit said. "People who study old bones for a living are called **paleontologists** — scientists who dig up fossils to figure out how these animals moved, ate, and lived."

Theo walked around the table, eyeing the giant jawbone, the size of a skateboard.

"That tooth is huge," Theo said. "What did it eat — buildings?"

Buckland looked up, startled, like he hadn't noticed a kid standing there the whole time. "Lizards don't normally grow teeth like this," he muttered. "This creature must have been enormous."

"How big?" Theo asked.

"I don't fully know yet," Buckland admitted. "That is rather the problem."

Theo looked at the scattered bones on the table — some stacked in the wrong order, like somebody had dropped their inventory. "You've got these backwards," he said, pointing. "That piece goes at the back, not the front. It curves the same way as the other one."

Buckland frowned, picked up the bone, and turned it over. He went quiet for a second. Then he slotted it into place at the back of the row.

"...Yes," Buckland said slowly. "Yes, that's better."

"Called it," Theo said.

A third coin blinked into his pocket.

"First dinosaur name in history," Bit said, "and you helped sort the bones that proved it was real. Not bad for a Tuesday."

"It's not even a school night anymore," Theo pointed out. "It's whatever this is."

"Fair."

chapters.heading: Level 4: Boss Design Review (Horns and Spikes)
chapters.text:
The level dropped him into tall ferns, warm air, bugs the size of his hand buzzing past his ear.

Something enormous shifted in the brush. Theo froze.

A dinosaur the size of a pickup truck stepped out, three horns pointed forward, a wide bony shield curving up behind its head.

"That's a—" Theo started.

"**Triceratops**," Bit said. "Three horns on its face, a big bony **frill** — that shield-shaped plate — to protect its neck."

"It's basically a tank unit," Theo said. "Max armor, low speed."

"Pretty much."

The triceratops gave them one long look, decided they weren't worth the trouble, and went back to chewing a fern.

Further down the path, something else caught Theo's eye — a dinosaur with square bony plates running up its back like a row of shark fins, and a spiked tail swinging slowly side to side.

"Okay, that tail," Theo said. "That's a weapon."

"That's a **Stegosaurus**," Bit said. "And those spikes on the tail even have their own name. People call it a **thagomizer**."

Theo snorted. "A what?"

"**Thagomizer**," Bit repeated. "Somebody thought that was funny enough to actually make official."

"That's the best boss name I've ever heard," Theo said. "I'm renaming my game's final boss attack right now. Thagomizer Smash."

"Patch notes incoming," Bit said.

The stegosaurus swung its tail once, slow and lazy, like it was stretching rather than attacking, and a low THWUMP echoed through the ferns as it caught a low branch instead of anything living.

Theo laughed. "Friendly fire."

A fourth coin appeared. Theo was starting to recognize the little jingle it made, like a level-up sound.

"Two dinosaurs built like walking tanks," Bit said. "Not every dinosaur needed sharp teeth to stay safe."

"Defense build instead of damage build," Theo said. "Respect."

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Biggest Save File (South Dakota, 1990)
chapters.text:
Dust blew across cracked orange rock, hot enough Theo could feel it through his sneakers.

A huge skull lay half-buried in the ground, teeth longer than Theo's whole hand.

"Those teeth are insane," Theo said, crouching to look closer without touching.

"**Tyrannosaurus rex**," Bit said. "Its teeth got up to **thirty centimeters** long — about twelve inches, root and all. Longer than a ruler."

"That's not a tooth, that's a dagger," Theo said.

"This exact skeleton has a nickname," Bit said. "People call it **Sue**. Found right here in **South Dakota**, in **1990**. One of the biggest, most complete T. rex skeletons anyone's ever dug up."

Theo walked the length of the skeleton, counting bones like he was checking a model for broken parts. "This whole thing was buried out here for how long?"

"Sixty-six million years, give or take," Bit said.

"And somebody just found it. Walking around."

"That's the job," Bit said. "You walk, you look down, and sometimes the ground hands you a T. rex."

"There's actually a story some people tell," Bit went on, "about a farmer's dog digging up part of a famous dinosaur bone, back before anyone knew what it was. Nobody can really prove that one happened — it's probably gotten bigger with every retelling — but it's a fun way to remember that huge finds sometimes start by total accident."

Theo grinned. "A dog found a dinosaur. That's the best glitch story I've ever heard."

"Allegedly," Bit said.

Theo crouched by one massive tooth, close but not touching, and did the math out loud. "If this tooth is a foot long, and my soccer cleat is like ten inches, this thing's whole head is bigger than my body."

"Give or take an arm," Bit said. "Speaking of arms — T. rex had tiny ones. Don't ask it to high-five."

Theo laughed so hard he nearly sat down in the dust. "That's so unfair. All that and you can't even reach your own face."

A fifth coin appeared, warm against his palm.

"Biggest bite in the game," Bit said, "and the shortest arms. Balance patch, dinosaur edition."

chapters.heading: Level 6: The Glitch in the Movies
chapters.text:
The level shifted to a forest floor covered in soft fallen leaves, and something rustled low in the undergrowth — too low, too small, to be scary.

Theo braced anyway, remembering every movie he'd seen. "Okay. Velociraptor. I know this one. These things are terrifying—"

A turkey-sized animal strutted out of the bushes, covered head to tail in feathers, chirping at a bug.

Theo blinked. "...That's not what I pictured."

"Movies lie," Bit said cheerfully. "Real **Velociraptor** was about the size of a **turkey**. And yes — **feathers**. Lots of dinosaurs had them, Velociraptor included."

"So the movie version is basically a mod," Theo said. "Someone reskinned it to look way scarier."

"A very popular mod," Bit agreed. "But the real one couldn't open a door if it tried."

Something glided overhead between two tree trunks — not flying exactly, more like jumping and catching air, four little wings spread wide like a kite made of feathers.

"Whoa, what is THAT," Theo said, ducking on instinct.

"**Microraptor**," Bit said. "Four wings instead of two. It couldn't fly like a bird — more like it glided, tree to tree."

Theo watched it land clumsily on a low branch and immediately start preening its feathers, like it was embarrassed about the landing. "That's basically wallhacking through a level," Theo said. "No flap, just glide straight from spawn to spawn."

"Exactly."

Theo crept closer to the little raptor on the ground, careful to keep his hands to himself, just watching the way its feathered head tilted at every sound.

"It's kind of cute," Theo admitted. "I really thought these things were going to try to eat me."

"Some of the bigger hunting dinosaurs might have," Bit said. "This one just wants that bug."

The raptor snapped up the bug and trotted off, satisfied, and a sixth coin blinked into Theo's hand.

"Most surprising reskin in dinosaur history," Bit said. "Turkey-sized and feathery, the whole time."

"I'm never trusting a movie poster again," Theo said.

chapters.heading: Level 7: Not Everyone Here Is a Dinosaur
chapters.text:
The ground dropped away into cliffs over a bright blue sea, and something huge swooped low overhead, wide leathery wings blotting out the sun for a second.

Theo ducked, then looked up, amazed. "Okay THAT'S a dinosaur, right? Please tell me that's a dinosaur."

"Nope," Bit said. "That's a **pterosaur** — a flying reptile. Related to dinosaurs, cousins almost, but not technically one of them."

"That seems like a technicality," Theo said. "It's huge and it flies. Feels pretty dinosaur to me."

"Game rules are game rules," Bit said. "Ask the judges, not me."

Out past the waves, something long-necked surfaced, paddled in a slow circle, and dove again.

"That one too?" Theo guessed. "Also not a dinosaur?"

"**Plesiosaur**," Bit confirmed. "There's another ocean reptile called a **mosasaur** out there too. Both lived at the same time as dinosaurs. Neither one counts as one. Dinosaurs were land animals — these guys never joined that server."

"So it's like the ocean biome and the land biome are different game modes," Theo said. "Same world, different rules."

"That's actually a really good way to put it," Bit said.

Something massive thrashed in the shallows near the shore — a dinosaur with a huge sail-like fin on its back, hunting half in and half out of the water.

"**Spinosaurus**," Bit said. "Might be the biggest meat-eating dinosaur ever found — maybe even longer than T. rex. Looks like it spent real time swimming, too."

"It's got a whole water level built in," Theo said. "That's unfair design. Give the other dinosaurs a chance."

Far off across the plain behind them, something so long it barely fit on the horizon moved slowly between the trees, its neck stretching higher than any building Theo had ever stood next to.

"And that," Bit said, "might be **Argentinosaurus** — maybe the biggest dinosaur of them all. Estimates put it at over a hundred feet long."

Theo tried to count the length in soccer fields and lost track around three. "That's not an animal, that's a stadium."

A seventh coin appeared, and Theo pocketed it without looking away from the horizon, still watching the impossible shape of it move.

"Biggest flyer, biggest swimmer, biggest everything," Bit said. "Not all of them dinosaurs. All of them real."

chapters.heading: Level 8: The Save Points Nobody Meant to Leave
chapters.text:
The ground here was cracked and pale, baked hard by old sun, and Theo's sneaker landed square in a dip in the dirt shaped exactly like a giant foot.

"Whoa — footprint!" he said, crouching to measure it against his own shoe. His whole foot fit inside one toe.

"**Trace fossil**," Bit said. "A footprint left in soft mud that hardened into rock over time, instead of the bone turning to rock. Places like **Texas** and **China** have whole trails of them."

"So it's basically a replay file," Theo said. "No actual dinosaur here, just a recording of where it walked."

"Exactly that."

Further along, a cluster of round shapes sat half-buried in a shallow dip in the ground, arranged in a neat circle, like someone had carefully set up a checkpoint.

"Eggs?" Theo guessed.

"A nest," Bit said. "This kind of dinosaur was called **Maiasaura**. Scientists found whole nesting sites like this one in **Montana** — proof that some dinosaur parents stuck around and took care of their babies, instead of walking off."

Theo looked at the ring of eggs, careful not to get too close in case a parent was watching. "That's actually kind of sweet. I figured they'd all just be out for themselves."

"Not this one," Bit said. "Good parent, as far as dinosaurs go."

"And where's the best place to find all this stuff?" Theo asked. "Like, if I wanted a hundred of these in one map."

"The **Gobi Desert**," Bit said, "in Mongolia and China. One of the richest fossil spots on the planet. Paleontologists still dig there every year."

"Add it to the map," Theo said, already imagining the level. "Egg nest checkpoint, footprint trail, loot everywhere."

An eighth coin appeared, and this time Theo caught it out of the air without looking, like he'd done it a hundred times already.

"You're getting good at this," Bit said.

"I build maps for a living," Theo said. "Well. For fun. Same thing, basically."

chapters.heading: Final Level: New Game Plus
chapters.text:
The level loaded one more time, and this time the sky over Theo's head had gone a strange, heavy orange, like a sunset that wouldn't finish.

"Something's different," Theo said. "Feels like a final boss level."

"Sixty-six million years after it all started," Bit said, "this is where the age of dinosaurs ends. Most scientists think a huge **asteroid** — a giant space rock — smashed into Earth near what's now **Mexico**. It changed everything, fast."

Theo looked around at the quiet plain, the dinosaurs in the distance going about their day, unaware. "Is this gonna be sad?"

"It's gonna be true," Bit said. "A lot changed that day. Most non-bird dinosaurs didn't make it through. But that's not really the end of the save file — it's more like a save point before New Game Plus."

"What do you mean?"

"Watch the sky," Bit said.

Something small and feathered flapped overhead, chirping, landing on a branch near Theo's shoulder, bold as anything.

"That's... a bird," Theo said.

"Birds are what's left of a whole branch of dinosaurs," Bit said. "The ones with feathers, the little hunters like Velociraptor's cousins — they never fully logged off. They just respawned smaller, with wings, and kept playing."

Theo watched the bird hop along the branch, completely unbothered by the strange orange sky, and felt something in his chest unknot that he hadn't noticed was tight. "So dinosaurs are still around. Just a different build."

"The best build," Bit said. "The one that's still here."

A ninth coin appeared — and then, without warning, a tenth, both landing in Theo's palm at once.

"Bonus level," Bit said. "You cleared the whole map."

The orange sky folded in on itself like a closing tab, and the ground went soft and familiar under Theo's feet — carpet, not cracked dirt.

He was back in his room. His laptop glowed quietly on the desk, Bit's little green pixels shrinking smaller and smaller inside it.

"Hey," Theo said. "You're not gonna disappear again, right?"

"**Level complete**, Player One," Bit said, voice getting squeakier, pixels blinking fast like static. "I always come back. New map, new level, same deal."

Something that looked almost like water gathered at the corners of Bit's blocky eyes — pixels rearranging themselves into something wobbly and bright.

"You okay?" Theo asked.

"8-bit guides don't cry," Bit said. "This is just rendering error."

Theo laughed, and when he looked down, all ten golden coins in his hand had melted together into one small, heavy trophy shaped like a dinosaur skull, sitting right there on his rug.

He turned it over once, then set it carefully on his shelf, next to the soccer trophy and the pile of half-finished sticky notes.

Tomorrow, he had a whole new world to build.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a whole new world to build.
