story.title: Eli and the Beacon
story.subtitle: One long night, eighteen years of history, and a radio that should not have worked.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Static
chapters.text:
Eli was supposed to be asleep. Instead he was on the floor of his room, soldering iron warm in one hand, trying to get the igniter wire on his model rocket to sit flush against the terminal. The rocket was a B6-4 motor job, nothing fancy, but he'd been chasing a stable flight for three weekends and tonight felt like the night.

His grandfather's old radio sat on the shelf above his desk, dead for as long as Eli had owned it — a boxy, wood-cased shortwave set that was supposed to be decoration. It had never once turned on. Tonight, with no warning, its dial light flickered green, and a sound came out of it that was not static.

**Beep. Beep. Beep.** Steady, metronomic, patient.

Eli set down the iron. He knew Morse code the way most kids his age knew a TikTok sound — not fluently, but enough to notice this wasn't Morse. It was simpler than that. A single tone, on, off, on, off, like a pulse.

"That's not a real transmission," he said out loud, to nobody. "That's a carrier wave with nothing on it."

"Wrong," said the radio. The voice was dry, a little tinny, like it was coming through sixty years of wire. "That is the realest transmission in human history. You're listening to a satellite the size of a beach ball, talking to the whole planet at once, and it's only saying one word. *Here.*"

Eli's mouth went dry. "Radios don't talk."

"This one does. Call me the Beacon. I pick up signals other radios can't — because I'm not picking them up now. I'm picking them up *then*. Dial's yours if you want to find out when."

Eli looked at the tuning dial. There was a date etched beside it, faint with age: **October 4, 1957.**

He turned it.

The beeping got louder, and louder, and the room around him folded away like a photograph curling in a flame — and then he was somewhere else, somewhere colder, standing on a dark field under a sky full of more stars than his city ever showed him, the beeping now coming from directly overhead.

"That," said the Beacon, floating beside him now as a dim green glow, "is **Sputnik 1**. Launched by the Soviet Union tonight, **October 4, 1957**. First man-made object ever to circle the Earth."

"How big?" Eli asked, squinting up at a bright point crossing the stars.

"**About 58 centimeters wide** — smaller than your bike wheel. No camera, no weapons, no instruments worth mentioning. Just a radio, a battery, and that beep, built simple enough that any ham radio operator on the planet could pick it up on an ordinary receiver."

"So the first satellite in history," Eli said slowly, working it out, "wasn't a spy tool or a science lab. It was a flex. A proof of concept, broadcast on repeat."

"Now you're getting it," the Beacon said. "Welcome to the Space Race, Eli. It's going to get a lot less simple from here. **Signal acquired.**"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: A Dog Named Laika
chapters.text:
The dial spun on its own this time, and the cold field became a different kind of cold — a launch pad lit by floodlights, steam venting off a rocket that looked thrown together out of welded pipe.

"**November 3, 1957**," the Beacon said. "One month after Sputnik 1. The Soviets wanted a second first before anyone caught up."

Eli heard something small bark, once, from inside the capsule stacked on top of the rocket.

"There's a dog in there," he said, and it wasn't a question.

"**Laika**," the Beacon confirmed. "A stray picked up off the streets of Moscow. She became the first living creature to orbit the Earth, aboard **Sputnik 2**."

Eli watched the rocket go, a long tongue of fire unzipping the dark, and felt something twist in his chest that was not excitement. "Did she make it back?"

The Beacon didn't dodge it. "No. She didn't survive the flight. It's one of the harder chapters in this story, and people have argued about it for sixty years. But she went up first, and because of her, the people who came after her — human people — had better odds."

Eli was quiet for a second, watching the light shrink to a star among stars. "Okay," he said eventually. "Where next?"

"Less than a year later," the Beacon said, and the scene dissolved into a sunlit lawn in front of a very official-looking building, flags out front, men in narrow ties walking briskly between doors. "**October 1, 1958**. The United States, badly rattled by Sputnik, stood up a brand-new agency to catch up in a hurry."

"NASA," Eli said, reading a sign being bolted to the wall by a man on a ladder.

"**NASA**," the Beacon agreed. "Founded that day. Before Sputnik, America's rocket programs were scattered across different branches of the military, barely talking to each other. Sputnik was the wake-up call that got them all under one roof."

Eli watched the sign go up — four letters, no logo yet, nothing to suggest it would end up on jackets and coffee mugs for the next seventy years. "One beach ball," he said, "and an entire country reorganizes its government."

"That's fear for you," said the Beacon. "Good motivator. Terrible long-term strategy. Luckily for them, it worked anyway."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Belt Nobody Expected
chapters.text:
The next stop smelled like jet fuel and nerves. Eli found himself in a crowd of engineers standing well back from a floodlit gantry, all of them staring at a thin white rocket with their arms folded like they were bracing for bad news.

"**January 31, 1958**," the Beacon said. "America's answer. **Explorer 1**, their first satellite — four months behind Sputnik, and they knew it."

Eli watched the countdown tick down on a hand-lettered sign one of the engineers was holding, and the rocket went up clean, no hesitation, a tight white line climbing into a sky that was just starting to go pink at the edges.

"They got something Sputnik didn't," the Beacon said, once the cheering below had died down. "A real instrument on board this time — a detector built by a physicist named James Van Allen."

"Detecting what?" Eli asked.

"Radiation. And it found way more of it than anyone expected — a whole belt of charged particles trapped by Earth's magnetic field, invisible, wrapped around the planet like a donut nobody knew was there."

Eli's brain, which lit up for exactly this kind of thing, caught fire a little. "So Earth's magnetic field is basically a force field, and it's been grabbing charged particles out of space this whole time, and nobody noticed until they flew an instrument through it?"

"Exactly. They named it the **Van Allen radiation belt**, after the guy who found it. First real scientific discovery of the Space Race, and it happened by accident, because somebody thought to point a Geiger counter at the sky instead of just waving a flag."

Eli watched Explorer 1's light climb and vanish, turning that over. "That's the part nobody tells you about," he said. "Everyone remembers the flags. Nobody remembers the guy who found an invisible donut of radiation around the entire planet."

"Write that on a T-shirt," said the Beacon. "I'd wear it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: One Hundred and Eight Minutes
chapters.text:
The dial clicked forward three years in an instant, and the air changed completely — warmer, louder, a crowd somewhere cheering in a language Eli didn't speak but understood anyway.

"**April 12, 1961**," the Beacon said, and above them a tiny silver sphere rode a pillar of fire into a blue morning sky. "Vostok 1. On board: a twenty-seven-year-old pilot named **Yuri Gagarin**."

"First human in space," Eli said. He'd known that one since he was eight.

"First human in space," the Beacon agreed. "One full orbit of Earth, about **108 minutes**, start to finish. He came back smiling — there's a famous photo of it, missing a shoe from the landing, grinning like he'd just gotten away with something."

"How fast would he have needed to be going to stay in orbit instead of falling back down?" Eli asked, already doing the math in his head out of habit.

"Fast enough that you'd need your own rocket to find out," the Beacon said dryly. "Which, incidentally, is the entire reason this is hard. Point straight up and you come straight back down. Go sideways fast enough and the ground curves away from you just as quick as you're falling toward it. That's an orbit. Gagarin's capsule did it at roughly **17,000 miles an hour**."

Eli let out a breath. "That's not flying. That's falling and missing."

"Astronaut humor got there before you," the Beacon said. "Less than a month later, the Americans answered."

The scene shifted to a launch pad in Florida, swampy heat instead of Russian cold. "**May 5, 1961**. **Alan Shepard**, aboard Freedom 7. Didn't orbit — his flight was short, up and back down, no full lap around the planet. But he made history too: first American in space."

"Second place," Eli said. "But first for his country."

"There's a lot of that in this story," the Beacon said. "Firsts come in more flavors than you'd think."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Dare
chapters.text:
The next scene put Eli in a packed hall, wood paneling, a podium, a man with a Boston accent gripping both sides of it like he meant every word.

"**May 25, 1961**," the Beacon said. "Twenty days after Shepard's flight. President **John F. Kennedy**, addressing Congress."

"I believe this nation should commit itself," the man at the podium said, "to landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to the Earth — before this decade is out."

Eli stared. "He just... said that. Out loud. With no idea if it was even possible."

"That's the dare," the Beacon said. "America had put one man in space, for fifteen minutes, and couldn't even get him into orbit yet. And the President just bet the entire country's reputation on reaching the Moon within nine years. Pure nerve."

"Did it work?"

"Patience," said the Beacon. "You'll see. But first — two years on, the Soviets had one more surprise in them."

The hall dissolved into a launch field again, and this time the pilot climbing into the capsule wore her hair pinned under her helmet, and the crowd around her was quieter, more intent, like they knew they were watching something that mattered.

"**June 16, 1963**. **Valentina Tereshkova**. Former textile factory worker, amateur skydiver, about to become the first woman in space."

Eli watched the capsule go up, trailing fire. "How long was she up there?"

"Long enough to orbit Earth **48 times**. Longer, in total flight time, than every American astronaut who'd flown before her, combined."

"So while the US is still figuring out how to get a guy into orbit for one lap," Eli said, "the Soviets just put a woman up there for forty-eight."

"The Space Race," the Beacon said, "was never a straight line. Keep that in mind. It's about to get stranger."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Secret Designer
chapters.text:
The Beacon's dial this time didn't glow toward a launch pad. It pointed somewhere darker — an office with the shades drawn, a man bent over blueprints by lamplight, his face deliberately never quite in view.

"Who's that?" Eli asked.

"**Sergei Korolev**," the Beacon said. "Chief designer. The man behind Sputnik, behind Gagarin, behind almost every Soviet triumph in this story so far. And almost nobody outside a tight circle knew his name while he was alive."

"Why hide him?"

"State secret. The Soviet government was terrified that if the West knew who their chief rocket designer was, he'd become a target — of rivals, of foreign agents, of anyone who wanted to slow the program down by taking him out of it. So they simply never printed his name. He died in **1966**, and only then did the world learn who'd been running the show the whole time."

Eli looked at the bent shoulders in the lamplight, turning that over. "That's wild. You can build the machines that start a whole space race and the public doesn't even get your name."

"History's full of people like that," the Beacon said. "Now — look up."

The office vanished, and Eli found himself staring at the black curve of Earth from somewhere that was very obviously not the ground. A capsule floated nearby, and tethered to it, drifting slowly against a backdrop of stars, was a man in a bulky white suit.

"**March 18, 1965**," the Beacon said. "**Alexei Leonov**, Voskhod 2. First human to leave a spacecraft and float free in space — what they'd start calling a spacewalk."

"How long was he out there?"

"**About ten minutes.**" The Beacon paused. "His suit puffed up in the vacuum so badly he almost couldn't fit back through the hatch. He had to bleed air out of his own suit to squeeze back in. Nobody watching from the ground could do a single thing to help him. He just had to solve it, alone, floating above the planet."

Eli watched the tiny white figure drift, utterly calm against all that black. "And he did."

"He did. Ten minutes that must have felt like ten years, and then he was back inside, and the hatch sealed, and everyone on the ground finally breathed again."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Earthrise
chapters.text:
"**December 1968**," the Beacon announced, and this time there was no launch pad at all — just the inside of a cramped capsule, three men strapped into seats no wider than Eli's desk chair, a small round window in front of them.

"Apollo 8," Eli said, recognizing the mission patch stitched on a sleeve.

"First crewed spacecraft to leave Earth's orbit entirely and circle the Moon. They didn't land — that wasn't the plan yet — but they went all the way around it and came back, which nobody in history had ever done."

One of the astronauts leaned toward the window, camera in hand, and went still.

"That's **William Anders**," the Beacon said quietly. "Watch."

Over the gray, cratered horizon of the Moon, a small blue marble rose into view — half-lit, swirled with white cloud, achingly bright against the black.

"Oh my God, look at that picture over there!" Anders said. "There's the Earth coming up. Wow, is that pretty."

He took the photo. Eli didn't say anything for a second.

"That's Earthrise," the Beacon said. "One of the most reproduced photographs in human history. Taken by three men who went to look at the Moon and came back having really seen their own planet for the first time."

"Who built the rocket that got them there?" Eli asked, because his brain always circled back to the hardware.

"Good question. Come look." The scene shifted to a hangar the size of a football stadium, a white rocket lying on its side like a sleeping giant. "**Wernher von Braun**. Built rockets in Germany before the war, then led the NASA team that built this — the **Saturn V**. **363 feet tall.** Taller than the Statue of Liberty, base to torch."

Eli walked the length of it in his mind, doing the math on thrust and mass ratios without meaning to. "That's not a rocket," he said. "That's a skyscraper that's decided to leave."

"Best way anyone's put it yet," the Beacon said. "And in seven months, it's going to do exactly that — with the whole world watching."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Giant Leap
chapters.text:
The hangar fell away, and Eli stood on a dark, dusty plain under a black sky with no air to soften the stars at all. A ladder stretched down from a spindly four-legged lander beside him.

"**July 20, 1969**," the Beacon said, and its voice, for the first time all night, had gone very quiet. "You're standing on the Moon. Or close enough to it that it won't matter."

A boot touched the dust below the ladder, kicking up a small, slow-motion cloud that drifted and settled strangely in the low gravity.

"That's one small step for man," said the figure on the ladder, "one giant leap for mankind."

"**Neil Armstrong**," the Beacon said. "First human being to stand on another world."

Eli realized he was holding his breath, and let it out slowly. "Who else is down here?"

"**Buzz Aldrin**, right behind him — second man on the Moon, twenty minutes later. And up there" — the Beacon tipped an invisible hand toward the black sky — "orbiting alone above you both, is **Michael Collins**, flying the command module **Columbia**, keeping it ready for the ride home. He never set foot on the surface. Spent the whole mission circling overhead, further from another human being than anyone in history ever had been."

"That's got to be the loneliest job in the entire program," Eli said, looking up at a sky with no Collins visible in it at all, just stars.

"He said as much, later. Also said he wouldn't have traded it. Somebody had to fly the ride home."

Eli crouched down and pressed his palm flat against the dust, feeling nothing through the dream of it, but trying anyway. "Eight years," he said. "Kennedy said nine, and they did it in eight. From a guy who couldn't even get fifteen minutes of suborbital flight, to this."

"**1969 to 1972**," the Beacon said. "Six landing missions, in total. **Twelve astronauts** walked on the Moon in that stretch — and nobody's done it since."

Eli looked at the footprints leading away across the dust, perfectly sharp-edged with no wind or rain to ever soften them. "They're still up there, aren't they. The footprints."

"Still up there," the Beacon said. "Waiting for somebody to add more."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Splashdown and a Handshake
chapters.text:
"Not every mission went the way this one did," the Beacon said, and the Moon dust dissolved into the cramped interior of a different capsule, warning lights blinking red, three men working fast and calm in a space the size of a car's interior.

"**1970**," the Beacon said. "Apollo 13. An oxygen tank exploded on the way to the Moon."

Eli's stomach dropped. "Did they—"

"They made it home," the Beacon said immediately, before the thought could even finish. "Every one of them. Engineers on the ground, working with whatever the astronauts had on board — duct tape, cardboard, a checklist rebuilt from scratch — figured out a fix in time. The mission to the Moon turned into a mission to just get three men back alive. It worked."

Eli let his shoulders drop. "That's — okay. Good. That's really good, actually."

"It's one of the best stories in the whole program," the Beacon agreed, "precisely because nobody died telling it."

The capsule scene faded, and the last stop arrived gently, without any drama at all — two spacecraft, one American, one Soviet, drifting toward each other against the curve of the Earth, slow as two hands reaching across a table.

"**July 17, 1975**," the Beacon said. "Apollo-Soyuz. The race ends here — not with one side winning, but with both sides docking together in orbit, and the crews climbing through the hatch to shake hands."

Eli watched an American astronaut grip a Soviet cosmonaut's hand through the open hatchway, both of them grinning the exact same grin Gagarin had worn fourteen years earlier.

"Eighteen years," Eli said. "From a beeping beach ball to that handshake."

"Eighteen years," the Beacon agreed, "and you watched most of it in one night. Not bad."

The dial spun backward on its own, fast, and the stars and capsules and dust all poured away like water down a drain — and Eli was on his bedroom floor again, soldering iron cold now in his hand, his half-finished rocket sitting exactly where he'd left it.

The old radio sat dark and silent on its shelf, dial light out, looking exactly like the dead decoration it had always pretended to be. Except the date dial, which had read October 4, 1957 when he started, now read a different date entirely — tonight's.

Eli looked at his model rocket for a long moment. Then he picked the soldering iron back up, finished the last joint clean, and set it down to cool properly this time.

Somewhere out past the ceiling, past the roof, past the sky his model would never reach, twelve sets of footprints sat undisturbed in gray dust, waiting.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, the rocket would finally fly — and so, probably, would he, eventually.

true_facts.text: **Sputnik 1** went up on **October 4, 1957** — the first man-made object ever to circle the Earth.
Sputnik 1 was only **about 58 centimeters wide** and just broadcast a steady beep anyone with a radio could pick up.
A month later, on **November 3, 1957**, the Soviets sent a dog named **Laika** into orbit aboard Sputnik 2, the first living creature ever to circle the planet.
Sputnik's shock pushed the US to found **NASA**, which started operating on **October 1, 1958**.
On **April 12, 1961**, **Yuri Gagarin** became the first human in space, circling the Earth once in about **108 minutes**.
On **May 25, 1961**, President **Kennedy** dared the US to land a man on the Moon and bring him home before the decade was out.
On **June 16, 1963**, **Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman in space, circling Earth **48 times**.
On **March 18, 1965**, **Alexei Leonov** became the first person to float free outside his spacecraft, a spacewalk that lasted **about ten minutes**.
On **July 20, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon.
While Armstrong and **Buzz Aldrin** walked on the Moon, **Michael Collins** orbited alone above them in the command module **Columbia**.
In **1970**, an oxygen tank exploded aboard Apollo 13 on the way to the Moon, but the whole crew made it home safely.
Between **1969 and 1972**, **twelve astronauts** walked on the Moon across six successful landing missions.
The **Saturn V** rocket that carried astronauts to the Moon stood **363 feet tall** — taller than the Statue of Liberty.
The Space Race ended on **July 17, 1975**, when American and Soviet spacecraft docked in orbit and the crews shook hands.

story.title: Mia and the Added-Time Referee
story.subtitle: A stoppage-time tour through the history of soccer.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Whistle That Still Worked (c. 200 BCE–1314 CE)
chapters.text:
Mia had the away-form data open in eleven tabs and absolutely no plan to go to bed.

It was the predictive model, really — the one she'd built to check whether her club's conversion rate (how often a shot actually went in) held up across two seasons of away games. The number refused to behave. At 11:52 p.m. she gave up on the spreadsheet and looked instead at the one piece of soccer equipment on her wall that couldn't be put into a cell: her grandfather's whistle, silver, scratched, hanging from a thumbtack since before she could tie her own cleats.

She picked it up because her hands needed something to do. She blew it, soft, half a joke to the empty room.

The whistle did not sound like a whistle. It sounded like the exact, specific noise a stadium floodlight makes when fifty thousand people go quiet at once — which is to say, enormous, and then nothing.

Green light poured out of the mouthpiece like someone had opened a window onto a pitch that wasn't there, and a man stepped through it holding a glowing board the exact size and shape of a fourth official's added-time sign. Except where the board should say +4, it said -2,206.

"That's years, not minutes," the man said, by way of introduction. He had a whistle of his own, a flag folded under one arm, and the permanently unimpressed face of someone who has watched a lot of replays for a living. "I'm the Fourth Official. Not *a* fourth official — sort of all of them, across time, which is its own headache. You blew the whistle. That buys us stoppage time, tonight, for as long as history needs. Interested?"

Mia looked at her spreadsheet, which was still wrong, and then at the hole in the air where a stadium smelled like cut grass.

"Obviously," she said.

He flipped the board. **-2,206.**

"Han China," he said. "Before soccer was soccer, before it even had a name people argued about, there was a kicking game called **cuju** — you moved a leather ball through a gap in a net without ever using your hands. People played it for more than **two thousand years**. It's one of the oldest known ancestors of the sport you watch on Saturdays."

Through the light, Mia could see it: a courtyard, a ball flicked boot to boot to shoulder, no hands anywhere. "That's basically keepie-uppies with extra steps," she said.

"Most good ideas are." He flipped the board again. **1314.**

London now — a street full of men, a ball, and no rules Mia could identify. A royal messenger nailed a notice to a post.

"**King Edward II**," the Fourth Official said, "banned this — they called it 'mob football' — right here in **1314**. Too many bruised shins, not enough net."

Mia watched a man trip over a cabbage cart and laugh about it. "Doesn't look banned."

"History's full of rules nobody followed yet," he said. "Give it time. That's sort of the whole tour."

He blew the whistle himself, and the board flipped again.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Ball Behind the Wall (1540s)
chapters.text:
The board read **1540** when the light cleared, and they were standing in a stone room so cold Mia could see her own breath — not that ghosts touring through time usually have breath, but nobody had explained the rules of that part yet.

"Stirling Castle," the Fourth Official said. "Scotland. Somebody's about to find something they weren't looking for."

A workman up on a ladder, replacing roof beams, reached into a gap above a ceiling and pulled out something round, flattened with age, stitched in thick strips of leather. He turned it over twice, clearly unsure if it was a ball or a very old potato.

Mia leaned in. "That's a bladder ball," she said, before the Fourth Official could get there first. "Before rubber, you'd blow up an animal bladder like a balloon and wrap it in leather so it held its shape. It's the same word we still use for what's inside a modern ball — the bladder."

The Fourth Official actually looked impressed, which from him seemed to take effort. "Correct. That ball is believed to date from the **1540s**, which would make it the oldest football anywhere in the world — found hidden in a wall where nobody touched it for roughly four hundred years."

"Found by accident," Mia said. "Nobody was even looking for soccer history. They were just fixing a roof."

"Most of history," he said, "is somebody fixing a roof."

Mia asked the obvious statistics question: how many games had that actual ball been in, how battered was it before it ended up in the rafters, could you even still kick it today. The Fourth Official didn't know — nobody had logged minutes played in the 1540s — and admitted that was the one stat history simply hadn't kept. Mia decided this bothered her more than it probably should have.

"Somebody should've had a spreadsheet," she muttered.

"Six hundred years early," he agreed, "but noted. I'll pass it along."

He flipped the board, and the castle folded away like a photograph closing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: One Rulebook to Rule Them All (1848–1863)
chapters.text:
**1848** flashed up next, and they landed in the middle of an argument.

A dozen university students stood in a field, two of them holding a ball, the rest shouting different versions of "that's not allowed" at the same time. Every school in England, it turned out, played some version of football, and every school's version disagreed with every other school's version about which parts of the body were legal.

"Cambridge University," the Fourth Official said. "**1848**. These students sat down and wrote the Cambridge Rules — a first attempt at one shared rulebook, so a team from one school could play a team from another without both sides arguing the entire match."

"Did it work?" Mia asked, watching two players nearly come to blows over whether shins were a legal target.

"Sort of. Took another fifteen years to really stick."

The board flipped to **1863**, and they were in a London tavern, where a stiff, serious-looking man was writing with the focus of someone finishing an assignment an hour before it was due.

"**Ebenezer Cobb Morley**," the Fourth Official said. "Founder of the Football Association, formed right here in London, **October 26, 1863**. He personally sat down and wrote the first official rulebook — the Laws of the Game — that soccer still traces itself back to."

Mia read over Morley's shoulder, scanning for the detail she already half-suspected. "No hands," she said. "He banned carrying the ball."

"NO HANDS!" 

"Correct," the Fourth Official said. "That one rule is the entire difference between the sport you play and the sport you'd call rugby. Before this, 'football' covered both — carrying and kicking, same word, same mess. Morley's rulebook is where they split for good."

Mia did the math out loud, the way she did everything out loud when numbers were involved. "So the rules are older than I thought — a hundred and sixty-some years — but the idea of kicking a ball without hands goes back way further, to the stuff we just saw."

"That's the whole shape of this sport," the Fourth Official said. "People had been kicking balls for millennia. Morley just made everyone agree on the paperwork."

Mia liked that line enough to repeat it under her breath, filing it away the way she filed away a good stat.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Tables Start (1871–1904)
chapters.text:
The board started flipping fast now, the way a highlight reel skips between the good bits.

**1871**. A trophy, newly made, sitting on a table while men in long socks argued about brackets. "The FA Cup," the Fourth Official said. "First played **1871 into '72**. It's the oldest football competition still running anywhere in the world — a hundred and fifty-odd years, and it has never once taken a season off."

**1872**. A damp field in Glasgow, two national teams, a scoreline that refused to move all match. "First official international match," he said. "**Scotland versus England**, **1872**. Final score: nothing-nothing."

Mia pulled a face. "The very first international game ever played was a scoreless draw?"

"Soccer's always had a sense of humor about its own milestones."

**1888**. A man with a notebook — an actual notebook, Mia noted with professional respect — walking between a dozen club chairmen, trying to convince them to play each other on a fixed schedule instead of whenever they felt like it.

"**William McGregor**," the Fourth Official said. "**1888**. He organized the Football League — the first football league anywhere in the world. Before this, clubs just played friendlies whenever. McGregor's idea was the one you'd recognize: everyone plays everyone, home and away, and you keep a running table of who's winning the season, not just the match."

Mia actually laughed. "HE INVENTED THE TABLE! The actual, literal league table. I have stared at that man's invention my entire life and never once knew his name."

"Most stats fans don't. Fair to say he started your whole hobby."

The board clicked to **1904**, Paris — a small room with seven men from seven different countries, none of whom fully trusted each other's accents, signing a document none of them yet realized would end up running the sport.

"FIFA," the Fourth Official said. "Founded right here, **1904**, by seven European federations, to run the game across borders instead of just inside them. Well over a hundred countries belong to it today."

Mia looked at the growing pile of institutions — a rulebook, a cup, a league, a world body — and did what she always did with a pile of data: looked for the pattern.

"It's not one invention," she said slowly. "It's like every ten or twenty years somebody adds one more piece of infrastructure, and the sport gets bigger because the *system* got better, not because the ball changed."

The Fourth Official actually smiled at that, which Mia suspected did not happen often. "Now you're doing my job for me."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Dog Who Saved the World Cup (1930–1966)
chapters.text:
**1930**. Montevideo, Uruguay — a stadium built specifically for one tournament, packed to a roar Mia could feel in her teeth.

"The first FIFA World Cup," the Fourth Official said. "**1930**, hosted by Uruguay. Thirteen teams traveled here, some by boat for over two weeks, just to play. The host beat **Argentina** in the final and lifted the very first trophy."

"The man who pushed for all this to happen in the first place," he went on, nodding at a mustached FIFA official pacing the touchline like he hadn't slept in a decade, "is **Jules Rimet**. His idea, his tournament. They named the original trophy after him."

Mia watched the small gold statue get handed over, gleaming under stadium lights that, to be fair, were basically just torches on poles in 1930. "That's a very small trophy for a very large idea."

"Wait till you see what happens to it."

The board jumped to **1966**, London, and a headline Mia actually gasped at: the World Cup trophy, on display before that year's tournament, had been stolen.

"Just — gone? In England? Before their own home World Cup?"

"For about a week," the Fourth Official said, entirely unbothered. "Which is the correct amount of suspense for this story, so don't worry. It turned up safe, found in a garden hedge by a dog out on his evening walk. His name was **Pickles**."

Mia stared at him. "A DOG NAMED PICKLES?!"

"A dog named Pickles," he confirmed. "England got their trophy back in plenty of time, hosted the tournament that same year, and then — still **1966** — won the whole thing. Their only title to date."

"So the dog is arguably the most important player of the tournament," Mia said.

"Pickles would agree with you. He got a medal."

The board clicked forward once more, and Mia noticed, not for the first time that night, that every disaster in this sport's history seemed to resolve itself within one flip of the board. She filed that away too — not as a stat, exactly, but close.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Three Stars and Two Cards (1958–1974)
chapters.text:
The board read **1958**, then **1962**, then **1970**, flipping almost too fast to follow, and each time the same player was on the field wearing yellow, scoring like it was arithmetic.

"**Pele**," the Fourth Official said. "Brazilian forward. He's the only player in history on three World Cup–winning squads — **1958**, **1962**, and **1970**. Brazil, as a country, has won it a record **five times** total: those three, plus **1994** and **2002**."

Mia, who ran numbers for fun, did this one instantly. "Five titles for one country, three of them with one guy on the roster. That's not luck. That's a dynasty with a name attached."

"Most dynasties have a name attached. That's usually how you spot one."

The board flipped back to **1970**, a different angle this time — not the final, but a referee standing at a dusty intersection outside the stadium, watching a yellow light turn red, an idea landing on his face in real time.

"**Ken Aston**," the Fourth Official said. "Referee. He's sitting at this exact traffic light when it hits him: soccer needs a signal that doesn't depend on which language the players speak. Yellow card for a caution, red card and you're off. He got them introduced at the **1970 World Cup**, and every referee on earth has used some version of them since."

"He invented a whole penalty system," Mia said, "by sitting at a red light."

"Great ideas rarely announce themselves. They just sit there being traffic lights until somebody's paying attention."

One more flip, **1974**: the original trophy, small and gold, locked permanently into a Brazilian case after their third title, retired for good because the rules said whoever won it three times got to keep it.

"Which meant," the Fourth Official said, "FIFA needed a brand new trophy for **1974** onward — the one still handed out today. The one you've actually watched being lifted."

Mia looked at the old trophy, small and a little scuffed, sitting behind glass, and then at the shinier one that replaced it. "So the current trophy," she said, "is only the second one that's ever existed. In the entire history of the tournament."

"Two trophies," the Fourth Official agreed, "over nearly a century. Most things in soccer, it turns out, don't change as often as you'd think. They just get handed to someone new."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Fifty Years Added Back On (1921–1991)
chapters.text:
The next stop had the biggest crowd yet, and Mia noticed it before the Fourth Official said a word.

Fifty-three thousand people, packed into a stadium in England, watching a women's football match like it was the biggest fixture of the year — because in 1920, it basically was.

"The Dick, Kerr Ladies," the Fourth Official said. "One of the most popular football teams in England, full stop, men's or women's. Their best player was **Lily Parr** — left foot like a cannon, by every account anyone ever wrote down."

Mia watched Parr take a free kick from an angle that looked, frankly, unfair to the goalkeeper. "They're drawing fifty thousand people. That's a massive crowd for *any* team."

"It was. Which is, depressingly, part of why what happens next happens."

The board flipped to **1921**, and the stadium emptied overnight — not because anyone stopped showing up, but because the Football Association banned women's football from its grounds, calling it unsuitable, which Mia translated, correctly, as too popular for comfort.

"That's not a rule," she said, flat. "That's jealousy wearing a rulebook."

"I won't argue with you," the Fourth Official said. "Nobody involved in this sport's history would, not anymore. It was unfair, it cost the women's game decades it should never have lost, and the Association itself has said as much since. I'm not going to pretend otherwise just to make the tour tidier."

Mia appreciated that he didn't. "How long did it last?"

He flipped the board to **1971**. "Fifty years," he said. "Exactly fifty, the sort of round number that makes a stats person wince. That's when the ban was finally lifted."

"Fifty years added on," Mia said quietly, "to a match that should never have had a whistle blown on it in the first place."

"Then this," the Fourth Official said, and flipped once more: **1991**, China, a packed stadium, a trophy lifted by a team in white and blue.

"The first official Women's World Cup. **1991**. Won by the **United States**."

Mia watched the American players pile on top of each other at the final whistle, and thought about Lily Parr's free kick, seventy-one years earlier, in front of fifty thousand people who weren't supposed to have been let back in for another five decades.

"They just picked it back up," Mia said. "Like it had never stopped."

"It never really had," the Fourth Official said. "It just wasn't allowed on the stat sheet for a while. That's different from not happening."

Mia thought that was, maybe, the best thing anyone had said to her all night.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Full Time
chapters.text:
The board in the Fourth Official's hand clicked down to **00:00**, and the green light folded itself back into the whistle the way water goes back down a drain.

Mia was sitting exactly where she'd started, cross-legged on her floor, laptop open to the same stubborn spreadsheet. The clock said barely four minutes had passed since she'd first picked up the whistle, which felt, statistically speaking, impossible.

The Fourth Official was still there, just barely, more outline than man now, the green light draining out of him like stoppage time finally expiring.

"One thing before I go," he said. "You kept asking the right question all night — not just what happened, but how do we know, and who wrote it down, and who didn't get to. That's the whole job. Every number in this sport, going back to a bladder ball in a castle wall, is somebody's decision about what was worth keeping."

"So keep better numbers," Mia said.

"Exactly the job," he said, and was gone.

She looked down at her spreadsheet. The conversion rate was still wrong, technically, in the sense that it still refused to match her model — but she found she minded less than she had an hour ago. A stat that didn't fit wasn't a failure. It was a question somebody hadn't answered yet, the same way nobody had ever logged how many matches that leather ball from Stirling Castle had played before it ended up behind a wall for four hundred years.

She picked her grandfather's whistle back up off the carpet, turned it once in her hand, and noticed — or thought she noticed, she'd check again in daylight — one more scratch along the barrel that hadn't been there before.

She hung it back on its thumbtack, closed the laptop, and for the first time all night, actually felt tired.

Monday's match report was going to need a new footnote.

Medieval 'mob football' got so rough that **King Edward II** banned it in London in **1314**.
A leather ball stuffed with a blown-up animal bladder, found hidden at **Stirling Castle**, may date back to the **1540s** — possibly the oldest football ever found.
The **Football Association** was founded in London on **October 26, 1863**, and banned players from carrying the ball by hand.
**William McGregor** organized the **Football League** in **1888** — the first football league table anywhere in the world.
**FIFA** was founded in Paris in **1904** by seven countries, to run the sport across borders.
The first **World Cup** was played in **Uruguay** in **1930**, with the host beating **Argentina** in the final.
In **1966** the World Cup trophy was stolen in London — and found safe a week later by a dog named **Pickles**.
**Brazil** has won the World Cup a record **five times**.
**Pele** is the only player ever on **three** World Cup–winning squads: 1958, 1962, and 1970.
Referee **Ken Aston** invented yellow and red cards, inspired by a traffic light, debuting at the **1970 World Cup**.
Star player **Lily Parr** helped make the Dick, Kerr Ladies one of England's most popular teams.
The Football Association's ban on women's football was finally lifted in **1971**, exactly **fifty years** after it began.
The first official **Women's World Cup** was held in **1991** and won by the **United States**.

story.title: Noah and the Eleven O'Clock Boss Fight
story.subtitle: One gamer, one glitching phone, and the science of why anybody sleeps at all.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Boy Who Watched Eyes Twitch (Chicago, 1953)
chapters.text:
Noah had the brightness turned all the way down; 1:47 a.m. light hits different than daylight light, and his mom thought he'd been asleep for hours. He was deep into a speedrun clip, earbuds in, volume low — the usual.

His phone's sleep-tracker icon, a cartoon moon meant to shame him into bed, flickered. Black, then sick green, then black. A pixel sprite popped up where the moon had been — two closed eyes, a blinking cursor for a mouth.

"You're up late," it typed, line by line, like a loading screen. "Name's REM. Want to see what you're missing?"

Noah's thumb hovered over the power button. Then the screen did something screens shouldn't do — it pulled, like a drain, and the room folded into a flickering lab decades older than his parents.

A man in a cardigan watched a sleeping kid's eyelids. A pen scratched jagged lines across paper.

"Those eyes," Noah said. "They're moving, under the lids. Is that normal?"

"Good catch," said REM. "**In 1953**, a scientist named **Eugene Aserinsky** noticed exactly that — a sleeping boy's eyes twitching — and he and his professor, **Nathaniel Kleitman**, at the **University of Chicago**, realized it meant something. They'd just found a whole stage of sleep nobody had named. Mine, as it happens."

"You're named after a sleep stage?"

"I *am* the sleep stage. Rapid Eye Movement. REM for short. Keep up — this game's got levels."

Noah grinned despite himself. "Level one, complete?"

The lab dissolved into static. LEVEL UP flashed across the dark, and pulled him somewhere quieter.

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Ninety-Minute Loop
chapters.text:
The corridor looped like a racetrack, same turn, same flicker, over and over. Noah clocked it after three laps — about the time it takes to half-finish a round of his favorite game, over and over, forever.

"Ninety minutes," REM said, before Noah could ask. "**A full night isn't one long sleep — it's cycles, roughly ninety minutes each**, bouncing between two settings. Quiet mode." The hallway dimmed, slow and steady. "And active mode." The lights spiked, flickering fast, music-video fast. "That one's me. REM sleep. Brain's almost as busy as when you're awake."

Through a window in the wall, Noah saw a sleeping kid about his own age, eyelids twitching exactly like the boy in the lab. The kid's hand jerked once, like he was reaching for a controller that wasn't there, then went still.

"Why'd he stop?" Noah asked. "Looked like he was about to do something."

"**During REM, your muscles basically switch off** — gone limp, nothing working — so you can't act out whatever your brain's playing. Good system. Otherwise sleepwalkers would be the least of anyone's problems."

"So my brain's got a controller lock during cutscenes."

"That's... annoyingly accurate," REM admitted. "Four, maybe five of those ninety-minute laps a night, and you're through."

The loop sped up, lights strobing, and Noah's stomach did the elevator-drop thing right before the next level started.

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Clock Behind Your Eyes
chapters.text:
Level three dropped him in a control room no bigger than his closet, every wall covered in dials, one tiny door marked DO NOT SLEEP ON THE JOB.

"That door's it," REM said. "**Suprachiasmatic nucleus**. Say it however you want, nobody's grading you. It's a clump of brain cells sitting right behind your eyes, roughly where the nerves from each eye cross. Works as your body's master clock — tells you when to feel sleepy, when to feel awake, on its own rough schedule."

"Like a built-in alarm nobody set."

"Exactly. It's why the word for that daily schedule is **'circadian'** — old Latin for 'about a day.' Your body's already running one, whether you check a clock or not."

Past the control room, a second door hissed open onto something that looked suspiciously like a growth chart taped to drywall, pencil marks climbing year by year.

"Deepest stage of the quiet kind of sleep," REM said, "**is when your body releases the most growth hormone**. One reason a growing kid's body wants more sleep than it's currently getting."

Noah glanced at his own height, marked on a door frame two years and four inches ago, and decided not to argue with the data.

"So staying up till two doesn't just make me tired."

"It makes you shorter than you could've been, theoretically. I don't make the rules. I just run the clock."

The little door marked DO NOT SLEEP ON THE JOB swung open on its own.

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Nobel-Winning Night Shift (2017)
chapters.text:
The next room looked like an achievement screen, gold borders and all, three portraits lit up like unlocked badges.

"**2017**," REM said. "**Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young** won the **Nobel Prize** — science's biggest trophy — for finding the actual genes that keep your circadian clock ticking. Turns out the clock isn't just a vibe. It's wiring."

"Genes that tell time."

"Genes that tell time. Down the hall's an older unlock."

A dim case held a small glass vial, label yellowed, next to a photo of a researcher in a lab coat that had clearly seen better decades.

"**1958**. **Aaron Lerner's** team isolated **melatonin** — that's the hormone that makes you sleepy — after years chasing it down. It's the reason blackout curtains work and bright phone screens don't help your case."

Noah looked down at his own phone, still faintly glowing in his hand even inside the game.

"So this," he said, holding it up, "is basically telling my melatonin to take the night off."

"Correctly diagnosed," REM said. "Want the badge?"

A small pixelated trophy appeared, labeled MELATONIN MASTER, and dropped into Noah's hand with a chime that sounded suspiciously like his own phone's notification sound.

"Rude," Noah said, pocketing it anyway.

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Brain's Rinse Cycle
chapters.text:
Level five was a library that kept rearranging itself, shelves sliding on invisible tracks, books flying into place.

"This is where last night's stuff gets filed," REM said, as a shelf slammed shut three feet from Noah's head. "**Sleep sorts your day into long-term memory** — whatever you practiced, crammed, or embarrassingly rewatched, this is when it gets saved instead of lost to a crash."

"So if I actually slept before a test—"

"You'd remember more of what you studied. Groundbreaking, I know."

A hidden door led into something that looked exactly like an automatic car wash, brushes spinning, except the car was a cross-section of a human skull.

"The **glymphatic system**," REM said, raising his voice over the noise. "**A nightly rinse cycle that flushes waste out of your sleeping brain.** Skip the wash too many nights running and the grime builds up."

"That is disgusting and also kind of comforting."

"Most true things are both. Shelf's closing. Let's move."

The library folded itself into a single glowing book, which slammed shut behind them like a level-complete screen.

chapters.heading: Level 6: Eleven Days Awake (San Diego, 1964)
chapters.text:
Level six opened on a school gym in **San Diego**, banners for a science fair strung across the ceiling, a year painted on a poster: **1964**.

A teenager stood at a folding table, eyes red-rimmed, grinning anyway, next to a sign reading WORLD RECORD ATTEMPT.

"**Randy Gardner**," REM said. "**Seventeen years old. Stayed awake about eleven days straight**, for a science-fair project. One of the longest stretches anybody's ever gone without sleep on record."

"Eleven *days*? How's he still standing?"

"Barely, by the end. Mood tanked, focus went first, memory next. Scientists learned plenty watching him fall apart in slow motion — which is exactly why none of them recommend trying it."

Noah watched the boy on stage misname a simple object, laugh too long at nothing, sway slightly on his feet.

"**Doctors are clear on this one,**" REM added, flatter now. "**Going without sleep wrecks your mood, your attention, your memory, fast.** This is a story, not a dare."

"Relax, I wasn't about to try beating an eleven-day record for a game guide."

"You say that. It's 2 a.m. and you're reading about sleep science instead of sleeping. I'm not entirely convinced."

Fair, Noah thought, and said nothing.

The gym lights dimmed, banners folding up like a stage set struck after a show, and the next level loaded in.

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Animal Kingdom's Sleep Settings
chapters.text:
Level seven looked like a nature documentary built by someone with an unlimited budget and no sense of scale.

A newborn baby slept in an oversized crib the size of a car, waking every so often for a snack.

"**Newborns sleep fourteen to seventeen hours a day**, in short bursts," REM said. "**Almost half of it in REM.** Tough life, mostly naps."

Past the crib, a pool held a bottlenose dolphin cruising in slow circles, one eye open, one eye shut.

"**Dolphins and some seals sleep with half their brain at a time**," REM said. "One side rests, one side stays on watch, so they don't drown or get caught off guard mid-nap."

A giraffe stood nearby, legs folded, head drooping, then snapping back up almost instantly.

"**Giraffes get by on under two hours a day**, sometimes, in short standing naps. Shortest sleepers of any big mammal going."

From a dark cave came a rustle: a small bat, hanging upside down, barely stirring.

"And this guy sleeps **up to twenty hours a day**. Some bats are basically professional nappers."

"What about sleepwalkers?" Noah asked, remembering a cousin who'd once wandered into a kitchen at midnight. "Are they acting out a dream?"

"Nope — **sleepwalking happens in deep, quiet sleep, not during REM dreaming**. They're not performing anything. Just up, confusingly."

"Even bugs sleep?" Noah guessed, pointing at a fruit fly drifting lazily mid-air.

"**Even fruit flies go into rest states that look like sleep**," REM said. "Which means this whole business is ancient. Older than bones, probably."

The safari dimmed into pixels, one more loading bar crawling across the dark.

chapters.heading: Level 8: Respawn
chapters.text:
The last level didn't look like a level at all. It looked like Noah's own room, slightly too bright at the edges, the way a loading screen looks right before it finishes.

REM's sprite sat on the home screen, eyes half-closed, like it too was ready for bed.

"Before you go," it said, "one more stat. **People spend roughly a third of their life asleep** — add it up over a lifetime, and it's years, not hours."

"A third of my life. That's actually a lot of levels."

"It's the whole game, really. Also — a guy named **Sigmund Freud** wrote a whole book in **1899** arguing dreams were secret wishes in disguise. Catchy idea. Most scientists today don't buy the specifics. Still, people have been trying to crack this code a long time. You're just doing it at 2 a.m. with better graphics."

Noah checked the clock in the corner of the screen: 2:11 a.m.

"I should probably log off."

"Rare wisdom for someone your age," REM said. "Night classes resume whenever you next decide bedtime is optional."

The screen faded, green to black to the ordinary glow of a moon icon, timer resetting. On the nightstand, his phone buzzed once with the regular sleep-app reminder, the same one he'd ignored at 1:47. This time he actually set it down, screen-side-down, and reached for the lamp switch instead.

Whatever level eight had been, it could wait till he was actually awake to beat it.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow night, he figured, he'd at least try to beat his own record for falling asleep on time.
